title: Late Fee Cap: 8% of Rent Due
bodyText: If your lease provides for a late charge on rent not paid when due, Hawaii caps it at 8% of the amount of rent due. On $2,000 of rent, the most you can charge is $160 for that late payment. The cap was added for rental agreements entered into or renewed on or after November 1, 2017; a month-to-month tenancy renews each month, so the cautious course is to apply it to every tenancy. Hawaii has no statutory grace period, and the late charge must be in your lease. This library's default clause does not treat an unpaid late fee, apart from the rent itself, as grounds for ending the tenancy. Separately, a service charge of up to $30 is allowed for a dishonored check.

title: Snow and Ice Removal
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule on snow or ice removal at a rental and do not divide that work between landlord and tenant. Snow falls in Hawaii only on the high summits, where there are no ordinary rentals, so a Hawaii lease does not need a snow clause. If a lease assigns any outdoor upkeep to the tenant, the general rules on tenant maintenance agreements still apply.

title: Lease with an Option to Buy: Seller Disclosure
bodyText: If you give a tenant an option to buy the home, Hawaii treats the lease with the option as a sale of residential real property for its seller disclosure law. That law covers fee simple or leasehold property with one to four dwelling units, or a residential condominium or cooperative unit used mainly as a residence. Before the sale, you must sign and date a written disclosure statement of all material facts about the property that you know of or control, that can be seen in visible, accessible areas, or that the law specially requires (including the flood, military-noise and other items in the separate disclosure rows). Sign it within six months before or ten calendar days after the tenant accepts the contract, and deliver it no later than ten calendar days after acceptance. The tenant must acknowledge receipt, then has fifteen calendar days to examine it and rescind in writing, with any deposit returned at once; you and the tenant may agree in writing to shorten or extend these periods. Prepare the statement in good faith and with due care. A few transfers are exempt, such as a sale to a co-owner or to your spouse, parent or child. An ordinary lease with no option to buy is not covered.

title: No Algorithmic Rent-Setting Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule on setting rents with algorithmic pricing software or on landlords sharing rent or occupancy data with each other. That does not make coordinated pricing safe. Hawaii's antitrust law makes every contract, combination or conspiracy in restraint of trade illegal and bars any person from agreeing or combining with another to fix, control or maintain the price of any commodity, a term the law defines broadly enough to include any business. A person injured in business or property can sue for at least $1,000 or three times the damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees. Federal law may also apply. If you use a tool that recommends rents from competitors' nonpublic data, or agree with other landlords on rents or lease terms, get legal advice first. Setting your own rent from public market information is not otherwise restricted by any Hawaii statute. Hawaii's emergency price law does limit it: when the governor or a county mayor declares a state of emergency, or a severe weather warning is issued, rent increases for residential dwellings in the affected area are barred (for 72 hours after a declaration, or until 24 hours after a warning is canceled, unless a proclamation continues the ban), apart from documented added operating expenses and increases in a written instrument the tenant signed before the declaration. A continued ban now covers the island of Maui through October 23, 2026 unless ended or extended: rent there may not exceed the level in effect on August 9, 2023, with limited exceptions.

title: Application Screening Fee
bodyText: You may charge a rental applicant an application screening fee, collected when you process the application, only to cover the cost of getting information about the applicant, such as personal reference checks, tenant reports, criminal background checks and credit reports. You may charge it only for an applicant who is 18 or older or an emancipated minor, so charge nothing for a younger household member. If the applicant asks, give a receipt for the fee and a breakdown of the costs it covers. Return any part of the fee you did not use for those costs within 30 days after you submit the screening requests. Hawaii's statutes set no dollar cap or yearly adjustment, require no written disclosure before the applicant applies, and say nothing about holding a fee while earlier applicants are screened. The cautious course is to charge no more than your actual screening cost, take the fee only when you are ready to process that application, and refund it in full if you never screen the applicant. The screening fee is separate from move-in money: at the start of the tenancy you may collect only the first month's rent and the security deposit. Your application form and questions may not indicate a limitation or preference based on a protected class under Hawaii's fair housing law. And unless an exemption applies (for example, you own four or fewer units in the State), you may not impose different conditions on an applicant in a section 8 voucher or permanent supportive housing program, though you may verify income and creditworthiness in a commercially reasonable way.

title: Collection Fees on Tenant Debts
bodyText: Hawaii limits charging a tenant for the cost of collecting a debt. A collection agency may not collect any collection fee, attorney's fee or commission from the debtor, except that after a lawsuit is filed an attorney's fee or commission of up to 25% of the unpaid principal may be collected and must go to the attorney. An agency also may not collect its own fees or charges for its services, or any interest or other fee incidental to the debt unless the lease expressly authorizes it and it is legally chargeable, or a law authorizes it. (A licensed real estate broker or salesperson residing in Hawaii and acting in the regular practice of that profession is not a collection agency.) If you collect your own tenants' consumer debts in the regular course of business, you may not collect any interest, charge, fee or expense incidental to the debt unless the lease or a law authorizes it, or say the debt can be increased by fees that cannot legally be added; a violation is an unfair or deceptive practice. Your attorney's fees for unpaid rent are capped by the landlord-tenant code: the lease may provide for reasonable fees of no more than 25% of the unpaid rent after default and referral to an attorney who is not your salaried employee, and a lease term beyond what the code allows is unenforceable. The library offers no collection-fee clause. Because an agency cannot collect its commission from the tenant, a lease fee that passes on that commission is unlikely to be collectible; recover rent, lawful late charges, agreed interest, and the fees and costs a court awards.

title: No Rental Fee Transparency Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rental fee transparency or all-in pricing rule for ordinary residential tenancies: nothing requires you to advertise one total price including mandatory fees, to state a total monthly payment on the lease's first page, or to use a set fee-disclosure sentence. (A 2026 total-price law covers short-term lodging such as vacation rentals, not ordinary tenancies.) Other rules still shape how you charge fees. At the start of the tenancy you may collect only the first month's rent and the security deposit, so a move-in, administrative or amenity fee charged at the beginning is barred. Hawaii's unfair and deceptive practices law defines a purchase to include a lease, and a consumer injured by a deceptive practice can recover at least $1,000 or three times the damages, plus attorney's fees. Late charges are allowed only where the lease provides for them and are capped at 8% of the rent due (a cap that reaches agreements made or renewed since November 1, 2017; treat it as applying to every tenancy). The cautious course is to state every recurring charge, with its amount and purpose, in your advertising and in the lease, and to charge none the lease does not state.

title: No Unprovided-Service Fee Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no general rule barring a residential landlord from charging a fee for a service that is not provided. Related rules still apply. Every agreement on the terms of the tenancy, written or oral, is part of the rental agreement, so a service you promise and charge for is one you must deliver. If you do not, and the failure is a material breach of the rental agreement, the tenant may, after written notice, have the work done and deduct the cost from rent within statutory limits, or end the tenancy if the condition deprives the tenant of a substantial part of the bargain and you do not fix it within a week (neither remedy applies to a condition caused by the want of due care of the tenant, the tenant's family or a guest). You may not cut services to retaliate against a tenant's protected complaint or repair request, and wilfully cutting off water, electricity, gas or another essential service to force a tenant out brings damages of at least three times the monthly rent or $1,000. Charge only for services you actually provide, describe each in the lease, and stop the charge if the service stops.

title: Fees and Charges as Rent
bodyText: Hawaii lets you and the tenant agree to any lawful consideration as rent, and the landlord-tenant code has no other definition of rent. One rule makes a charge rent by statute: if the tenant fails to keep up the unit, you give written notice allowing at least ten days after the tenant receives it to fix the problem, and the tenant does not, you may do the cleaning, repair or replacement yourself and bill the actual and reasonable cost, and that bill is treated as rent due on the next regular rent date (or immediately, if the tenancy has ended). Such a failure lets you end the tenancy only if it is a material breach of the building and housing laws affecting health and safety. If you want another recurring charge, such as parking or pet rent, to be part of the rent, the lease must say so clearly. Be careful with late fees and other one-time charges. A nonpayment termination notice gives the tenant 10 calendar days to pay the rent due. Until February 4, 2028, the 10-calendar-day nonpayment notice must also list the items the statute requires, including the current rent due after applying all rent paid from all sources, a copy must go to a state-funded mediation center, and if mediation is scheduled within the 10 days you must wait 20 calendar days after the tenant receives the notice before filing, unless the tenant fails to attend or cancels the mediation. On February 4, 2028 those notice-content and mediation rules are repealed unless the Legislature extends them, but the 10-calendar-day period remains, with a posted notice received on the date of posting and a mailed notice two business days after the postmark. The court's current summary possession complaint form for nonpayment asks for unpaid base monthly rent separately from additional charges such as parking, late fees and utilities, so keep late fees and similar charges out of the rent figure in the notice. Calling a late fee additional rent does not lift the 8% late-charge cap (a cap that reaches agreements made or renewed since November 1, 2017; treat it as applying to every tenancy). The security deposit may be used only for the items the deposit statute lists, so a fee that is neither unpaid rent nor one of those items may not be deducted. Never make attorney's fees rent: the code limits what a lease may say about fees.

title: No Government Fee Pass-Through Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no statewide registration or licensing fee for long-term residential rentals and no rule letting you pass a government fee through to a tenant as a separate charge. County ordinances, including short-term rental rules, may impose their own registration or fees; this row does not cover them. If you want to recover a new government fee or tax from tenants, build it into the rent. For a month-to-month tenancy that takes written notice at least 45 consecutive days before the higher rent takes effect (15 consecutive days if the tenancy is shorter than month to month); during a fixed term you can raise rent only if the lease allows it, and otherwise at renewal. A substantial increase in property taxes or other operating costs that you became liable for at least four months before you demand the increase allows an increase even after a tenant's protected complaint, but only up to the prorated net increase. At the start of the tenancy you may collect only the first month's rent and the security deposit, so a move-in charge for a government fee is barred. General excise tax is a separate case covered in the rent tax row.

title: No Lease-Type Parity Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not require the same rent or terms for month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies, and do not cap the difference between them. What changes with the tenancy type is notice. Unless you and the tenant agree in writing to a term, the tenancy is month to month (week to week for boarders). For a month-to-month tenancy you must give written notice at least 45 consecutive days before a rent increase and at least 45 days before ending the tenancy, and the tenant must give at least 28 days' written notice to end it. For a tenancy shorter than month to month, a rent increase needs 15 consecutive days' written notice and either side may end the tenancy on 10 days' notice. A fixed-term lease sets its rent for the term. A termination notice given to get around the rent-increase notice periods is void. Fair housing and source-of-income rules still apply to how you set terms for different applicants.

title: No Rent Concession Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule on rent concessions such as a free month, a rent credit or a move-in discount. If you give one, put it in the lease with its amount and the rental periods it covers, and state the full rent that applies when it ends. Three Hawaii rules affect how a concession works. A discount that is lost, or a concession you take back, because rent is paid late may be treated as a late charge; together with any late charge for that period, keep it within 8% of the rent due (a cap that reaches agreements made or renewed since November 1, 2017; treat it as applying to every tenancy). If a fixed-term tenant abandons the unit, your damages are limited by statute to the lesser of the rent for the rest of the term or the rent during a reasonable re-renting period plus any shortfall in rent and a reasonable commission, so a clause making the tenant repay an earlier concession on default risks being unenforceable. And a concession is a credit, not money you collect, so it does not conflict with the rule that you may collect only the first month's rent and the security deposit at the start.

title: No Statewide Rent Control
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no statewide rent control: none caps how much or how often you may raise the rent on an ordinary tenancy. What limits increases is notice (written notice at least 45 consecutive days ahead for a month-to-month tenancy, 15 for a shorter one, and only as the lease allows during a fixed term) and the ban on raising rent to retaliate against a tenant's protected complaint or repair request. The one statewide cap is temporary: after the Governor or a mayor declares an emergency, or during a severe weather warning, price increases on residential dwellings in the affected area are barred while the limit is in force (see the emergency rent freeze row; one now applies on the island of Maui). An old provision of the eviction law refers to county rent control ordinances adopted under statutes since repealed. Hawaii's statutes contain no provision expressly allowing or barring county rent control; county ordinances were not searched, so check your county's rules.

title: No Rent-Demand Bar
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule that bars you outright from demanding or collecting rent while a unit has code violations or is unfit. Instead, rent is tied to your repair duties in several ways. If you fail to deliver possession at the start of the term, the tenant owes no rent while unable to move in. If fire or another casualty that the tenant or a family member did not wilfully cause makes part of the unit unusable, a tenant who stays and vacates the unusable part owes only the fair rental value of the part still used. If the tenant ends the tenancy because a condition deprives the tenant of a substantial part of the bargain, or after such a casualty, you must refund advance rent for the remaining days within 14 days (a mailed refund complies if sent by certified mail, return receipt requested, to an address the tenant supplied, postmarked by midnight of the 14th day). When you fail to start repairs on time after notice, the tenant may have the work done and deduct the cost from rent, up to $1,000 or one month's rent, whichever is greater, and no more than three months' rent in six months. The termination and repair-and-deduct remedies do not apply to a condition caused by the want of due care of the tenant, the tenant's family or another person on the premises with the tenant's consent; the casualty remedies are lost only if the tenant or a family member wilfully caused the fire or casualty. In a court case where rent is disputed, either side may ask the court to have the disputed rent paid into court, and the court pays it out to whichever side was right. A tenant who keeps paying rent, or tenders receipts for rent lawfully withheld, is protected from retaliation. Court decisions may also let a tenant raise the unit's condition as a defense to nonpayment; no published case was searched.

title: Emergency Rent Increase Freeze
bodyText: When the Governor declares a state of emergency for all or part of the State, a mayor declares a local emergency, or an area is under a severe weather warning, Hawaii law bars any increase in the price of commodities in the affected area, and residential dwellings are commodities. The bar lasts 72 hours after a declaration takes effect (24 hours after a severe weather warning is canceled) unless the proclamation continues it, and a proclamation may limit it to particular commodities. Two exceptions apply: you may pass on documented additional operating expenses the emergency caused, and a rent increase set out in a written instrument the tenant signed before the declaration may take effect as written. A violation is an unfair or deceptive practice with civil penalties, unless you prove it was unintentional, you rolled the price back on discovering it, and you set up restitution for those overcharged. The Thirty-Second Proclamation Relating to Wildfires (August 24, 2026) continues this limit for the island of Maui only, through October 23, 2026 unless ended or superseded: residential rents there may not exceed the regular prices in effect on August 9, 2023, except for documented added operating expenses and increases in a written instrument the tenant signed before August 9, 2023, and the limit does not cover projects wholly owned by one entity under a government regulatory agreement that limits rent increases. Proclamations are reissued often, so check the current one before raising any rent on Maui, and after any new emergency declaration anywhere in the State. Any increase that is allowed still needs the normal written notice (45 consecutive days for month to month, 15 for shorter tenancies). The same statute can also limit ending tenancies during an emergency.

title: Rent Increase Notice
bodyText: For a month-to-month tenancy you may raise the rent only by written notice given at least 45 consecutive days before the increase takes effect; for a tenancy shorter than month to month (for example, week to week), at least 15 consecutive days. During a fixed-term lease the rent is what the lease says; you can raise it mid-term only if the lease provides for it (see the optional mid-term increase clause). When a fixed term ends, set any new rent in the renewal; if the tenancy continues month to month, the 45-day rule applies. A termination notice given to get around these notice periods is void. You may not demand a rent increase to retaliate against a tenant who keeps paying rent and has complained in good faith to a government agency or to you about conditions violating health law or the landlord-tenant code, or has requested repairs in good faith. An increase is still allowed in those cases if the health department has certified the unit was in compliance, if you became liable at least four months earlier for a substantial increase in property taxes or operating costs (and the increase does not exceed the prorated net increase), for a capital improvement (within its straight-line depreciation), if the complaint concerned only a condition caused by the want of due care of the tenant, a household member or a guest, or if the new rent is no more than comparable units in the building or market value. Hawaii's statutes set no general cap on the size or frequency of increases, but during a declared emergency increases may be barred (see the emergency rent freeze row; one applies on Maui now).

title: Rent Due Dates and Public Assistance Option
bodyText: Rent is payable at the time and place you and the tenant agree. If the lease is silent, rent for a term of one month or less is due in full at the start of the term, and rent for a longer term is due in equal monthly installments at the start of each month. Rent is apportioned day by day, so a partial month is prorated. Hawaii gives tenants who receive public assistance a due-date option. If your lease with such a tenant requires rent to be paid on or before the third day after the day the tenant's public assistance check usually arrives, the tenant may set a new due date by making a one-time payment covering the days between the original due date and the new one. The new date may be no more than three days, not counting Saturdays, Sundays and holidays, after the date the checks are mailed. The one-time payment is the monthly rent divided by 30, multiplied by the number of days between the two dates. The statute does not say how the tenant exercises the option; ask for the request in writing, confirm the new due date in writing, and from then on treat rent paid by the new date as on time.

title: Rent Receipts
bodyText: You must give the tenant a written receipt for rent at the time it is paid. A canceled check counts as a written receipt, so for rent paid by check you need to give a separate receipt only if the tenant asks for one. Rent paid in cash, by money order or by another method needs a written receipt when it is paid. Whether an electronic confirmation satisfies the written-receipt rule depends on Hawaii's electronic transactions law, which this row does not cover; the cautious course is a receipt the tenant can keep, on paper or by e-mail if the tenant has agreed to electronic records. If you fail to give a required receipt within ten days after the tenant properly demands it, you may owe the tenant $100 plus reasonable attorney's fees. Receipts also protect you: in a court case where rent is disputed, a tenant who shows the rent was already paid need not deposit it into court, and your records are your proof of what was and was not paid.

title: No Rent Reporting Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes neither require nor limit a landlord's reporting of rent payments to a credit bureau. There is no state rent-reporting program, no duty to offer positive rent reporting, and no rule barring you from requiring a tenant to enroll in a reporting service. Two limits apply. If you collect your own tenants' consumer debts in the regular course of business, you may not falsely tell a credit reporting agency, or threaten to tell it, that a debt has not been paid. And a reporting-service fee charged at the start of the tenancy runs into the rule that you may then collect only the first month's rent and the security deposit. Federal law may also apply, including federal consumer reporting rules on accuracy and disputes.

title: General Excise Tax on Rent
bodyText: Hawaii taxes the landlord, not the tenant: rent you receive is gross income subject to the 4% general excise tax, plus any county surcharge of up to 0.5%. You may pass the tax on to the tenant if the lease says so. Hawaii's tax law recognizes written contracts that require passing the tax on, and any amount you collect and separately state as the tax is held in trust for the State and must be paid over. State the base rent and the tax charge (or a total rent that includes it) in the lease so the tenant agrees to the total. Because the amount you pass on is itself taxable income, the State's landlord-tenant handbook gives a maximum pass-on rate of 4.166%, or 4.712% where the 0.5% county surcharge applies; check the Department of Taxation's current guidance. Do not add a tax charge to the security deposit: the deposit is held for the tenant. At the start of the tenancy, collect only the first month's rent (with any agreed tax charge on it) and the security deposit. Renting a dwelling to a transient for less than 180 consecutive days can be a transient accommodation subject to the transient accommodations tax (10% from January 1, 2026, plus any county tax of up to 3%); counties also regulate short-term rentals, which this row does not cover. Rentals in certain certified affordable housing projects may be exempt from general excise tax. You must also give every tenant your general excise tax number (see that clause).

title: Tax Statement in Rent Collection Agreements
bodyText: If you hire a property manager or anyone else to collect rent for you, Hawaii tax law puts duties on the collection agreement, not the lease. Every written agreement authorizing a person to collect rent on your behalf must show on its first page your name, address, social security number and, if available, general excise tax number, the address of the rental property, and this statement in bold print and ten-point type: "HAWAII GENERAL EXCISE TAXES MUST BE PAID ON THE GROSS RENTS COLLECTED BY ANY PERSON RENTING REAL PROPERTY IN THE STATE OF HAWAII. A COPY OF THE FIRST PAGE OF THIS AGREEMENT, OR OF FEDERAL INTERNAL REVENUE FORM 1099 STATING THE AMOUNT OF RENTS COLLECTED, SHALL BE FILED WITH THE HAWAII DEPARTMENT OF TAXATION." The collector must file a copy of that first page with the Department of Taxation within 30 days after entering the agreement, or instead file the federal Form 1099, with your social security number and (if available) excise tax number, when the 1099 is due. Under an oral agreement, the collector gives the Department the same information and gives you a copy of the notice. For transient accommodations (stays under 180 consecutive days), the agreement must also show your transient accommodations tax registration number and carry the transient accommodations statement; it may be combined with the general excise statement by adding "HAWAII TRANSIENT ACCOMMODATIONS TAXES AND" to the front, and a collector who complies with the transient rule is treated as complying with the general one. Failing to comply is unlawful, and the Department may fine up to $500 per violation. The lease with your tenant does not need the statement.

title: No Required Fee Listing Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not require the lease to list every fee with its purpose, and set no notice period for adding a fee later. Several rules still push fees into the lease. A late charge is allowed only where the rental agreement provides for one, and it is capped at 8% of the rent due (a cap that reaches agreements made or renewed since November 1, 2017; treat it as applying to every tenancy). At the start of the tenancy you may collect only the first month's rent and the security deposit, so no move-in fees. A rule or obligation you adopt after the tenant moves in binds the tenant only once it is brought to the tenant's attention and, if it substantially modifies the tenant's bargain, only if the tenant consents in writing; a new recurring charge is likely such a modification. On a month-to-month tenancy, a new recurring charge that works as a rent increase also needs written notice at least 45 consecutive days ahead (15 for shorter tenancies). List each fee, its amount and when it is due in the lease, and add new fees only at renewal or by written agreement.

title: No Government Shutdown Rent Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes give no special protection to tenants who are federal, state or other government workers during a government shutdown or furlough: no delay of rent, no late-charge bar and no eviction defense. The ordinary rules apply, including the 8% late-charge cap (only if the lease provides for a late charge; the cap reaches agreements made or renewed since November 1, 2017, so treat it as applying to every tenancy) and the written notice giving the tenant at least 10 calendar days to pay before you may end the tenancy for nonpayment. Until February 4, 2028, that notice must also list the items the statute requires, a copy must go to a state-funded mediation center, and if mediation is scheduled within the 10 days you must wait 20 calendar days after the tenant receives the notice before filing, unless the tenant fails to attend or cancels the mediation; a posted notice is received on the date of posting and a mailed notice two business days after the postmark. On February 4, 2028 the notice-content and mediation rules are repealed unless extended, but the 10-calendar-day period and the receipt rules remain. If a tenant's pay is interrupted, consider a written payment plan. Federal law may also apply.

title: Hawaii Money Limits at a Glance
bodyText: Hawaii sets these money limits for residential rentals, whatever the lease says. Move-in money: only the first month's rent and the security deposit. Security deposit: one month's rent, plus an agreed pet deposit of up to one month's rent, only for a pet that lives in the unit and never for an assistance animal. Late charge: only where the lease provides for one, and no more than 8% of the rent due (the cap was added for agreements made or renewed from November 1, 2017; apply it to every tenancy). Dishonored check: a service charge of up to $30. Application screening fee: only your actual screening costs, only for applicants 18 or older or emancipated minors, with unused amounts refunded within 30 days after you submit the screening requests. Attorney's fees: for unpaid rent, reasonable fees of up to 25% of the unpaid rent after default and referral to an attorney who is not your salaried employee; otherwise only prevailing-party fees in matters under the landlord-tenant code; court-taxed contract fees are capped at 25% of the judgment. Holdover without your consent: up to twice the monthly rent, prorated daily, for each day the tenant stays (bring a summary possession case within the first 60 days of holdover, or a month-to-month tenancy at the old rent arises). Deposit penalties: miss the 14-day written notice and you may keep none of the deposit (unless the tenant wrongfully quit); wrongful retention costs the amount kept, and wilful wrongful retention up to three times that amount, plus costs. Interest: 10% a year when no written contract sets a different rate, and 10% on judgments; a tenant who stops a writ for nonpayment pays rent with 8% interest, costs and a reasonable attorney's fee. Rent increases: no cap on the amount, only notice periods, except during a declared emergency. Tenant repair and deduct: up to $1,000 or one month's rent, whichever is greater, and no more than three months' rent in six months, never for a condition caused by the want of due care of the tenant, the tenant's family or a guest. Penalties you can face: an overnight lockout without cause or court order, two months' rent or two months' free occupancy plus costs and fees; cutting off utilities to force a tenant out, at least three times the monthly rent or $1,000; a disclosure failure after demand, $100 plus fees; source-of-income discrimination (if no exemption applies), civil penalties up to $2,000 for a first violation and $2,500 for a later one.

title: No Subsidy Rent Proration Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes have no special rule for reducing rent when part of a subsidized unit becomes unusable, and nothing says how a reduction is split between the tenant's share and the subsidy. The general rules apply to every tenant under the landlord-tenant code. After a fire or other casualty that the tenant or a family member did not wilfully cause makes part of the unit unusable, a tenant who lawfully stays and vacates the unusable part owes no more than the fair rental value of the part still used. A tenant who ends the tenancy after such a casualty, or for a condition that deprives the tenant of a substantial part of the bargain, gets back advance rent for the remaining days within 14 days (a mailed refund complies if sent by certified mail, return receipt requested, postmarked by midnight of the 14th day); a tenant may not end the tenancy for a condition caused by the want of due care of the tenant, the tenant's family or a guest. For a voucher or other federally subsidized tenancy, the program's conditions control wherever they conflict with the code, so follow your housing assistance contract on abatement and on how any reduction is shared. Housing owned or managed by the Hawaii Public Housing Authority is outside the landlord-tenant code entirely.

title: No Subsidy Late-Fee Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes have no rule on late charges for the part of the rent a housing subsidy pays. The general rule applies: a late charge only where the lease provides for one, and no more than 8% of the amount of rent due (a cap that reaches agreements made or renewed since November 1, 2017; treat it as applying to every tenancy). Charging a voucher tenant a late charge because the housing agency paid its share late is risky. Federal program conditions control wherever they conflict with the landlord-tenant code, and your housing assistance contract may forbid it. And unless an exemption applies, you may not impose rental conditions on a tenant in a section 8 voucher or permanent supportive housing program that differ from those for other tenants. The exemptions include owning four or fewer units in the State (unless you hold more than a 10% interest in more than four), renting in an owner-occupied two-family building or renting up to four rooms in a home you live in, publicly subsidized affordable projects, and commercially reasonable checks of income and creditworthiness. The cautious course is to charge any late charge only on the tenant's own share of the rent, as the lease states, and never for the agency's late payment.

title: No Tax Escalation Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule on a lease clause that passes real property tax increases to a residential tenant, and the library does not offer one. Raise rent instead: at renewal; on a month-to-month tenancy, by written notice at least 45 consecutive days before the increase (15 for tenancies shorter than month to month); or during a fixed term only if the lease allows mid-term increases (see the optional mid-term increase clause). A substantial increase in property taxes or other operating costs that you became liable for at least four months before you demand the increase is a recognized reason for an increase even after a tenant's protected complaint, as long as the increase does not exceed the prorated net increase in those taxes or costs. Do not deduct a tax share from the security deposit; it may be used only for the items the deposit statute lists. During a declared emergency, rent increases may be barred except for documented operating expenses the emergency caused.

title: Interest on Unpaid Amounts
bodyText: When no written contract fixes a different rate, Hawaii's legal interest rate is 10% a year on money due under a written instrument after it becomes due, and judgments carry 10% a year. In a contract case the court may start prejudgment interest as early as the date of the breach. A lease may set its own rate. For a consumer credit transaction a written contract may not exceed 12% a year; whether a residential lease is consumer credit is not settled by statute, so keep any lease rate at or below 10%. A tenant who stops a writ of possession for nonpayment by paying before it issues pays the rent due with interest at 8% a year, plus the costs of the case and a reasonable attorney's fee. Be careful stacking interest on rent with a late charge: the late charge (allowed only if the lease provides for one) is capped at 8% of the rent due (a cap that reaches agreements made or renewed since November 1, 2017; treat it as applying to every tenancy), and a lease interest charge on late rent could be counted toward that cap, so the library's optional clause charges interest only on amounts other than rent. If you collect your own tenants' consumer debts in the regular course of business, or use a collection agency, interest may be collected only if the lease or a law authorizes it.

title: Move-In Inventory and Inspections
bodyText: Before the tenant first moves in, you must inventory the unit and make a written record detailing its condition and the condition of any furnishings or appliances you provide. You and the tenant each sign duplicate copies, and each tenant gets a copy. The statute does not distinguish written from oral rental agreements, so do it for every tenancy. In an action under the landlord's repair-duty section, the signed inventory is presumed correct. If you skip it, the unit's condition at the end of the tenancy is rebuttably presumed to be the same as when the tenant moved in, which can defeat a deposit deduction for damage unless you prove otherwise. Hawaii's statutes do not require a move-out inspection, a separate notice of inspection rights, or a damage list that the tenant must sign or dispute. A joint walk-through at move-out, with dated photos compared against the move-in inventory, is still a good way to prevent deposit disputes. The library's move-in inventory clause puts this duty in the lease.

title: No Preset Deposit Charges
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not let a lease preset cleaning, carpet or repair charges that you may keep from the deposit. You may use the deposit only for the purposes the statute lists, including the cost of cleaning the unit at the end of the tenancy so it is as fit as when the tenant moved in, and of remedying damage from the tenant's failure to meet the tenant's maintenance duties, but not for normal wear and tear (items missing from the unit are not wear and tear). If you keep any part, your written notice within 14 days must give the particulars and grounds and include written evidence of the costs, such as estimates or invoices for materials and services, or receipts for supplies and equipment or charges for cleaning services; the notice is not needed if the tenant wrongfully quit. A price list in the lease can tell the tenant what typical work costs, but deduct the actual, documented cost. Treat carpet cleaning like any other cleaning: deduct only what is needed to return the carpet to its move-in condition.

title: Unclaimed Deposit Refunds
bodyText: A deposit refund the tenant never claims is not yours to keep. Return the deposit, with the written notice of anything you keep (not needed if the tenant wrongfully quit), within 14 days after the rental agreement ends, by mail to the address the tenant supplied if you can. If the refund then goes unclaimed, Hawaii's unclaimed property law treats money you owe in the course of your business as property you hold for the tenant. It is generally presumed abandoned five years after the tenant's right to demand it arose, if the tenant has not communicated with you about it in a way your records show. You then report it to the State's unclaimed property administrator before November 1 for the twelve months ending the preceding July 1, and pay it over with the report. If your records have an address for the tenant that you have no reason to think is wrong and the amount is $50 or more, send the tenant written notice no more than six months before you report. If the tenant's last known address is in another state, that state's law may apply instead. Late reporting brings interest and daily civil penalties (larger if the failure is wilful). A lease clause forfeiting an unclaimed refund to you would conflict with the deposit-return rule, and a contract time limit on the tenant's claim does not stop the refund from being presumed abandoned; you may deduct a dormancy charge only under a valid written contract that you regularly enforce, in an amount that is not unconscionable; the library offers no such clause.

title: No Deposit Installment Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes give tenants no right to pay a security deposit or pet deposit in installments, and neither require nor forbid an installment plan. You may agree to one. If you do, put each installment's amount and due date in writing and keep the total within the cap: one month's rent, plus a pet deposit of up to one month's rent only for a pet that lives in the unit and never for an assistance animal. Do not charge a fee for the plan; at the start of the tenancy you may collect only the first month's rent and the security deposit. An installment paid after move-in is still part of the security deposit and may be used only for the purposes the deposit statute lists.

title: Deposit and Last Month's Rent
bodyText: You may not collect last month's rent in advance at the start of a Hawaii tenancy: at the beginning you may collect only the first month's rent and the security deposit. And no part of the security deposit counts as payment of the last month's rent unless you and the tenant agree in writing, which the statute allows only if the tenant gives 45 days' notice of vacating. Agreeing does not waive your right to recover damages the tenant causes, but once the deposit has gone to rent there may be nothing left to cover cleaning or damage, so weigh that before agreeing. Without such an agreement, the tenant must pay the final month's rent when due, and you account for the deposit within 14 days after the tenancy ends (no itemized notice is needed if the tenant wrongfully quit). On a month-to-month tenancy the tenant's own termination notice need only be 28 days, so a tenant who gives only that notice has not given the 45 days the statute requires for applying the deposit to the last month.

title: Refund Not Conditioned on Notice
bodyText: You may not make the deposit refund depend on the tenant giving advance notice of moving out, a forwarding address or keys by a deadline: Hawaii's deposit rules contain no such condition, and a lease cannot waive the tenant's rights under the landlord-tenant code. Your deadline is 14 days after the rental agreement ends. Two things the tenant does matter. If the tenant is absent for 20 or more days in a row without written notice to you, during a period for which you have not received rent, the tenant is treated as having wrongfully quit; you may then keep the entire deposit (on top of your other remedies) and the itemized notice is not required. And your timely return is presumed only if you mail it to an address the tenant supplied, with acceptable proof of mailing, postmarked before midnight of the 14th day, or the tenant acknowledges receipt within the 14 days. So ask in the lease for a forwarding address in writing, as the library's deposit return clause does, but refund on time even without one, using the best address you have. Keys, key fobs, parking cards, garage door openers and mailbox keys you furnished and the tenant does not return are a permitted deduction.

title: Deposits After Early Termination
bodyText: Hawaii lets a tenant end a rental agreement of one year or less early, without fees or liability for future rent, if the tenant or an immediate family member living there was a victim of domestic violence in the last 90 days (on at least 14 days' written notice with the documentation the statute requires), and lets a servicemember tenant do so under qualifying military orders (30 days' notice for a term of a year or less, 15 days for month to month). The deposit rules change with who stays. If the terminating tenant was the only tenant, the agreement ends on the early termination date and you return the deposit under the normal rule: within 14 days after termination, with a written notice of anything you keep (unless the tenant wrongfully quit). If other tenants remain on the agreement, you need not refund any deposit or prepaid rent until the agreement ends for all tenants and the unit is surrendered. If you end the remaining tenants' tenancy early because they cannot show they can pay the rent, each terminating tenant gets a prorated share of the deposit and prepaid rent when the agreement ends; the share is set by the court (domestic violence cases) or by the parties in writing, and if neither sets it you may refund in equal shares to each tenant on the agreement. You may withhold a prorated amount for damage the terminating tenant caused by breaching the tenant's maintenance duties, but you may charge no early-termination fee or penalty, and if a domestic violence victim instead has the locks changed (at the tenant's expense, within three days of the request), you may not require any additional rent, fees or deposit because the abuser is excluded (the lock-change right does not apply where the abuser is a party to the rental agreement unless a court has ordered the abuser to vacate and you have a copy). Keep information a domestic violence victim gives you confidential unless the tenant consents in a signed statement, it is required or relevant in a court case, or other law requires disclosure.

title: No Expedited Deposit Procedure
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no expedited security deposit procedure and no fee for handling a deposit early. Your deadline is 14 days after the rental agreement ends, and you may always return the deposit sooner. Do not deduct a processing, administrative or accounting fee: the deposit may be used only for the purposes the statute lists (damage from the tenant's breach of the tenant's maintenance duties, unpaid rent, unreturned keys and similar items, cleaning to move-in condition, damages from wrongfully quitting, pet damage, and unpaid landlord-provided utilities not included in the rent), and anything you keep needs a written notice with the particulars and written evidence of the costs.

title: No Deposit-Alternative Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule on fees in lieu of a security deposit, deposit insurance or surety bond programs for tenants. Two Hawaii rules limit them. At the start of the tenancy you may collect only the first month's rent and the security deposit, so a deposit-alternative fee charged at move-in is barred. And money a tenant deposits with you to cover damage, unpaid rent or the other listed items is a security deposit under the statute, with its cap, closed list of uses and 14-day accounting, whatever you call it. A product that promises to pay you for a tenant's damage may be insurance, governed by insurance law this library does not cover. The library offers no deposit-alternative clause; if a vendor offers one, make it optional for the tenant, collect nothing for it at move-in, and get advice.

title: Furnished Rentals
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes set no higher deposit limit for a furnished unit and no separate furniture deposit: anything you hold to secure the furniture is part of the security deposit and counts toward the one-month cap (the only addition allowed is a pet deposit of up to one month's rent for a resident pet that is not an assistance animal). What Hawaii does require is that your move-in inventory record the condition of any furnishings and appliances you provide, signed in duplicate by you and the tenant; without it, their condition at move-out is presumed to be the same as at move-in. The tenant must keep the furniture and furnishings you supply in fit condition, reasonable wear and tear excepted, and you may deduct from the deposit for damage from the tenant's failure to do so, but not for normal wear and tear; items missing from the unit are not wear and tear. You must keep appliances you supply in good working order, subject to reasonable wear and tear. A furnished rental for less than 180 consecutive days may be a transient accommodation subject to the transient accommodations tax.

title: No Holding Deposit Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule on holding deposits or other money taken from an applicant to reserve a unit before the lease is signed, and do not say whether such money falls under the deposit statute. Treat it cautiously. A rental agreement can be oral, so an agreement may exist before anything is signed. Once one exists, you may collect at its beginning only the first month's rent and the security deposit, so any holding money you keep must be credited to one of those, with the deposit staying within the one-month cap. If the tenant clearly backs out after agreeing but before moving in, the tenant owes you the least of: all money deposited with you, one month's rent at the agreed rate, or the rent accrued until you re-rent at fair rent plus any shortfall in rent, reasonable costs and a reasonable commission. Put the holding terms in writing: the amount, how long you will hold the unit, that it will be credited to the first month's rent or the deposit, and that you will refund it if you do not offer the lease or the applicant is not approved. If the applicant withdraws, keep no more than that statutory measure. An application screening fee is separate, limited to actual screening costs and charged only for applicants 18 or older or emancipated minors.

title: Consequence of Skipping the Inventory
bodyText: Hawaii's consequence for skipping the move-in inventory is evidentiary, not a forfeiture. If you do not make the signed written inventory of the unit's condition and of the furnishings and appliances you provide before the tenant moves in, their condition at the end of the tenancy is rebuttably presumed to be the same as at move-in, so you must overcome that presumption with other evidence to deduct for damage. The missing inventory does not by itself stop you from keeping the deposit for unpaid rent or other items that do not depend on the unit's condition. Hawaii's statutes contain no move-out inspection or inspection-notice requirement, so no penalty is tied to one. Hawaii's deposit penalties attach instead to the 14-day written notice: if you miss it you may keep none of the deposit (the notice is not needed if the tenant wrongfully quit), and a wrongful retention costs you the amount kept, or up to three times that amount if wilful.

title: No Nonrefundable Deposits
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes have no category of nonrefundable deposit and no notice rule for one. A security deposit is money held for the tenant for the purposes the statute lists, and whatever is not properly kept for those purposes must be returned within 14 days after the tenancy ends (with a written notice of anything you keep, unless the tenant wrongfully quit), so do not describe any part of a deposit as nonrefundable. Nonrefundable fees fare no better at move-in: at the start of the tenancy you may collect only the first month's rent and the security deposit, which rules out move-in, administrative, cleaning or pet fees charged then. Hawaii's statutes do not bar a separately stated charge later in the tenancy for a real service, but put it in the lease and do not let it work as a disguised deposit or late charge. An application screening fee, charged when you process the application, is the one pre-tenancy fee the code addresses; you may charge it only for applicants 18 or older or emancipated minors, and must refund any unused part.

title: No Nonrefundable Deposit Notice
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes have no rule requiring a separate written notice, when you collect a deposit, that part of it is nonrefundable. That is because no part of a Hawaii security deposit can be made nonrefundable: it is held for the tenant, may be used only for the items the deposit statute lists, and the rest must be returned within 14 days after the tenancy ends, with a written notice giving the particulars and written evidence of the costs for anything you keep (not needed if the tenant wrongfully quit). Giving the tenant a written statement of the deposit amount, and of any pet deposit, when you collect it is still good practice.

title: Security Deposit Cap: One Month's Rent
bodyText: Hawaii caps the security deposit at one month's rent. You may also take an additional pet deposit, in an amount you and the tenant agree, of up to one month's rent, to cover damage by a pet allowed to live in the unit under the lease; you may not require it from a tenant who has no pet living in the unit, or for an assistance animal that is a reasonable accommodation for a tenant with a disability. So the most you may hold is one month's rent, or two months' rent when a pet deposit applies. At the beginning of the tenancy you may collect only the first month's rent and the security deposit, so there is no prepaid last month's rent and no separate key, cleaning or furniture deposit outside the cap. The cap applies to every tenancy under the landlord-tenant code, whatever its length; arrangements the code excludes, such as transient day-to-day hotel or motel stays and housing owned or managed by the Hawaii Public Housing Authority, are outside it. Hawaii's statute does not say whether you may raise a deposit after a later rent increase; the cautious course is to leave it as collected or, by written agreement, keep the total within one month's rent at the new rate.

title: How Deposits Are Held
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not require you to keep tenants' deposits in a separate, trust or escrow account, at a particular bank, or to tell tenants where they are held. It protects the tenant's claim directly instead: you hold the deposit for the tenant, and the tenant's claim to it comes before the claim of any of your creditors, including a bankruptcy trustee, even if the deposits are mixed with your other money. Keep a separate record for each tenant anyway. When you sell or otherwise transfer the property you must give the new owner an accounting of each unit's deposit at or before the transfer, and the new owner must tell each tenant in writing within 20 days how much is credited. If a licensed real estate broker manages the property, real estate licensing rules on client trust accounts may also apply; this row does not cover them. Hawaii's statutes do not require you to pay interest on deposits.

title: No Deposit Interest Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not require you to pay the tenant interest on a security deposit or pet deposit, and do not say who keeps any interest a bank account earns on it. If you want to pay interest, or to keep it, say so in the lease so there is no dispute at move-out.

title: Deposit Rights Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: A lease may not make the tenant give up any right or remedy under Hawaii's landlord-tenant code, including the deposit rules: the one-month cap (plus a pet deposit of up to one month's rent for a resident pet that is not an assistance animal), the closed list of permitted uses, the 14-day written notice with evidence of costs and the loss of your right to keep any of the deposit if you miss it, the tenant's priority over your creditors, the rules for a sale of the property, and the small claims remedies, including up to three times an amount wilfully and wrongfully kept. A lease term that tries to waive them does not bind the tenant, and a court may refuse to enforce a term that was unconscionable when made. The code's rights cannot be waived by the landlord either. Once a real dispute over the deposit arises in good faith, you and the tenant may settle it by agreement, and any claim may be settled for less than the amount claimed, but a settlement that gives up code rights is invalid if a court finds it was unconscionable when made.

title: Deposits When the Property Is Sold
bodyText: If you transfer your interest in the rental, whether by sale, assignment, death, appointment of a receiver or otherwise, your successor is bound by the deposit statute. You must give the successor an accounting of the security deposits received for each unit at or before the transfer, and within 20 days after the transfer the successor must give each tenant written notice of the deposit amount credited to that tenant. If the successor does not meet these requirements, the tenant is presumed to have paid a deposit of at least one month's rent at the rate charged when the tenant first rented, and the successor is bound by that amount. Unless otherwise agreed, a landlord who sells in good faith to an unconnected buyer, with the written disclosure the statute calls for in the sale contract, is relieved of liability under the rental agreement and the code for events after the conveyance, and the buyer becomes liable; a manager is likewise relieved for events after the management ends. Transfer the deposit funds to the buyer at closing and keep a record, since the tenant's claim to the deposit comes before your creditors, including a bankruptcy trustee.

title: Deposit Penalties and Disputes
bodyText: Hawaii's deposit penalties are strict. If you do not give the tenant, within 14 days after the rental agreement ends, the written notice of what you are keeping, with the particulars and grounds and written evidence of the costs, you lose the right to keep any part of the deposit and must return all of it. The notice is not needed if the tenant wrongfully quit, which includes being absent 20 or more days in a row without written notice to you during a period for which you received no rent. A disagreement about the deposit goes to the small claims division of the district court in the circuit where the rental is located, which hears residential deposit disputes whatever the amount (a district court hearing a summary possession case between you may also decide it). Neither side may be represented there by an attorney or a salaried employee, and there is no appeal from the judgment. If the court finds you wrongfully and wilfully kept any part, it may award the tenant up to three times the amount wrongfully and wilfully kept, plus costs; if you kept it wrongfully but not wilfully, the tenant gets the amount wrongfully kept plus costs; and if you were entitled to keep it, the court awards you the disputed amount and costs. The tenant must sue within one year after the rental agreement ends. When a tenant ends the tenancy under the code's remedies for your failure to deliver a conforming unit, a serious condition, or a fire or casualty, you must also refund unused advance rent within 14 days (those remedies are not available for a condition caused by the want of due care of the tenant, the tenant's family or a guest, or for a casualty the tenant or a family member wilfully caused), and a mailed refund complies only if sent by certified mail, return receipt requested, postmarked by midnight of the 14th day.

title: No Deposit Standards Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not require you to post or disclose the standards you use to set deposit amounts, even if different tenants pay different deposits. Three limits apply. Every deposit is capped at one month's rent, plus a pet deposit of up to one month's rent only for a resident pet that is not an assistance animal. Hawaii's fair housing law bars discrimination in the terms or conditions of a rental because of race; sex, including gender identity or expression; sexual orientation; color; religion; marital status; familial status; ancestry; disability; age; or HIV infection, with narrow exemptions (an owner-occupied building for two families, an owner-occupant renting up to four rooms, certain religious housing, and housing for older persons). And unless an exemption applies, such as owning four or fewer units in the State, you may not require different rental conditions, such as a higher deposit, of a tenant in a section 8 voucher or permanent supportive housing program; commercially reasonable verification of income and creditworthiness is allowed. Base any difference on documented, neutral criteria and apply them consistently.

title: Utility Charges and Deposits
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes have no separate category of landlord-held utility deposit. Money you hold to secure utility charges is part of the security deposit and counts toward the one-month cap. Hawaii does let you use the deposit to cover amounts the tenant owes under the lease for electricity, water, sewer or natural gas service you provide that is not included in the rent, so state in the lease which of those utilities you provide and how they are billed. Any amount you keep for utilities must appear in your 14-day written notice with written evidence of the charges (the notice is not needed if the tenant wrongfully quit). Deposits a utility company takes from the tenant are governed by that utility's own rules, not by your lease; a utility's unclaimed customer deposit or refund is presumed abandoned one year after it becomes payable.

title: No Utility Lien for Tenant Bills
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not make a tenant's unpaid water, sewer or garbage bill a lien on your property, and they set no lease clause or affidavit procedure for keeping one off it. A county board of water supply fixes its own rates and may enforce collection by discontinuing service to delinquent consumers or by suing, and its rules have the force of law; whether a board bills the owner or the occupant, and how it treats an owner whose tenant leaves a balance, is set in those rules and in county ordinances, which this library did not search. Check your county's water and sewer rules before deciding whose name goes on the account. If you supply a utility yourself and bill the tenant separately from rent, the security deposit may cover what the tenant owes for that service at the end of the tenancy. Whatever is owed, you may never cut off or reduce running water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service to force a tenant out.

title: No Bed Bug Statute
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule on bed bugs, pest treatment or a tenant's duty to cooperate with it. The general rules apply. You must make all repairs and arrangements needed to keep the premises habitable and comply with building and housing laws materially affecting health and safety. The tenant must keep the part of the premises the tenant occupies and uses as clean and safe as conditions permit, and dispose of garbage and other waste in a clean and safe manner. The tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to your entry to inspect or make necessary repairs, and is liable for damage caused by an unreasonable refusal; except in an emergency or where it is impracticable, give at least two days' notice and enter only at reasonable hours. If you want specific cooperation duties, such as preparing the unit for treatment or reporting signs of infestation promptly, put them in the lease or in written rules given to the tenant at signing. Rules must serve the tenants' convenience, safety or welfare or protect the property, be reasonably related to that purpose, apply fairly to all tenants and be explicit. Where an infestation results from the tenant's failure to meet those duties, you may give written notice allowing at least ten days to fix it, then remedy it and bill the reasonable cost as rent.

title: No Professional Carpet Cleaning Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule letting you require professional carpet cleaning at move-out. What Hawaii does allow: you may use the security deposit to clean the unit, or have it cleaned, when the tenancy ends so as to put it in as fit a condition as when the tenant moved in. A cleaning deduction must appear in your written notice of retention, with written evidence of the cost, such as receipts for supplies and equipment or charges for cleaning services, within 14 days after the tenancy ends (no notice is needed if the tenant wrongfully quit). The signed move-in inventory is your evidence of the starting condition. A lease term charging for professional carpet cleaning whatever the carpets' condition goes beyond what the deposit may cover; the cautious course is to charge only when the carpets need cleaning to reach their move-in condition, at the documented actual cost. You may not collect a cleaning fee up front: at the start of the tenancy you may collect only the first month's rent and the security deposit.

title: No Cold-Weather Vacancy Notice
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule requiring a tenant to tell you before leaving the unit empty in cold weather. If you want to know when a tenant will be away for a long period, for any reason, Hawaii lets the lease require the tenant to notify you of an anticipated extended absence no later than the first day of the absence. If the lease includes that duty and the tenant fails to make reasonable efforts to comply, the tenant must indemnify you for any damage resulting from the absence, and during an extended absence you may enter as reasonably necessary to inspect, maintain and safeguard the unit. Use the Notice of Extended Absence clause for this. Separately, for deposit purposes, a tenant who is absent for 20 days in a row without written notice to you, during a period for which you have not received rent, is treated as having wrongfully quit.

title: No Key-Control Mandate
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not require you to adopt a key-control policy or to run background checks on employees or contractors who have access to tenants' units. Two rules make key control worth having anyway. First, entry is limited to the purposes and notice Hawaii allows, for you and anyone you authorize. Second, except for an emergency entry such as a fire, you are liable for any theft, casualty or other damage caused by an entry by you or by a person you permit if the tenant, after notice of the proposed entry, refused consent to that specific entry while absent, if the tenant was present and able to consent but did not actually consent, or if the damage was caused by your negligence. Possessing a master key without authorization, intending to use it for an unlawful entry or theft, is a crime. A written key log, limited master-key access and prompt re-keying when keys go missing are sound practice. A tenant who has been a victim of domestic violence may require you to change the locks (see the domestic violence lock-change row).

title: No Smart Lock Statute
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule on smart locks, keypads, app-based or biometric entry systems in rentals, and no requirement to offer a non-app or non-biometric alternative. The general rules apply whatever the lock technology. You may enter only to inspect, make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations or improvements, supply agreed services, or show the unit to prospective purchasers, mortgagees or tenants; except in an emergency or where it is impracticable, give at least two days' notice and enter only at reasonable hours; and you have no other right of entry except by court order, when the tenant appears to have abandoned the unit, or during an extended absence. A remote unlock is an entry like any other. Electronic access devices you furnish, such as key fobs and parking cards, count as keys for the security deposit: the deposit may cover devices the tenant does not return at the end of the tenancy. Hawaii's privacy and data laws were not researched for entry-log data; if your system records when tenants come and go, get advice before using or sharing that data.

title: No Rule on Tenant Insurance Claims
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule on whether you may require a tenant to claim on the tenant's own renter's insurance, or may claim on that policy yourself. Two Hawaii rules limit how far such a term could go. A lease term that exempts or limits your liability, or requires the tenant to indemnify you, for damage to persons or property caused by the acts or omissions of you, your agents, servants or employees in or about the unit or the premises is void. And your duties to keep the premises habitable and to repair and maintain the facilities and appliances you supply cannot be waived by the tenant. So a term making the tenant's insurance pay for damage you caused, or for repairs that are yours to make, is a term to avoid (drafting judgment). You may require a tenant to carry renter's insurance; the premium is paid to the insurer, not to you. A claim on the tenant's policy is between the tenant and the insurer, so get the tenant's written agreement at the time before submitting anything on the tenant's behalf.

title: No Home Business Protection
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not make a home-based business a protected use of a rental, so your lease may limit or prohibit business use. Hawaii's default rule supports you: unless the lease provides otherwise, a tenant's use of the unit for any purpose other than as the tenant's home, or not using it at all, is a breach you may address with Hawaii's written rule-breach notice, which must give at least ten days to stop before you may end the agreement and sue for possession. If you are willing to allow working from home or a small business, say what is allowed (for example no customer visits, employees, signs or inventory) so the term is explicit. One use has special status: Hawaii treats a family child care home as a residential use for zoning and voids recorded restrictions against it (see the family child care row). County zoning rules on home occupations also apply.

title: No Right to Cut Off Landlord-Billed Utilities
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes set no special rules for electricity, water or gas that you submeter or bill to tenants, and give you no right to interrupt a utility because the tenant has not paid for it. You may not take back possession by wilfully interrupting or reducing running water, hot water, electricity, gas or any other essential service contrary to the lease or your maintenance duties, except after the tenant abandons or surrenders the unit. Doing so is an unfair or deceptive practice, with minimum damages of three times the monthly rent or $1,000, whichever is greater, on top of other penalties. To collect an unpaid utility bill you provide, use the lease remedies and court process; at the end of the tenancy the security deposit may cover amounts the tenant owes for utility service you provided but did not include in the rent. If you sell tenants electricity from a solar or other renewable system on your property, the lease must include specific rate and tariff disclosures for you to stay outside public utility regulation, and it may not override the utility tariffs on shutoff for nonpayment (see the on-site renewable electricity clause). Public Utilities Commission rules on resale of utility service were not searched.

title: Disability Modifications
bodyText: Hawaii's fair housing law makes it a discriminatory practice to refuse to let a person with a disability make reasonable modifications to the premises the person occupies or will occupy, at that person's expense, if the modifications may be necessary to give the person full enjoyment of the premises. Hawaii does not shift the cost to owners of larger buildings or assisted housing: the person making the modification pays, whatever the size of the property. The statute lets a real estate broker or salesperson, where it is reasonable, condition permission on the person agreeing to restore the interior to its condition before the modification, reasonable wear and tear excepted; the chapter defines that term to include anyone, licensed or not, who rents or leases real property for consideration, so the condition is likely available to you too, but this is not settled, and the cautious course is to ask for a restoration agreement only for interior changes and only where it is reasonable, and to get advice before refusing a modification over restoration. Federal law may also apply. The rule does not apply to renting a unit in a building of no more than two units where you live in the other, or to renting a room or up to four rooms in a home where you live. A finding of a discriminatory practice can bring orders, damages, which may be set at $500 for each violation unless greater damages are proven, and attorney's fees, and a tenant may sue within two years. The No Alterations clause keeps this right.

title: Family Child Care Homes
bodyText: Hawaii does not require you to let a tenant run a family child care home in a rental, and its statutes set no lease conditions such as liability waivers or insurance for one. But Hawaii favours these homes in two ways, so if you want to restrict one, say so expressly in the lease. For zoning, a family child care home (a private residence, including an apartment, unit or townhouse, where care may be provided for up to six children unrelated to the caregiver at any one time) is a residential use permitted in all residential zones, with no conditional use permit, variance or special exception needed. And every recorded restriction or prohibition, by covenant, condition on use or occupancy, or condition on transfer of title, that directly or indirectly restricts or prohibits family child care homes on residential real property is void; this does not apply to housing for older persons or to limited-equity or cooperative housing corporations. An ordinary unrecorded lease is not a recorded restriction, but whether a recorded lease would be caught is unsettled, so the cautious course is not to record a lease that bans family child care. A townhouse association may not prohibit a family child care home run by an owner-occupant, which gives a tenant no protection against the association; an association may allow one by owner approval and may require indemnity, insurance and parent waivers protecting the association. Anyone operating a family child care home must be registered with the Department of Human Services. If you allow one, you may require the tenant to carry liability insurance for it, but a lease term that excuses you from, or makes the tenant indemnify you for, your own negligence is void.

title: Illegal-Use Nuisance and Forfeiture
bodyText: Hawaii has no statute that makes a lease void just because the tenant uses the property for a forbidden purpose, but three rules attach consequences. First, unless the lease provides otherwise, using the unit for any purpose other than as the tenant's home, or not using it at all, is a breach you may address with Hawaii's written rule-breach notice giving at least ten days to stop; if it continues or recurs you may sue for possession within 30 days. Second, a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy (one for an indefinite time with periodic rent) is subject to forfeiture if the tenant or the tenant's invitee or employee commits an act or causes a condition on the premises that is a nuisance under Hawaii's nuisance-abatement law, which covers places used for drug manufacture or distribution, prostitution, non-social gambling and the other listed public health and morals offenses. You must first deliver a written notice warning the tenant to abate the nuisance within 24 hours; if it is not abated, you may end the tenancy by a written notice to vacate within five days, and you must refund rent paid in advance for the period after the tenant leaves. For a fixed-term tenancy, use the rule-breach route or the Criminal Activity clause; Hawaii's landlord-tenant code controls where it conflicts with this forfeiture rule. Third, a government official, a resident of the county or a tenant organization may sue to abate such a nuisance against the owner, lessee or agent; the court may bar the persons responsible from the property, close it for up to a year, and make fees, costs and fines a lien on the owner's interest. A court weighing contempt against an owner must consider the owner's notice to the lessee that the lease will be revoked if the nuisance continues, so act promptly and in writing.

title: Smoke-Free Common Areas
bodyText: Hawaii's smoke-free law prohibits smoking in the lobbies, hallways and other common areas of apartment buildings, condominiums, multifamily dwellings (buildings with more than two dwelling units) and other multiple-unit residential facilities. Smoking includes using an electronic smoking device such as an e-cigarette or vape, and covers any lighted or heated tobacco or plant product intended for inhalation, so it reaches marijuana too. Smoking is also prohibited within a presumptively reasonable distance of 20 feet from entrances, exits, windows that open and ventilation intakes serving an enclosed or partially enclosed area where smoking is prohibited; enclosed or partially enclosed means closed in by a roof or overhang and at least two walls, and includes lanais, interior courtyards, patios and covered walkways. The units themselves are private residences and are exempt unless used as a licensed child care, adult day care or health care facility, so smoking inside a unit is a matter for your lease. The law requires the owner, operator or manager to post clearly legible signs reading "Smoking Prohibited by Law" in letters at least one inch high, or the international No Smoking symbol, in and at the entrance to places where smoking is prohibited; the cautious course is to post them at your residential common areas. Owners and managers must also tell people who violate the law about it. An owner, manager or operator who fails to comply can be fined up to $100 for a first violation, $200 for a second within a year and $500 for each further violation within a year; a person who smokes where it is prohibited can be fined up to $50. You may also declare the whole property, or any part of it, non-smoking by posting conforming signs. County ordinances may add rules.

title: Liens for Tenant Improvements
bodyText: In Hawaii, a contractor or supplier who furnishes labor or material to improve real property has a lien on the improvement and on the interest of the owner who contracted for the work, and owner includes a lessee for a term of years. So when a tenant hires the work, the lien reaches the tenant's leasehold. Your own interest is exposed in a defined case: where the terms of a lease require the improvement, your interest in the improvement and the land is also subject to the lien, and a lease provision that forfeits the lease or penalizes the tenant if a lien is filed does not affect the lienors' rights. Hawaii's statute offers no lease wording or recorded notice that keeps your interest free of liens for improvements the lease requires.
