To limit exposure, do not make a residential lease require the tenant to build or improve; keep alterations to your prior written consent, as the No Alterations clause does; and if you consent to a tenant project, ask for proof of payment or lien releases before the work is accepted. Whether a lease that merely permits an improvement exposes your interest is not settled by the statute (the case annotations, which this library did not read, say a lien cannot exist unless the owner authorized the improvement).

title: Storage Areas and the Self-Storage Lien
bodyText: Hawaii's self-service storage law gives a storage facility owner a lien on stored property for unpaid rent and a notice-and-sale procedure, but it covers real property designed and used for renting storage space, and it does not include a garage or other storage area in a private residence. Storage space you provide to a residential tenant, such as a locker, garage or storage room that comes with the unit, is part of the rented premises under Hawaii's landlord-tenant code, which defines premises to include facilities held out for tenants and any area whose use is promised to the tenant. Treat it that way: do not use the self-storage lien or sale procedure against a residential tenant's stored belongings, and do not lock a tenant out of a storage area for unpaid rent. If a tenant leaves property in a storage area after wrongfully quitting or at the end of the tenancy, follow Hawaii's abandoned-property procedure (see the Handling of Property Left Behind clause). A separately rented storage unit in a stand-alone self-storage facility, under its own storage agreement, is governed by the self-storage law instead.

title: No Special Entry for Animal Care
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes give you no special right to enter a unit to check on, feed or remove a tenant's animal, and no procedure for taking custody of an animal a tenant leaves behind. The general entry rules apply: you may enter without the usual two days' notice in an emergency (an animal in obvious distress may be one) or where notice is impracticable; during an extended absence of the tenant you may enter as reasonably necessary for inspection, maintenance and safe-keeping; and you may enter when the tenant appears to have abandoned the unit. You have no other right of entry except by court order, so a lease term letting you enter to remove a pet at your discretion would go beyond Hawaii law. Deserting a pet animal (leaving it without intending to return) is a crime for its owner, but Hawaii's abandoned-property procedure for a tenant's belongings (sell, store or donate after notice) does not say whether it covers live animals; the cautious course is to contact the tenant and your county's animal control or humane society rather than treat an animal as property to sell or donate. You may ask the tenant to name, in the lease or a pet addendum, a person you may call to collect or care for an animal in an emergency.

title: Assistance Animals: Hawaii Verification Rules
bodyText: Hawaii's fair housing law requires you to make reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices and services when they may be necessary to give a person with a disability an equal opportunity to use and enjoy housing, and an assistance animal is a common one. Hawaii defines an assistance animal broadly: an animal needed to perform disability-related work, services or tasks, or to provide emotional support that alleviates symptoms or effects of the person's disability; it may be a service, therapy, comfort or emotional support animal, trained or untrained, and of a species other than a dog. You may impose reasonable restrictions on an assistance animal. If the disability is not readily apparent, you may ask for information verifying that the person has a disability (a physical or mental impairment that substantially limits a major life activity), and if the disability-related need for the animal is not readily apparent, you may ask for verification that the animal is needed to alleviate one or more symptoms of the disability. Verification may come in a letter or other communication from the person's treating health care professional, mental health professional or social worker. You may not ask for medical records or access to health care providers, or ask about the diagnosis, nature or severity of the disability. A vest, tag or registration document of the kind commonly bought online is not valid verification. You may not require a pet deposit for an assistance animal that is a reasonable accommodation. These rules do not apply where you rent a unit in a two-unit building you live in, or rent up to four rooms in your own home. Federal law may also apply.

title: No Pet Eviction Fact Sheet
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes require no state fact sheet on pets and eviction that you must give a tenant who has a dog or cat, at signing or later, and its summary possession statutes have no special rule for animals left behind after an eviction. Hawaii does make it a crime for a pet's owner, or anyone in possession of a pet, to desert it, meaning to leave it without intending to return. If an eviction involves a pet, plan ahead with the tenant, the officer serving the writ and your county's animal control or humane society, and do not treat a live animal as abandoned property to sell or donate without advice.

title: Pet Deposits, Pet Rent and Pet Fees
bodyText: Hawaii treats a pet deposit as part of the security deposit. You may take one only for a pet allowed to live in the unit under the lease, in an amount you and the tenant agree of no more than one month's rent, on top of the regular deposit of up to one month's rent; you may not require it from a tenant with no pet living in the unit or for an assistance animal that is a reasonable accommodation. Like the rest of the deposit it is refundable: it may be used only for damage caused by the pet (along with the deposit's other listed uses), and it must be accounted for in writing and returned within 14 days after the tenancy ends. Because you may collect only the first month's rent and the security deposit at the start of a tenancy, a nonrefundable pet fee or pet cleaning fee charged at move-in is not allowed. A monthly pet charge that the lease makes part of the rent is rent, since Hawaii lets the parties agree to any lawful consideration as rent; state that in the lease, and a late fee on it is limited the same way as a late fee on the rest of the rent. If a tenant gets a pet partway through the tenancy, the cautious course is to add any pet deposit by written amendment, within the one-month cap.

title: Condominium Pet Rules for Tenants
bodyText: If your rental is a condominium unit, the association's bylaws control which pets may be kept, but Hawaii protects tenants in one way. Where the bylaws do not prohibit owners from keeping pets in their units, the bylaws may not prohibit tenants from keeping pets either, provided that you, as the unit owner, consent in writing to your tenant keeping a pet, and the tenant keeps only the types of pets owners may keep. The bylaws may limit each owner or tenant to one pet, may restrict excessive noise and other problems caused by pets and pets running at large in common areas, and bar animals described as pests or prohibited from importation. Exceptions in the bylaws for pets kept before a ban apply equally to owners and tenants, and the association may act immediately to remove vicious animals. So, for a condominium rental, check the bylaws before approving a pet, give your consent in writing (the Pets clause can serve), and require the tenant to follow the association's pet rules. Hawaii's statutes give tenants no general right to keep a pet in other rentals, including senior housing.

title: Penalties for Refusing Service and Assistance Animals
bodyText: In housing, refusing a reasonable accommodation for an assistance animal is a discriminatory practice under Hawaii's fair housing law. The consequences are civil, not criminal: the Civil Rights Commission can order you to stop and take corrective action, award damages (which may be set at $500 for each violation unless greater damages are proven) and attorney's fees, and the tenant may sue within two years, where a court may also award punitive damages. Hawaii's statutes contain no criminal penalty for a housing denial. A separate Hawaii law covers public places: a person with a disability has the right to be accompanied by a trained service dog in hotels, lodging places, places of public accommodation and other places to which the general public is invited, without paying an extra charge, but is liable for any damage the animal does. Violating it can bring a fine of up to $1,000, and the injured person may sue for three times actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater, per violation, plus fees. A rental unit itself is not one of the listed places; whether a leasing office or common areas open to the public are is not settled, so the cautious course is to admit service dogs there without charge. Intentionally striking, poisoning or otherwise harming a service animal while it is working is a crime.

title: Service Animal Misrepresentation
bodyText: Hawaii makes it unlawful for a person to knowingly misrepresent as a service animal any animal that is not one. For this rule a service animal is a dog individually trained to do work or perform tasks directly related to a person's disability; emotional support, comfort or companionship is not such work. On clear and convincing evidence the penalty is a fine of $100 to $250 for a first violation and at least $500 for each later one, and other civil remedies remain available. The section is not limited to particular places. Use it carefully in housing: a tenant who asks to keep an emotional support or other assistance animal as a reasonable accommodation is not claiming it is a service animal, and Hawaii's fair housing law protects that request even for an untrained animal or one of another species. Handle a doubtful housing request through the verification Hawaii allows (a letter from the tenant's treating health care professional, mental health professional or social worker where the disability or need is not readily apparent); a vest, tag or online registration is not valid verification, and is not itself proof of misrepresentation.

title: No Tenant EV Charging Right
bodyText: Hawaii gives tenants no statutory right to install or use an electric vehicle charger at a rental. Hawaii's charging law protects owners: no covenant, bylaw, lease or similar agreement may prevent a person from installing a charging system on or near the parking stall of a multi-family residential dwelling or townhouse that the person owns, and an association may adopt only reasonable rules on placement and use, may not ban chargers altogether, and may not charge the owner fees for placement (it may require reimbursement for electricity). As the owner of a condominium or townhouse unit you rent out, that protection is yours, not your tenant's. Whether to let a tenant install or use a charger is your decision; if you agree, put the terms in writing (see the optional EV charger installation clause). If you provide charging and bill the tenant for it, a facility used primarily to charge vehicle batteries is not a public utility, so you may charge for charging.

title: No Landlord-Tenant EV Conditions
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes set no conditions that a landlord may or must impose on a tenant's electric vehicle charging. The conditions in Hawaii law (following the association's reasonable rules and specifications, registering the system with the association within 30 days of installation, and, for a system on a common element or limited common element, using a licensed contractor, following the association's design specifications and providing a certificate of insurance naming the association within 14 days of its approval) apply between an association and the unit owner. If you rent out a condominium or townhouse unit and let your tenant install a charger, those duties stay with you, along with responsibility for damage, insurance and removal of a system on a common element, so pass them through in writing (see the optional EV charger installation clause). Anything you hold to secure the tenant's obligations for a charger is part of the security deposit and counts toward its limit.

title: No EV Charger Removal Rule
bodyText: Hawaii has no statute on who owns, or who must remove, an electric vehicle charging system a tenant installed when the tenancy ends. The only removal rule is between an association and a unit owner: for a system on a common element or limited common element, the owner of the parking stall and each successive owner are responsible for damage caused by installing, maintaining, repairing, removing or replacing it, must keep insurance covering that responsibility, and must remove it if reasonably necessary or convenient for repair, maintenance or replacement of the common elements. If you let a tenant install a charger, say in writing who will own it, whether the tenant must remove it and restore the space, and who pays (see the optional EV charger installation clause). A deduction from the security deposit for removal damage must fit the deposit's listed uses and be documented in your written notice within 14 days after the tenancy ends.

title: No Shared-Area EV Rule for Rentals
bodyText: Hawaii has no statute on tenant electric vehicle charging in shared parking at a rental property, on charging a tenant to reserve a charging space, or on sharing a charger among tenants; those are matters for your lease and parking rules. Rules you adopt for shared charging must meet Hawaii's tests for rental rules (serve the tenants' convenience, safety or welfare or fair distribution of facilities, be reasonably related to that purpose, apply fairly to all tenants and be explicit), and a later rule that substantially changes a tenant's bargain needs the tenant's written consent. A charge for charging is not public utility service, since a facility used primarily to charge vehicle batteries is not a public utility. Hawaii also makes it a traffic infraction, with a fine of $50 to $100 plus a $50 enforcement fine, to park a non-electric vehicle in a space designated and marked as reserved for electric vehicles or to park any vehicle in a space equipped with a charging system while not actively charging; the statute's words are not limited to public lots, but whether officers enforce it in a private residential lot is unsettled. In a condominium, the association, not you, controls charging on common elements.

title: No Unbundled Parking Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes neither require nor regulate separating parking charges from residential rent. If you charge for parking under the lease, treat the charge as rent: Hawaii lets the parties agree to any lawful consideration as rent, and at the start of a tenancy you may collect only the first month's rent and the security deposit, so a separate parking fee, permit fee or parking deposit collected at move-in is not allowed. A parking card or similar device you furnish counts as a key for the security deposit, which may cover one the tenant does not return. A parking space leased under a separate agreement from the dwelling, such as in a commercial garage, is outside this rule only if it is truly not part of the residential rental arrangement; get advice before splitting them. County zoning or parking requirements for new buildings were not searched.

title: Parking Rules: When They Bind
bodyText: Hawaii has no special statute on parking rules in rentals: no required heading, no rule that they be delivered before signing, and no limit on the vehicle information you may ask for. Parking rules are rules under Hawaii's general rule section. A rule binds the tenant if it is brought to the tenant's attention when the tenant enters into the rental agreement, so attach your parking rules to the lease or give them with it. A rule adopted later binds once brought to the tenant's attention, but if it works a substantial modification of the tenant's bargain (for example, taking away an included space or adding a parking charge) it binds only if the tenant consents in writing. Every rule must be for the tenants' convenience, safety or welfare, the protection of your property from abusive use, or the fair distribution of facilities held out for tenants generally; be reasonably related to that purpose; apply to all tenants fairly; and be explicit enough to tell the tenant what to do. If a tenant breaks a parking rule, give Hawaii's written rule-breach notice allowing at least ten days to comply before you may end the tenancy. Towing a vehicle follows the separate towing rules (see the towing row).

title: Towing From Rental Property
bodyText: Hawaii lets the owner, occupant or person in charge of private property have a vehicle that is left there without authorization towed at the vehicle owner's expense, but only if a notice prohibiting unauthorized parking is posted. The sign must state, in light-reflective letters at least two inches high on a contrasting background, that a vehicle parked without authorization will be towed and held at the vehicle owner's expense, and give the name, address and phone number of the facility where it will be held. It must be large enough and placed so that it is clearly visible to a driver approaching any parking space; where the whole lot is restricted, a sign at each entrance is enough. A vehicle that complies with the sign and displays a visible prepaid receipt, or a placard, permit or written authorization from the owner, occupant or person in charge, is not parked without authorization. The tow company carries the duties on capped charges, police notice, owner notice, release and payment. A violation of the towing statute is an unfair or deceptive practice. The statute does not apply in a county that has adopted its own towing ordinances, so check your county's rules first. Wheel boots, tire locks and wheel clamps are prohibited on private property, with a $100 fine for each use. For tenants: tow only vehicles parked where they are not authorized, after posting the required signs; a tenant's car parked in the tenant's own authorized space with a visible permit is not "without authorization" under the statute even if it breaks another lease rule, so use the written rule-breach process for that. In a single-family rental where the tenant has exclusive use of the parking area, the tenant is the occupant who authorizes vehicles there; the cautious course is not to tow a vehicle the tenant has authorized.

title: Lock Change for Domestic Violence Victims
bodyText: If a tenant, or an immediate family member of the tenant, has been a victim of domestic violence and the tenant does not choose to end the rental agreement early under Hawaii's domestic violence release, the tenant may require you to change the locks to the unit by submitting a request. Within three days of receiving the request you must change the locks, at the tenant's expense. If you do not act within the three days, the tenant may change the locks without your permission and must give you a key to the new locks. If the person who committed the violence is also a party to the rental agreement, you may not change the locks unless a court has ordered that person to vacate the unit and you have been given a copy of the order. You may not require any additional rent, fees or security deposit because the abuser is excluded from the unit. The person who committed the violence has no claim against you or the tenant for complying in good faith. Once a court has ordered the abuser to vacate, you need not let that person into the unit unless accompanied by a law enforcement officer, or give the person keys, and if the person is a party to the rental agreement the person's interest in the tenancy ends. The statute does not require the tenant to provide documentation for a lock change, so the cautious course is not to delay a change while asking for proof. Domestic violence has the meaning of domestic abuse in Hawaii's protective order law: physical harm, bodily injury, assault or the threat of it, extreme psychological abuse, coercive control or malicious property damage between family or household members, which include current and former spouses, people who have a child in common, relatives, people who live or lived together in the same unit and people in a dating relationship, but not adults who are roommates only by an economic or contractual arrangement. The lock-change right applies whatever the length or type of the tenancy.

title: Entry: Consent, Liability and Remedies
bodyText: Hawaii's entry rule works through the tenant's consent. The tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to your entry to inspect, make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations or improvements, supply agreed services, or show the unit to prospective purchasers, mortgagees or tenants; you must not abuse that right or use it to harass the tenant, and except in an emergency or where it is impracticable you must give at least two days' notice and enter only at reasonable hours. Remedies run both ways. A tenant who unreasonably refuses access is liable for any damage the refusal causes. Except for an emergency entry such as a fire, you are liable for any theft, casualty or other damage caused by an entry by you or someone you permit if the tenant was absent and, after notice of the proposed entry, refused consent to that specific entry; if the tenant was present and able to consent but did not actually consent; or, in any other case, if the damage results from your negligence. Repeated demands for unreasonable entry, or an unreasonable entry without the tenant's consent, let the tenant end the rental agreement, and a circuit court may enjoin you and fine you up to $100. Any agreement exempting you from this liability is void, except the tenant's consent to a particular entry. So the lease cannot give blanket advance consent: treat a tenant's repair request as consent at most to the entry it asks for, and still give notice of when you will come or agree a specific time. Hawaii's statutes have no general procedure for relocating a tenant during non-emergency work; arrange any move by written agreement. During a declared emergency in which Hawaii's emergency limits on ending tenancies apply, a landlord may, on 45 days' written notice, require a tenant to relocate while repairs make the unit fit for occupancy, must offer the same tenant reoccupancy, and the term is extended by the repair period; check the current proclamation.

title: Entry for Scheduled Services
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes have no special entry rule for regularly scheduled services. Supplying agreed services is one of the purposes for which a tenant may not unreasonably refuse entry, but except in an emergency or where it is impracticable you must give at least two days' notice of your intent to enter and enter only at reasonable hours, and a lease term exempting you from liability for an entry is void except the tenant's consent to a particular entry. So for services inside the dwelling, such as changing air-conditioning filters or interior pest treatment, give notice before each visit or agree a specific time with the tenant. For yard and grounds the tenant uses exclusively, as in a single-family rental, Hawaii's text does not settle whether the entry rule applies; the cautious course is to treat those areas like the unit, with two days' notice and reasonable hours, unless the lease sets a written schedule for a landlord service the tenant agreed to (see the optional Scheduled Grounds Service clause). Common areas held out for all tenants are not part of any tenant's unit.

title: No Waiver of Showing Notice
bodyText: Hawaii lets you show the unit to prospective purchasers, mortgagees or tenants, and the tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent, but except in an emergency or where notice is impracticable you must give at least two days' notice and enter only at reasonable hours. A tenant cannot waive that notice in advance, in the lease or in a separate signed addendum: a tenant may not waive rights under Hawaii's landlord-tenant code, and an agreement exempting you from liability for entries is void except the tenant's consent to a particular entry. What does work is the tenant's consent to a particular showing, for example agreeing by text to a showing tomorrow at 3 p.m.; keep a record of it. A showing is not "impracticable" just because a prospect wants to see the unit sooner. Showings follow the same notice rule in every type of tenancy, including the last weeks of a month-to-month tenancy after notice of termination.

title: Smoke and CO Alarms: No Statute
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no rule requiring a landlord to install, test or maintain smoke alarms or carbon monoxide alarms in a rental, no rule making the tenant maintain them, and no notice, evidence or insurance rule tied to them. That does not make alarms optional. Alarm requirements come, if at all, from the State Fire Code adopted by the state fire council, which becomes part of the Hawaii state building codes, and from county building and fire codes; neither was searched for this row. Your rental duties pick those codes up: at all times during any tenancy you must comply with all applicable building and housing laws materially affecting health and safety. Separately, anyone who owns or controls a building may not permit its occupancy unless it is reasonably safe from fire, and a violation of any law, ordinance or rule relating to fire protection carries a fine of up to $2,500 or up to 30 days in jail, with each day a separate offense. If a state or county agency notifies you in writing of a health or safety violation, you must start repairs within seven calendar days (or tell the tenant the reason for a delay beyond your control and set a reasonable tentative start date); otherwise the tenant may have the work done and deduct the cost, up to $1,000 or one month's rent, whichever is greater, and no more than three months' rent in any six months, unless the tenant, a family member or a guest caused the condition through want of due care. The cautious course: install working smoke alarms, and carbon monoxide alarms where your county's codes call for them, before each tenancy; test them at turnover; note them on the move-in inventory; and ask the tenant to report any alarm that stops working.

title: No Alternate-Housing Duty
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not require you to provide or pay for alternate housing, a hotel room or relocation costs while you make repairs, even if a condition makes the unit unlivable, except that if a state or county agency forces tenants out because of a code violation you are responsible for, you may have to repay the relocation payments it makes (see the end of this entry). The tenant's remedies instead let the tenant leave. If a condition deprives the tenant of a substantial part of the bargain, the tenant may notify you in writing and end the tenancy if you do not remedy it within one week; no notice is needed if the unit is uninhabitable or there is an imminent threat to anyone's health or safety. The tenant may not end the tenancy over a condition caused by the want of due care of the tenant, a family member or someone on the premises with the tenant's consent. When a tenant ends the tenancy this way, you must return advance rent for the remaining days and any deposit you may not keep within 14 days (a refund mailed by certified mail, return receipt requested, to an address the tenant gave you and postmarked by midnight of the 14th day complies). After a fire or other casualty that occurs without wilful fault of the tenant or a family member, the tenant may quit at once, or stay and pay only the fair rental value of the part still usable. The one substitute-housing rule applies at the start of the tenancy: if you fail to put the tenant into possession in the agreed condition, the tenant owes no rent while unable to move in, may end the rental agreement, and may recover reasonable costs of adequate substitute housing, by suing or by deducting them from rent with receipts, and a court may add costs and attorney's fees. During a declared emergency in which the emergency statute's limits on ending tenancies apply (they apply automatically for 72 hours after a declaration unless a proclamation continues them; the current Maui wildfire proclamation does not invoke them), you may, on 45 days' written notice, require a tenant under a fixed-term lease or periodic tenancy to move out while you repair the unit to make it fit for occupancy, but you must first offer the unit back to the same tenant, the tenancy is extended by the length of the repair, and the tenant finds other accommodations. Relocation-payment laws apply only to people displaced by state or county action, but that includes code enforcement: if a state or county agency makes tenants move because of a building, zoning or housing code violation, it pays relocation costs to tenants who are not responsible for the violation and may recover them from whoever is responsible for the violation, and if that is the owner and the owner does not pay within 60 days after written demand, the agency may claim a lien on the property.

title: Appliances You Do Not Supply
bodyText: Your duty to keep appliances in good working order, subject to reasonable wear and tear, covers the facilities and appliances you supply, and the rule that you must start repairs within three business days of oral or written notice covers major appliances you provide under the rental agreement where they are needed for sanitary and habitable living conditions (except repairs needed because of the tenant's misuse). Hawaii's statutes do not presume that every appliance in the unit is yours to maintain, so the lease and the move-in inventory decide. List in the lease the appliances you supply, and list separately anything present that you do not supply, such as a washer the tenant owns or an old refrigerator a prior occupant left that you will not repair; then record the supplied items on the signed move-in inventory, which you must prepare before the tenant first moves in. Excluding an appliance never excuses your other duties: you must still comply with building and housing laws materially affecting health and safety and keep the premises habitable, and a lease cannot waive the tenant's rights or exempt you from liability for damage you or your agents cause. If you miss the three-business-day start for an appliance you do supply, the tenant may have it repaired and deduct up to $1,000 or one month's rent, whichever is greater, unless the tenant, a family member or a guest caused the problem through want of due care. The tenant must keep the appliances you supply in fit condition, reasonable wear and tear excepted.

title: No Common-Area Lighting Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule on charging a tenant for common-area lights, or other shared electricity, wired to the tenant's own meter, and no rule on how common areas must be lit. Your general duties still apply: in a multi-unit property you must keep the common areas clean and safe, and you must comply with building and housing laws materially affecting health and safety, which may set lighting standards (county codes were not searched). If hallway, stairway or exterior lights used by others run through one tenant's meter, the cautious course is to move them to a house meter or, if that is not practical, say so in the lease before it is signed and credit the tenant for the shared use. Never cut off or reduce a tenant's electricity to force the tenant out.

title: No Condemned-Unit Rent Bar
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule barring you from collecting rent or a deposit after a government agency condemns a unit, finds it unfit, posts it or orders it vacated, and no statutory penalty for renting such a unit. Other rules cover the situation. At all times you must comply with building and housing laws materially affecting health and safety. When a state or county agency notifies you in writing of a health or safety violation, you must start repairs within seven calendar days, or tell the tenant why a delay beyond your control is happening and set a reasonable tentative start date; if you do not, the tenant may have the work done and deduct the cost from rent, up to $1,000 or one month's rent, whichever is greater, and no more than three months' rent in any six months. A tenant may end the tenancy at once, without giving you a week to fix it, if a condition makes the unit uninhabitable or poses an imminent threat to anyone's health or safety; you must then return advance rent for the remaining days and any deposit you may not keep within 14 days (a refund mailed by certified mail, return receipt requested, to an address the tenant gave you and postmarked by midnight of the 14th day complies). After a fire or other casualty that occurs without wilful fault of the tenant or a family member, the tenant may quit at once, or stay and pay only the fair rental value of the part still usable. The condition-based termination and repair-and-deduct remedies do not apply to a condition caused by the want of due care of the tenant, a family member or someone on the premises with the tenant's consent; the casualty remedies are lost only if the tenant or a family member wilfully caused the fire or casualty. During a declared emergency in which the emergency statute's limits on ending tenancies apply, you may still end a tenancy if the county agency determines the unit is so damaged that it is dangerous or unsanitary. If a state or county agency's code enforcement forces tenants to move, the agency pays relocation costs to tenants who are not responsible for the violation and may recover them from the owner if the owner is responsible for the violation (see the alternate-housing row). The cautious course: do not collect rent for, or re-rent, a unit under a vacate order until it may lawfully be occupied, and check your county's code, which was not searched. Counties may also adopt ordinances under which, after a hearing, the owner of a dwelling unfit for human habitation can be ordered to repair it, to vacate and close it, or to remove or demolish it, and if the owner does not, a county officer may do so, with the county's costs a lien on the property; county ordinances were not searched.

title: Who Does Tenant Repair Work
bodyText: Hawaii lets you influence who does a tenant's repair-and-deduct work in only one situation. When a state or county agency has notified you in writing of a health or safety violation and you have not started repairs within seven calendar days, the tenant may either have the work done immediately in a competent manner, or first give you written, signed estimates from two qualified workers at least seven calendar days before the work and use the lower bidder. On that second route you may require, in writing, a reasonable substitute worker or substitute materials. Hawaii's statutes contain no rule letting the lease name who must do repairs the tenant makes at your expense, and a lease term that narrows the tenant's repair-and-deduct remedy is likely unenforceable, because neither side may waive or agree to give up rights or remedies under the landlord-tenant code. The other limits on the tenant are set by statute: the work must be done competently, the tenant must give you receipts at least equal to the amount deducted, a deduction may not exceed $1,000 or one month's rent, whichever is greater, total repair costs charged to you may not exceed three months' rent in any six-month period, the tenant must notify other tenants before working on shared facilities, and the tenant may never repair at your expense a condition caused by the want of due care of the tenant, a family member or someone on the premises with the tenant's consent. The practical way to control who does the work is to meet your own deadlines: start repairs within 12 business days after the tenant's written notice of a defective condition, and within three business days after oral or written notice for repairs to electrical, plumbing or other facilities, including major appliances you provide, that are needed for sanitary and habitable living conditions. You may give tenants a list of contractors you prefer, as a suggestion only.

title: Disability Modifications and Accommodations
bodyText: Hawaii's fair housing law makes it a discriminatory practice, in any rental, to refuse to permit a person with a disability to make, at that person's expense, reasonable modifications to the premises that may be necessary for full enjoyment of them, or to refuse reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices or services that may be necessary for equal opportunity to use and enjoy the housing. If an accommodation is an assistance animal, you may impose reasonable restrictions, and you may not require a pet deposit for it. If a disability is not readily apparent, you may ask for information verifying that the person has a physical or mental impairment that substantially limits a major life activity, but you may not ask for medical records or access to health care providers, or ask about the diagnosis, nature or severity of the disability. If the need for an assistance animal is not readily apparent, you may ask for verification from the person's treating health care professional, mental health professional or social worker; a vest, tag or registration bought online is not valid verification. For modifications, the statute lets a real estate broker or salesperson, where reasonable, condition permission on the person agreeing to restore the interior to its prior condition, reasonable wear and tear excepted. The chapter defines that term to include anyone, licensed or not, who rents or leases real property for consideration, and anyone acting for them, so the condition likely is available to you as well, but this is not settled. Hawaii's statutes do not require the restoration condition to appear in the lease and set no escrow or interest-bearing account rule for restoration money. These rules do not apply when you rent a unit in a two-family building you live in, or rent up to four rooms in a home you live in. Federal law may also apply.

title: No Double-Letting Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule on renting the same room or unit to more than one tenant for overlapping periods, and no special rent penalty for it. The general rules cover it. You must deliver possession to the tenant at the start of the agreed term, in the agreed condition. If you cannot because someone else is in the unit, the tenant owes no rent while unable to move in, may end the rental agreement at any time during that period, and may recover reasonable costs of adequate substitute housing, by suing or by deducting them from rent with receipts; a court may also award costs and attorney's fees. If a prior occupant is wrongfully holding over, either you or the new tenant may bring a summary possession case against that occupant. If you remove or exclude a tenant overnight without cause or a court order, the tenant may recover possession or end the tenancy and, either way, recover two months' rent or two months of free occupancy plus costs and attorney's fees. Before signing a new lease, confirm the current occupant's move-out date in writing and allow a margin.

title: No Staff Screening Mandate
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not require you to run background checks on maintenance workers, resident managers or other employees who have keys to tenants' units. If you choose to screen, Hawaii's employment law limits how: you may consider a conviction record only if it bears a rational relationship to the duties of the position, you may ask about or consider it only after making a conditional offer of employment (which you may withdraw on that basis), and you may consider only convictions within the most recent seven years for felonies and five years for misdemeanors, not counting time in prison. Condominium boards, managing agents and resident managers, and cooperative housing boards and managers, have their own authority: with the applicant's written authorization, they may run a background check on an applicant for security guard, resident manager or any position with access to unit keys or association funds, and those checks are exempt from the conditional-offer and look-back limits. Failing to run such a check does not by itself create a claim against the association. A private landlord outside those settings has no such exemption. Careful hiring and key control remain good practice. Federal law may also apply.

title: When a Repair Problem Is Material
bodyText: Hawaii's repair rules turn on several thresholds, and minor or cosmetic problems usually fall below them, but no statute lists which conditions count. Your code duty covers building and housing laws materially affecting health and safety, and an agency's written notice of a health or safety violation (noncompliance with that duty) gives you seven calendar days to start repairs. A tenant's written notice of a defective condition in material noncompliance with your fitness duties or with the rental agreement gives you 12 business days to start; for repairs to electrical, plumbing or other facilities, including major appliances you provide, needed for sanitary and habitable living conditions, you have three business days from oral or written notice (repairs needed because of the tenant's misuse excepted). If you miss a deadline, the tenant may repair and deduct up to $1,000 or one month's rent, whichever is greater, within a limit of three months' rent per six months. During the first week of occupancy the tenant may end the tenancy if you have not conformed to the rental agreement (no materiality test) or are in material noncompliance with your fitness duties, and keeps that right while staying on in reliance on your promise to fix the problem. At any later time the tenant may end the tenancy, after written notice and a week to remedy, only for a condition that deprives the tenant of a substantial part of the benefit and enjoyment of the bargain (no notice is needed if the unit is uninhabitable or there is an imminent threat to health or safety). The later termination right and repair-and-deduct are not available for a condition caused by the want of due care of the tenant, a family member or someone on the premises with the tenant's consent. Courts decide materiality case by case; no published case was searched. Treat problems with water, sewage, electricity, gas, structural safety or anything a code officer cites as material, and answer every other repair request in writing promptly.

title: What the Lease Can and Cannot Change
bodyText: A Hawaii lease cannot remove your basic fitness duties. At all times during the tenancy you must comply with building and housing laws materially affecting health and safety, keep common areas of a multi-unit property clean and safe, make all repairs and arrangements needed to put and keep the premises habitable, and keep the electrical, plumbing and other facilities and appliances you supply in good working order, subject to reasonable wear and tear. Neither side may waive or agree to give up rights or remedies under the landlord-tenant code except where the code allows it. Two duties are switched off by the statute itself, not by the lease: in a single family residence you need not provide rubbish receptacles and removal, or running water; and the running-water duty also does not apply where the building is not required by law to be equipped for it (a question for county codes, which were not searched). A unit that shares walls counts as a single family residence only if it has direct access to a street and shares no hot water equipment or other essential facility or service with another unit. Hawaii's statutes contain no special rule for homes served by a private well or catchment system; if your rental relies on one, say in the lease who maintains it, and remember that your code and habitability duties still apply. Beyond those exceptions, the only change the law allows is an agreement that the tenant performs specified repairs, maintenance tasks or minor remodeling, made in good faith and not to evade your obligations, that does not cover work needed to cure your code noncompliance, and that does not reduce your obligations to other tenants. The library's tenant repair agreement clause is built for that.

title: No Habitability Presumptions
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no presumption that you breached your repair duties, or took an unreasonable time to repair, in an eviction, rent or repair case. The presumptions that exist concern condition records: in an action under the landlord's fitness section, the signed move-in inventory is presumed correct, and if you made no inventory, the unit's condition at the end of the tenancy is rebuttably presumed to be the same as when the tenant moved in. Fixed deadlines do the work presumptions do elsewhere: you must start repairs within seven calendar days after an agency's written notice of a health or safety violation, within 12 business days after a tenant's written notice of a defective condition, and within three business days after oral or written notice for repairs to electrical, plumbing or other facilities, including major appliances you provide, needed for sanitary and habitable living conditions; when a delay is beyond your control you must tell the tenant why and set a reasonable tentative start date. If you miss a deadline, the tenant may repair and deduct up to $1,000 or one month's rent, whichever is greater, within three months' rent per six months, but not for a condition caused by the want of due care of the tenant, a family member or a guest. In a retaliation dispute, a Department of Health certification that the unit and facilities complied with health laws on the date of the tenant's complaint lets you recover possession, or raise the rent, despite the complaint. When rent is disputed in court, either side may ask that the disputed rent be paid into court, and the court pays it out to whichever side was right. Courts may apply their own burdens of proof; no published case was searched.

title: No Required Fitness Statement
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not require your lease to state that the unit is or will be fit to live in. Your duties apply whether or not the lease mentions them. At the start of the agreed term you must deliver possession in the agreed condition, unless you and the tenant agree otherwise before delivery. At all times during the tenancy you must comply with building and housing laws materially affecting health and safety, keep common areas of a multi-unit property clean and safe, make all repairs and arrangements needed to keep the premises habitable, and maintain the facilities and appliances you supply; outside a single family residence you must also provide rubbish receptacles and removal and, unless the building is not required by law to have it, running water. What Hawaii does require in writing is different: a signed move-in inventory, the names and addresses of the owner and manager, an on-island agent if the owner lives off-island or out of state, and your general excise tax number. Because the agreed condition is what you must deliver, describe in the lease or the move-in inventory any known defect you will not fix and any repair you promise to make, with its completion date. A tenant who stays on in reliance on your promise, written or oral, to fix a condition keeps the right to end the tenancy over it beyond the first week.

title: Habitability Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: A Hawaii lease cannot remove your habitability duties or the tenant's remedies. Except where the landlord-tenant code itself allows it, neither you nor the tenant may waive or agree to give up rights or remedies under it, and a lease clause that exempts or limits your liability, or makes the tenant indemnify you, for injury or property damage caused by your own acts or omissions or those of your agents, servants or employees is void. A court may also refuse to enforce an unconscionable lease provision. The only way to shift work is an agreement that the tenant performs specified repairs, maintenance tasks and minor remodeling, made in good faith and not to evade your duties, that does not cover work needed to cure your code noncompliance and does not reduce your obligations to other tenants. Hawaii's statutes contain no procedure for a tenant to accept a listed defect in exchange for a stated rent reduction, and no rule requiring a separate document for any agreement about heat or other services; an 'as is' discount cannot excuse your code and habitability duties. Once a dispute exists, a claim disputed in good faith may be settled by agreement and any claim may be settled for less than its full value, but a court will not enforce a settlement giving up rights under the code if it was unconscionable when made (the court looks at each side's competence, any deception or coercion, the legal advice received and the value given). If you and the tenant sign a written agreement that rent may be withheld or deducted, a court will not make the tenant pay that rent into court in a later dispute.

title: No Health-District Rental Rules
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes create no local health districts with their own rental-housing regulations and do not require you to give tenants health-department rental rules on request or to post a notice of occupants' rights. Health enforcement is statewide, through the Department of Health. The department examines nuisances and conditions dangerous to public or environmental health; on private property it notifies the owner to abate them at the owner's expense within the time it sets, and leaves a copy of the notice with a tenant or occupant. If the department or another state or county agency notifies you in writing of a health or safety violation, you must start repairs within seven calendar days (or tell the tenant the reason for a delay beyond your control and set a reasonable tentative start date); otherwise the tenant may have the work done and deduct up to $1,000 or one month's rent, whichever is greater, within three months' rent per six months, unless the tenant, a family member or a guest caused the condition through want of due care. A tenant who complains in good faith to the department, a building department, the Office of Consumer Protection or you is protected from retaliatory eviction, rent increases or reduced services, subject to the statute's exceptions (for example, a condition caused by the lack of ordinary care of the tenant, a household member or a guest, or a department certification that the unit complied). If you rent rooms to three or more unrelated people in a building with no more than nine rooming units, the building is a rooming house and you must first get a clearance from the county agency that the building complies with building and zoning codes, and must keep it in good sanitary condition as the law and department of health orders require. The Office of Consumer Protection may investigate and try to resolve any landlord-tenant dispute. Department of health rules were not searched.

title: No Heat or Cooling Standard
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes set no heating season, minimum indoor temperature or air-conditioning duty for rentals, so there is no rule on shifting heat to the tenant. Hot water and other services are still protected. You must keep the electrical, plumbing and other facilities and appliances you supply, such as a water heater or an air conditioner you provide, in good working order, subject to reasonable wear and tear. Repairs to electrical, plumbing or other facilities, including major appliances you provide, that are needed for sanitary and habitable living conditions must start within three business days after the tenant tells you, orally or in writing (repairs needed because of the tenant's misuse excepted); other defects in material noncompliance with your duties or the rental agreement must be started within 12 business days after written notice. If you miss those deadlines, the tenant may have the work done and deduct up to $1,000 or one month's rent, whichever is greater, within a limit of three months' rent per six months, unless the tenant, a family member or a guest caused the problem through want of due care. You may never interrupt or reduce running water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service to force a tenant out. For buildings permitted after December 31, 1992, county building codes must require pressure-balance or thermostatic shower valves unless shower water is limited to 110 degrees Fahrenheit. County codes may set other standards; they were not searched.

title: Tenant Remedies When You Breach
bodyText: If you breach the lease or your duties under Hawaii's landlord-tenant code, the tenant's statutory remedies include the following. If you fail to deliver possession at the start of the term in the agreed condition, the tenant owes no rent while unable to move in, may end the rental agreement, may recover reasonable substitute-housing costs, and may sue a holdover occupant for possession; a court may add costs and attorney's fees. During the first week of occupancy the tenant may end the tenancy on notice if you have not conformed to the rental agreement or are in material noncompliance with your fitness duties, and keeps that right while staying on in reliance on your promise to fix the problem. At any time, a tenant deprived of a substantial part of the bargain by a condition may give written notice and end the tenancy if you do not remedy it within one week, and may recover damages if you caused the condition wilfully or negligently. If you do not start repairs on time (seven calendar days after an agency's written notice, 12 business days after a tenant's written notice, or three business days after oral or written notice for facilities needed for sanitary and habitable living conditions), the tenant may repair and deduct up to $1,000 or one month's rent, whichever is greater, within three months' rent per six months. The termination for a condition and the repair-and-deduct remedy do not apply to a condition caused by the want of due care of the tenant, a family member or someone on the premises with the tenant's consent. After a fire or casualty without wilful fault of the tenant or a family member, the tenant may quit or pay only for the usable part. When a tenant ends the tenancy under these rules, you must return advance rent for the remaining days and any deposit you may not keep within 14 days (mailing by certified mail, return receipt requested, to the tenant's address, postmarked by the 14th day, complies). Removing or excluding a tenant overnight without cause or a court order costs two months' rent or two months' free occupancy plus costs and attorney's fees. Failing to make the owner and manager disclosures within ten days of the tenant's demand costs $100 plus attorney's fees. Entering improperly can make you liable for resulting theft or damage, and repeated unreasonable entry lets the tenant end the tenancy and seek an injunction and a fine of up to $100. Retaliating against a tenant's good-faith complaint or repair request exposes you to damages, costs and attorney's fees, subject to the statute's exceptions (such as a condition caused by the lack of ordinary care of the tenant or the tenant's household or guests). Interrupting essential services to force a tenant out is an unfair or deceptive practice with minimum damages of three times the monthly rent or $1,000, whichever is greater, plus civil penalties. A court may also refuse to enforce an unconscionable term, either side may ask that disputed rent be paid into court, and the Office of Consumer Protection may investigate disputes.

title: Your Maintenance Duties
bodyText: Hawaii's landlord-tenant code requires you, at all times during the tenancy, to comply with all applicable building and housing laws materially affecting health and safety; keep the common areas of a multi-unit property clean and safe; make all repairs and arrangements needed to put and keep the premises habitable; and keep the electrical, plumbing and other facilities and appliances you supply in good working order, subject to reasonable wear and tear. Except in a single family residence, you must also provide suitable rubbish and garbage receptacles and arrange frequent removal, and provide running water as reasonably required (unless the building is not required by law to have it). A unit that shares walls is a single family residence only if it has direct street access and shares no hot water equipment or other essential facility or service. These duties apply to tenancies the code covers; it excludes, for example, day-to-day hotel or motel stays and Hawaii Public Housing Authority housing. Repair deadlines: start within seven calendar days after an agency's written notice of a health or safety violation; within 12 business days after the tenant's written notice of a defective condition in material noncompliance with your duties or the rental agreement; and within three business days after oral or written notice for repairs to electrical, plumbing or other facilities, including major appliances you provide, needed for sanitary and habitable living conditions (except repairs needed because of the tenant's misuse). If a delay is beyond your control, tell the tenant why and set a reasonable tentative start date. If you miss a deadline, the tenant may repair and deduct up to $1,000 or one month's rent, whichever is greater, and no more than three months' rent in any six months, but never for a condition caused by the want of due care of the tenant, a family member or someone on the premises with the tenant's consent. The tenant must report defects the tenant believes you do not know about as soon as practicable. If the tenant damages the unit or fails to keep it as the tenant's duties require, you may give written notice allowing at least ten days to fix it (no time is needed if the damage threatens irremediable harm), then do the work yourself and bill the actual, reasonable cost, which is treated as rent due on the next rent date. You may agree with a tenant that the tenant performs specified repairs or maintenance only on the conditions the law sets (see the tenant repair agreement clause). Anyone who manages the property for the owner must use the rents to meet these duties.

title: Shifting Chores to the Tenant
bodyText: Hawaii lets you and a tenant agree that the tenant performs specified repairs, maintenance tasks and minor remodeling, in any kind of rental, but only if three conditions are met: the agreement is made in good faith and not to evade your obligations; the work is not needed to cure your noncompliance with building and housing laws materially affecting health and safety; and the agreement does not reduce your obligations to other tenants. The statute does not require a separate document, but list each task specifically in the lease or a signed addendum, and say what the tenant receives in return if anything (for example a stated rent reduction). Two of your duties do not apply at all in a single family residence (including a unit that shares walls but has direct street access and shares no hot water equipment or other essential facility or service): providing rubbish receptacles and removal, and providing running water. In such a home the lease may simply make the tenant responsible for trash service and for arranging water and other utilities. Everything else stays with you, because neither side may waive rights or remedies under the landlord-tenant code: code compliance, habitability, clean and safe common areas, and maintenance of the facilities and appliances you supply. The library's tenant repair agreement clause is drafted to meet these conditions.

title: Facilities You Must Provide
bodyText: Beyond keeping the premises habitable and up to code, Hawaii's statutes add few specific facility duties. In a multi-unit property you must keep the common areas clean and safe. Except in a single family residence, you must provide suitable receptacles for normal amounts of rubbish and garbage and arrange frequent removal, and provide running water as reasonably required, unless the building is not required by law to have it. You must keep the electrical, plumbing and other facilities and appliances you supply in good working order. The premises these duties cover include the unit, its appurtenances and grounds, facilities held out for tenants generally, and any other area or facility whose use you promise the tenant, so a pool, laundry room, storage area or parking you promise becomes part of what you must keep habitable and safe. Hawaii's statutes contain no state rule requiring window screens, a mail receptacle, telephone jacks, a posted street number or stair railings; county building and housing codes may, and were not searched. You may charge the deposit for keys, key fobs, parking cards, garage door openers and mailbox keys you furnish that are not returned at the end of the tenancy.

title: Promises to Repair
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not require your promises to clean, repair or improve a unit to be in writing, to carry a completion date, or to be made before the lease is signed. But promises bind you. Hawaii's landlord-tenant code treats every agreement, written or oral, that sets or changes the terms of the tenancy as part of the rental agreement. You must deliver possession at the start of the term in the agreed condition unless you agree otherwise before delivery, and if you do not, the tenant may withhold rent while unable to move in, end the rental agreement and recover substitute-housing costs. A tenant who stays on in reliance on your promise, written or oral, to correct a condition keeps the right to end the tenancy over that condition beyond the first week of occupancy. A defect in material noncompliance with the rental agreement, including a promised repair, starts the 12-business-day repair deadline after the tenant's written notice, and if you miss it the tenant may repair and deduct up to $1,000 or one month's rent, whichever is greater, within three months' rent per six months, except for conditions caused by the want of due care of the tenant, a family member or a guest. A facility whose use you promise, such as a pool or parking space, becomes part of the premises you must keep up. Put every promise in the lease or a signed addendum with a completion date, record it on the move-in inventory, and avoid oral assurances you do not intend to keep.

title: No Statutory Quiet-Enjoyment Covenant
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no covenant of quiet possession or quiet enjoyment for residential leases. A court may still read such a covenant into a lease (no published case was searched), so act as if one applies. The landlord-tenant code protects the tenant's possession directly. If you remove or exclude a tenant overnight without cause or a court order, the tenant may recover possession or end the tenancy and, either way, recover two months' rent or two months of free occupancy plus costs and attorney's fees. You may not abuse your right of entry or use it to harass the tenant; you must give at least two days' notice and enter at reasonable hours except in an emergency or where notice is impracticable; and you have no other right of entry except by court order, apparent abandonment or the tenant's extended absence. Improper entry can make you liable for resulting theft or damage, and repeated unreasonable entry lets the tenant end the tenancy and seek an injunction. You may not interrupt or reduce running water, hot water, electricity, gas or other essential services to force a tenant out, and you may not reduce services in retaliation for a good-faith complaint or repair request, subject to the statute's exceptions (such as a condition caused by the lack of ordinary care of the tenant, a household member or a guest). If your unit is in a condominium and your tenant repeatedly violates the association's governing documents or other occupants' quiet enjoyment, the association may bring a possession case against the tenant if you refuse to act, naming you as a defendant.

title: Rent Collection Carries Repair Duties
bodyText: In Hawaii no one can collect the rent free of the duty to maintain the property. Any agreement, conveyance or trust instrument that authorizes someone other than the beneficial owner to act as landlord, such as a property manager, master tenant or trustee, operates, whatever its terms say, to authorize and require that person to use the rents to comply with the landlord-tenant code and every other law, code, ordinance or regulation on maintaining and operating the premises. Hawaii's code counts any agent of the landlord as a landlord. If the person who rents the unit for you fails to disclose in writing the names and addresses of the manager and the owner or the owner's agent, that person becomes an agent of every landlord for receiving rents and notices and for performing the landlord's obligations, including spending the rent collected on them, and an owner who does not deal with the tenant directly is responsible for making sure the disclosure happens. When you sell in good faith and disclose the tenancy in writing in the sale contract, you are relieved of liability for later events unless otherwise agreed, and the buyer becomes liable under the rental agreement and the code; the buyer is also bound by the security deposit rules. A manager is relieved for events after the management ends, unless otherwise agreed. None of this can be waived in the lease.

title: Government Inspections of Rentals
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes set no general rental registration or inspection program and say nothing about a lease authorizing a housing inspector to enter. Your own right of entry is limited to the purposes and notice in the access rules, and a lease cannot excuse you from liability for improper entry except by the tenant's consent to a particular entry, so ask the tenant to agree to each government inspection rather than relying on blanket lease language. Some officials have their own entry rights: fire officials may enter a private dwelling when they have reason to believe a dangerous fire hazard exists or after a fire there. Rooming houses have a special regime. If you let space in a building with no more than nine rooming units to three or more unrelated people (a lodging or tenement house, group home or rooming house), you may not operate until you get a clearance from the county agency that enforces building and zoning codes, you must at all times allow police, Department of Health agents and county code agents access to inspect, and you must keep records identifying your tenants or lodgers; violations carry fines of $100 to $1,000 per day, and obstructing an authorized inspection is a misdemeanor. The statute does not define a rooming unit; renting rooms separately to unrelated people is the clearest case, so check with your county before renting by the room. If you accept a housing voucher, the approval process includes an inspection of the unit. County rental ordinances were not searched, and federal law may also apply.

title: No Small-Landlord Remedy Exemption
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no notice or other procedure that lets a landlord with only a few units opt out of tenants' repair remedies, and no rent escrow program to opt out of. The tenant's rights to end the tenancy over unrepaired conditions, to repair and deduct, and to the possession and casualty remedies apply however few units you own, and neither side may waive them. The landlord-tenant code excludes some kinds of occupancy, such as day-to-day hotel stays, employee housing tied to employment and Hawaii Public Housing Authority housing, but not small landlords. Size and owner-occupancy exemptions exist only in other laws: the source-of-income discrimination ban does not apply to a landlord owning four or fewer units in Hawaii (unless the owner holds more than a ten percent interest in more than four), and the fair housing law does not apply to renting a unit in a two-family building you live in or up to four rooms in a home you live in. If you live in the building and rent a unit that lacks its own toilet, refrigerator or stove and shares those facilities, the tenant is a roomer or boarder, whom you may evict for any material noncompliance with the tenant's duties after notice, but who keeps the repair remedies.

title: Repair Requests and Your Deadlines
bodyText: Hawaii ties your repair deadlines to how the tenant tells you. A written notice of a defective condition in material noncompliance with your duties or the rental agreement gives you 12 business days to start repairs. For repairs to electrical, plumbing or other facilities, including major appliances you provide, needed for sanitary and habitable living conditions (other than repairs needed because of the tenant's misuse), oral notice is enough and you have three business days. A state or county agency's written notice of a health or safety violation gives you seven calendar days. If you cannot start in time for reasons beyond your control, tell the tenant why and set a reasonable tentative start date; otherwise the tenant may repair and deduct up to $1,000 or one month's rent, whichever is greater, within three months' rent per six months, except for a condition caused by the want of due care of the tenant, a family member or a guest. When first notifying you, the tenant must list every condition the tenant knows or should know about; one left off cannot be charged to you under the repair-and-deduct rule for six months. To end the tenancy over a condition, the tenant must notify you in writing and give you a week, unless the unit is uninhabitable or there is an imminent threat to health or safety. The tenant must report defects the tenant believes you do not know about as soon as practicable. Because neither side may waive rights under the landlord-tenant code, a lease clause requiring written repair requests cannot take away the three-business-day oral-notice rule or the tenant's other remedies, which is why the library's repair-request clause keeps them. Notice in Hawaii also means what you actually know or have reason to know, and a notice is received when it comes to your attention or is delivered where you take such communications, so treat a phone call, text or e-mail about a serious problem as starting the clock. A tenant who requests repairs in good faith is protected from retaliation, subject to the statute's exceptions.

title: No Lock or Rekey Statute
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not require you to install deadbolts, door viewers or peepholes, window latches or other security devices, or to rekey locks between tenants; county building codes, which were not searched, may set hardware standards that your code-compliance duty picks up. Rekeying at each turnover is still the cautious course. The one statutory lock rule protects victims of domestic violence: if a tenant or the tenant's immediate family member has been a victim and the tenant does not end the tenancy, the tenant may ask you to change the locks, and you must do so within three days at the tenant's expense. If you do not act within three days, the tenant may change the locks without your permission and must give you a key. If the person who committed the violence is also a party to the rental agreement, the locks may not be changed unless a court has ordered that person to vacate and you have received a copy of the order. You may not charge additional rent, fees or deposit because the person was excluded. After a court orders the person to vacate, neither you nor the tenant has any duty to let that person in unless accompanied by a law enforcement officer, or to give that person keys. You may charge the deposit for keys, key fobs, parking cards, garage door openers and mailbox keys you furnished that are not returned at the end of the tenancy.

title: No Senior-Housing Work Card
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not require work cards or background checks for maintenance or management staff in housing for people 55 or older, or in any other private rental housing. If you choose to screen staff who will have keys to residents' units, Hawaii's employment law applies: you may consider a conviction record only if it is rationally related to the job, only after a conditional offer of employment, and only within the most recent seven years for felonies and five years for misdemeanors, not counting time in prison. Condominium and cooperative housing boards and managers have a separate authority to check applicants for positions with key access. Federal law may also apply.

title: No Stove or Refrigerator Mandate
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not require you to supply a stove or refrigerator; county housing codes may require cooking facilities, and they were not searched. If you supply them, you must keep them in good working order, subject to reasonable wear and tear, and a refrigerator or stove you provide under the rental agreement is a major appliance whose repair, where needed for sanitary and habitable living conditions, you must start within three business days after oral or written notice (repairs needed because of the tenant's misuse excepted); if you do not, the tenant may repair and deduct, unless the tenant, a family member or a guest caused the problem through want of due care. List the appliances you supply in the lease and on the move-in inventory. Whether a unit has its own kitchen facilities also matters for its classification: a tenant whose unit lacks a toilet, refrigerator or stove, who shares those facilities with other units, in a building where you live, is a roomer or boarder. A boarder's tenancy is week to week unless you agree otherwise in writing, and you may end a roomer's or boarder's tenancy for any material noncompliance with the tenant's duties that is not fixed within the time in your notice. If you run a rooming house, do not limit residents' access to refrigerators or food storage.

title: No Code-Enforcement Receivership
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no procedure for a county or tenants to have a receiver appointed to collect rents and repair a substandard rental building. Enforcement runs through other channels. A county fire chief who finds a fire-law violation or an unreasonable fire risk serves a written order on the owner or occupant; if it is not followed, the fire chief may have the work done at the owner's or occupant's expense and, if that expense is not paid within 30 days, the county gets a prior lien on the property. The Department of Health may order an owner to abate a nuisance or health hazard, go to court to carry out the order, and recover its costs from anyone who caused the problem and from an owner, tenant or occupant who failed to abate it after notice. If your condominium association forecloses its lien on your unit, the court may appoint a receiver, often the association's managing agent, to collect the rent from your tenant. In a court dispute over rent, either side may ask that disputed rent be paid into court. And anyone who manages the property for the owner must use the rents to comply with the landlord-tenant code and other housing laws. County code enforcement tools were not searched.

title: No Cable or Satellite Access Statute
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule requiring you to let cable, satellite or internet providers into a rental building, no rule on payments from providers for access, no rule against charging tenants differently depending on whether they subscribe, and no state rule on tenant-installed antennas or satellite dishes. Cable franchises cover public places and easements dedicated for compatible purposes, not private buildings. If your rental is a condominium unit, the association's board, not you, may install antennas, cables and other telecommunications equipment on the common elements. Treat a tenant's request to install equipment under the lease's alterations terms, and remember that federal law, including federal rules on antennas and satellite dishes, may also apply.

title: Repair and Deduct
bodyText: Hawaii gives tenants a repair-and-deduct remedy on three tracks. Agency track: when a state or county agency (such as the Department of Health) notifies you in writing of a health or safety violation (noncompliance with building and housing laws materially affecting health and safety), you must start repairs within seven calendar days and finish as soon as possible, or, if a delay is beyond your control, tell the tenant why and set a reasonable tentative start date. If you do not, the tenant may immediately have the work done competently and deduct the cost, or first give you two written, signed estimates from qualified workers at least seven calendar days before the work and use the lower bid; on that second route you may require in writing a reasonable substitute worker or materials. Tenant-notice track: after the tenant's written notice of a defective condition in material noncompliance with your fitness duties or the rental agreement, you must start within 12 business days. Essential-repair track: for repairs to electrical, plumbing or other facilities, including major appliances you provide, needed for sanitary and habitable living conditions (except repairs needed because of the tenant's misuse), you must start within three business days after oral or written notice. If you miss the tenant-notice or essential-repair deadline, the tenant may have the work done competently and deduct it. On every track the deduction may not exceed $1,000 or one month's rent, whichever is greater, the tenant must give you receipts at least equal to the deduction, and total repair costs charged to you may not exceed three months' rent in any six-month period. When first notifying you, the tenant must list every known condition; one left off cannot be charged to you under this remedy for six months. Before working on facilities shared with other units, the tenant must notify the other tenants and minimize inconvenience to them. The tenant may never repair at your expense, or end the tenancy over, a condition caused by the want of due care of the tenant, a family member or someone on the premises with the tenant's consent. Separately, a tenant deprived of a substantial part of the bargain may end the tenancy after written notice and one week (no notice if the unit is uninhabitable or there is an imminent threat), recover damages if you caused the condition wilfully or negligently, and get a refund of advance rent and the deposit you may not keep within 14 days (a refund mailed by certified mail, return receipt requested, to an address the tenant gave you and postmarked by midnight of the 14th day complies). Hawaii's statutes create no rent escrow program; in a court dispute over rent, either side may ask that disputed rent be paid into court.
