A tenant who requests repairs in good faith and keeps paying rent, or tenders receipts for rent lawfully withheld, is protected from retaliation, subject to the statute's exceptions.

title: Billing Tenants for Utilities
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule on submetering, ratio or formula billing, or reselling utility-company electricity, water or gas to tenants, and no prescribed disclosure for those arrangements. One arrangement is regulated directly: if you own or operate a renewable energy system (such as rooftop solar) on your property and sell its power to your tenants, you stay outside public-utility regulation only if you keep an interconnection with the electric utility so tenants can still be served by it, you do not use the utility's lines to deliver the power, the rate at signing is no higher than the utility's effective per-kilowatt-hour rate, the rate schedule or formula is fixed for the length of the lease and stated in it, and the lease discloses the rate schedule or formula, that the rate meets that limit at signing, that the lease does not override the utility tariffs on shutoff for nonpayment or health, safety and welfare rules, and whether the lease requires the tenant to buy the power. The library's on-site renewable power clause contains those disclosures. For any other resale or allocation, whether you could be treated as a public utility is not settled by statute, and public utilities commission rules were not searched, so get advice before billing tenants for utility-company service by meter or formula. If you provide a utility that is not included in the rent, the security deposit may cover unpaid charges the lease makes the tenant owe, and you may never interrupt or reduce running water, hot water, electricity or gas to force a tenant out.

title: No Utility Allowance Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule on utility allowances, caps on landlord-paid utilities, or overage charges when a tenant's use runs over an allowance. Hawaii lets you and the tenant agree to any lawful consideration as rent, so an allowance-and-overage term is a matter of the lease, but only if it is agreed in writing at the start: a later change for a month-to-month tenant is a rent increase needing 45 consecutive days' written notice (15 for a shorter periodic tenancy), and a fixed-term lease cannot be changed mid-term without the tenant's agreement. State the allowance, how usage is measured and how the overage is billed. Where usage is measured from a utility-company bill rather than a separate meter, the public-utility question discussed in the utility billing row applies, and public utilities commission rules were not searched. The security deposit may cover unpaid charges for a utility you provide that is not included in the rent. Never interrupt or reduce a utility to collect an overage or to force a tenant out.

title: No Utility Apportionment Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule on splitting a shared utility bill among tenants, no required apportionment method, and no rule that a lease term making a tenant pay for utilities not separately metered to the unit is unenforceable. If you apportion a shared water, sewer, gas or electric bill, the method is a lease term: state it in writing before the lease is signed, apply it the same way to every unit, show the tenant the underlying bill on request, and do not add a markup, because whether reselling utility-company service to tenants makes you a public utility is not settled by statute (public utilities commission rules were not searched). Outside a single family residence you must provide running water as reasonably required unless the building is not required by law to have it. In a condominium, the association may install unit meters and bill owners by actual use; that binds you as owner, not your tenant, unless your lease passes the charge on. The security deposit may cover unpaid charges for a utility you provide that is not included in the rent, and you may never interrupt or reduce a utility to force a tenant out.

title: Learning of a Tenant Utility Shutoff
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no procedure for a tenant or owner to authorize a utility to warn you before the tenant's own service is disconnected, and no rule requiring a utility to copy a landlord on a tenant's shutoff notice. Utility tariffs and public utilities commission rules, which were not searched, may let a customer name a third party to receive notices; you may ask the tenant to use any such option, but a lease cannot make the utility send them to you. Practical steps: require in the lease that the tenant keep tenant-paid utilities in service and give you a copy of any shutoff notice the tenant receives, and keep a record of which utilities are in whose name.

title: Utilities in Your Name
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no special rules for utilities held in the landlord's name: nothing on whether a utility may shut off tenants for your unpaid bill, nothing letting tenants pay your bill and deduct it, no notice to tenants before a building-wide shutoff, and no rent receiver when you fall behind. Utility tariffs and public utilities commission rules, which were not searched, may address some of this. Your general duties fill the gap. If the lease says you provide a utility, or the law requires it (outside a single family residence you must provide running water as reasonably required, unless the building is not required by law to have it), letting it lapse can breach the lease and your duties, and a lost essential service may let the tenant end the tenancy after written notice and a week if it deprives the tenant of a substantial part of the bargain (not if the tenant or a guest caused the problem through want of due care). A wilful interruption or reduction of running water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service to force a tenant out is an unfair or deceptive practice, with minimum damages of three times the monthly rent or $1,000, whichever is greater, plus civil penalties of $500 to $10,000 per violation, each day counting separately. Pay landlord-held utility accounts on time and keep the utility's contact information current.

title: No Utility Shutoffs to Force a Tenant Out
bodyText: You may not recover or take possession of a unit by wilfully interrupting or reducing running water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service to the tenant contrary to the rental agreement or your statutory duties. The only exceptions are abandonment and surrender. A landlord who does this is treated as having engaged in an unfair or deceptive practice under Hawaii's consumer protection law: the tenant recovers at least three times the monthly rent or $1,000, whichever is greater, and the State may seek civil penalties of $500 to $10,000 per violation, with each day a separate violation. The rule applies to every tenancy the landlord-tenant code covers, whatever its length, and to utilities in your name as well as services you control. You also may not reduce services in retaliation for a tenant's good-faith complaint or repair request, subject to the statute's exceptions. To end a tenancy, use the notice and court process instead. Hawaii's statutes set no seasonal or winter rule on utility disconnections; the public utilities commission's rules on how utilities disconnect customers were not searched.

title: No Cutoff for Untransferred Utilities
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule letting you shut off utilities still in your name because the tenant did not transfer them. A wilful interruption or reduction of running water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service contrary to the rental agreement or your duties, done to recover possession, is an unfair or deceptive practice with minimum damages of three times the monthly rent or $1,000, whichever is greater, plus civil penalties; and outside a single family residence you must provide running water as reasonably required unless the building is not required by law to have it. So require in the lease that the tenant put named utilities in the tenant's own name by a stated date, follow up in writing, and until the transfer happens keep the service on and bill the tenant for it as the lease allows. The security deposit may cover unpaid charges the lease makes the tenant owe for a utility you provide that is not included in the rent. If the tenant refuses, treat it as a lease breach and use the notice and court process. Utility tariffs and public utilities commission rules were not searched.

title: Habitability Rules Hawaii Lacks
bodyText: Several habitability rules found in other states have no counterpart in Hawaii's statutes. (1) No heat or cooling standard: there is no heating season, minimum indoor temperature or air-conditioning duty. (2) No smoke or carbon monoxide alarm statute: alarm requirements, if any, come from the State Fire Code and county codes, which your code-compliance duty picks up. (3) No presumptions: no statute presumes you breached your repair duties or took too long; fixed repair deadlines apply instead. (4) No relocation duty: you need not house a tenant during repairs. (5) No rent bar on condemned units, and no code-enforcement receivership. (6) No small-landlord exemption from tenant remedies. (7) No statutory list of serious or dangerous conditions. (8) No rent escrow program. What Hawaii does have: fitness duties that cannot be waived; repair deadlines of seven calendar days after an agency's written notice, 12 business days after a tenant's written notice, and three business days after oral or written notice for essential facilities; a repair-and-deduct remedy capped at $1,000 or one month's rent, whichever is greater, and three months' rent per six months, never available for conditions caused by the want of due care of the tenant, a family member or a guest; termination rights; and a court rent trust fund for disputed rent. State administrative rules, county codes and case law were not searched and may add duties.

title: Medical Cannabis Tenants
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes permit only medical cannabis. Possessing marijuana without medical authorization remains an offense under state law (three grams or less is a violation with a $130 fine). For registered medical cannabis patients and caregivers, two rules apply. First, you may not refuse to lease to, or otherwise penalize, a person solely for being a qualifying patient or primary caregiver, unless doing so would cost you a monetary or licensing-related benefit under federal law; the protection applies only if the person has strictly complied with the program and shows a registry card or certificate and photo identification. Second, a lease provision allowing you to evict a tenant who holds a valid certificate for the medical use of cannabis in any form is void, unless the lease allows eviction for smoking tobacco and the tenant smokes the medical cannabis. Medical use includes acquiring, possessing, growing (within the adequate supply of ten plants and four ounces of usable cannabis), using and transporting cannabis, so a lease cannot be used to evict a certificate holder for growing or for non-smoked use such as edibles. The practical result: a smoke-free lease that treats tobacco and cannabis smoking alike can be enforced against medical cannabis smoking, which is what the library's smoking policy does; that policy treats vaporizing as not smoking for the medical exception, the cautious reading because the landlord-tenant code does not define smoking. The medical authorization does not cover use that endangers another person or use in any place open to the public, and Hawaii's smoke-free law separately bans smoking, including heated plant products and electronic smoking devices, in the lobbies, hallways and other common areas of apartment buildings, condominiums and other multi-unit residences. The eviction rule does not apply where a condominium or planned community's governing documents prohibit the medical use of cannabis. A tenant without a valid certificate has none of these protections. Federal law may also apply.

title: Disaster-Displaced Guests
bodyText: Hawaii's landlord-tenant code does not cover transient occupancy on a day-to-day basis in a hotel or motel (unless the arrangement was created solely to avoid the code), and a current emergency order goes further for Maui. Under the Thirty-Second Proclamation Relating to Wildfires (August 24, 2026), a stay between a hotel, motel or condominium operated as a hotel or motel on the island of Maui and a person displaced by the wildfire emergency does not create a landlord-tenant relationship, or turn the room into a residential dwelling unit, under the emergency price law, the landlord-tenant code or the summary possession law, unless the stay agreement says otherwise. The proclamation runs through October 23, 2026 unless ended or superseded, and proclamations are reissued often, so check the current one before relying on it. Outside that order, Hawaii's statutes say nothing about when a displaced guest becomes a tenant, and nothing lets your tenants house displaced friends or family despite the lease's guest or occupancy limits; your lease terms apply, subject to fair housing law. Consider consenting in writing to temporary stays after a disaster, with an end date.

title: Firearms and Your Lease
bodyText: Hawaii's firearms law expressly preserves lease restrictions: nothing in it limits the enforceability of a provision in a private rental agreement restricting a tenant's possession or use of firearms, or a restrictive covenant or association rule doing so. So you may restrict or ban firearms in the lease if you choose, and the restriction is a lease term like any other. Separately, a person licensed to carry may not enter or remain on private property of another person while carrying a firearm, loaded or not, concealed or not, without express authorization from the owner, lessee, operator or manager, given by unambiguous written or verbal authorization or by clear and conspicuous signs at the entrance or on the premises; a violation is a misdemeanor. A tenant is a lessee, so this default rule does not bar a licensed tenant from carrying in the tenant's own rental, and the tenant may authorize the tenant's own guests there unless the lease restricts it. Whether a tenant counts as a lessee of shared areas of a larger property, such as lobbies or parking, is not settled, so if you want to allow or forbid carrying in common areas, say so in the lease and, if you allow it, post signs. People in categories exempt from Hawaii's firearm-licensing rules, such as on-duty law enforcement, are outside the default rule. Carrying is also banned in listed places regardless of authorization. Court challenges to these rules were not searched, and federal law may also apply.

title: No Guest-Rights Statute
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes give tenants' guests, visitors, caregivers, tradespeople and delivery people no access rights of their own, set no limit on lease guest terms, and do not bar guest fees, so your lease governs, within limits. Rules on guests must serve a legitimate purpose, be reasonably related to it, apply to all tenants fairly and be explicit enough to follow. Fair housing law still applies: a guest or occupancy rule may not discriminate on a protected basis such as familial status, and you must make reasonable accommodations, such as allowing a live-in aide a tenant with a disability needs (the fair housing law has narrow exemptions, such as renting a unit in a two-family building you live in or up to four rooms in your own home). The tenant answers for guests: a tenant must not permit anyone on the premises with the tenant's permission to wilfully damage the property, and if a tenant's invitee or employee commits a nuisance on the premises of the kind Hawaii's nuisance-abatement law covers (such as drug or prostitution offenses), a periodic (month-to-month or other period) tenancy is subject to forfeiture after a written 24-hour warning to abate and a five-day notice to vacate; for a fixed term, the lease's default terms and the landlord-tenant code's rule-breach procedure apply.

title: No Crime-Free Lease Statute
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule requiring or regulating crime-free lease addenda, no duty to give police or child-protection investigators information about tenants, and no statute limiting tenants' calls for police or emergency help; the library's criminal-activity clause nonetheless protects emergency calls and crime victims. What Hawaii does have is a nuisance-abatement law aimed at places used for drug, prostitution and similar offenses. Any building or place used to commit those offenses is a nuisance; a court may bar the people responsible from the property and, if that will not end the nuisance, order the building closed for up to a year, with costs becoming a lien. If you, as owner, warn the tenant in writing that the lease will be revoked if the nuisance continues and take steps to end it, a court must give that appropriate consideration if you are accused of contempt. For a periodic tenancy (month to month or other period), the summary possession law lets you end the tenancy when the tenant, or the tenant's invitee or employee, creates such a nuisance on the premises: deliver a written warning to abate it within 24 hours, then a written notice to vacate within five days, refunding any rent paid in advance for the period after the tenant leaves. After a court orders an abuser to vacate, you have no duty to let that person in unless accompanied by a law enforcement officer. Rooming houses must allow police access for inspection at all times. Two duties bind you as they bind anyone. Anyone who becomes aware of a death from violence, accident or suicide, a sudden death of someone in apparent health, a death unattended by a physician, or one in a suspicious or unusual manner, as when a tenant is found dead in a unit, must immediately notify the coroner or deputy coroner, and failing to report is subject to a fine of up to $100 (HRS § 841-3). And anyone at the scene of a crime who knows a victim is suffering serious physical harm must obtain or try to obtain aid from police or medical personnel if that can be done without danger to anyone; failing to is a petty misdemeanor (HRS § 663-1.6). The child-abuse and vulnerable-adult reporting duties bind listed professionals, not landlords as such (HRS §§ 350-1.1(a) and 346-224(a)), though anyone may report suspected abuse of a vulnerable adult (HRS § 346-224(d)).

title: No Candidate Access Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule requiring you to let political candidates, campaign workers or voter-registration workers into an apartment building, condominium or other multi-unit property to reach tenants' doors, and no duty to set aside an area for voter information. Access to locked common areas for canvassing is up to you, but apply any policy to all candidates and causes alike. A different rule protects display: in a rental agreement for a single family residence, you may not prohibit the tenant from putting up or keeping an otherwise legal sign urging a vote for or against a person or issue, though reasonable restrictions to comply with building and housing laws affecting health and safety are allowed.

title: No Window-Unit Right
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes give tenants no right to install a window or portable air conditioner or other cooling device, and set no cooling standard you must meet. Your lease may allow, limit or ban tenant-installed units, and a lease that restricts them need not say anything special. Any rule you adopt must serve tenants' convenience, safety or welfare, protect the property from abusive use or fairly distribute services; be reasonably related to that purpose; apply to all tenants fairly; and be explicit enough to follow, for example by stating approved unit types, installation methods and who pays for electrical work. If you supply an air conditioner, you must keep it in good working order, subject to reasonable wear and tear. A tenant with a disability may need a cooling device as a reasonable accommodation, unless a fair housing exemption applies (for example, renting a unit in a two-family building you live in).

title: No Tenant Solar Right
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes give tenants no right to install a plug-in, balcony or other portable solar device. Hawaii's solar-access law protects owners: no covenant, bylaw, deed, lease or other agreement may prevent a person from installing a solar energy device on a single-family home or townhouse that person owns, and a contrary lease term is void. That protects you as owner against your own association or ground lessor, but it does not extend to your tenant, who does not own the home. In a condominium, owners may install solar devices with the board's written consent. Treat a tenant's request under the lease's alterations terms; if you allow a device, state where and how it may be installed and who removes it at move-out. If you install a solar system yourself and sell its power to the tenant, the library's on-site renewable power clause sets out the lease disclosures Hawaii requires.

title: No Recycling Notice Duty
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not require you to tell tenants where or how to recycle, or to provide recycling service. Your related duty is about trash: except in a single family residence, you must provide suitable receptacles for normal amounts of rubbish and garbage and arrange frequent removal, and tenants must dispose of their rubbish and other waste in a clean and safe manner. Counties run their own recycling programs and may have rules for multi-unit properties; county ordinances were not searched. If recycling bins are available, saying in the lease or house rules where they are and what goes in them is good practice.

title: No Religious Display Statute
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule protecting a tenant's religious or cultural displays, such as a mezuzah on a door frame or a blessing item at the entry. Your lease and house rules govern, within limits. A rule restricting displays must serve tenants' convenience, safety or welfare, protect the property from abusive use or fairly distribute services; be reasonably related to that purpose; apply to all tenants fairly; and be explicit enough to follow. Hawaii's fair housing law bars discrimination because of religion in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental, so a rule that singles out religious items, or is enforced against one faith and not others, invites a complaint (unless a fair housing exemption applies, such as renting a unit in a two-family building you live in). If the unit is in a condominium, the tenant must also follow the association's bylaws. Federal law may also apply.

title: Smoke From Other Units
bodyText: Hawaii's smoke-free law bans smoking, including electronic smoking devices and heated plant products intended for inhalation, in lobbies, hallways and other enclosed or partially enclosed common areas of apartment buildings, condominiums and other multi-unit residences (a multifamily dwelling is a building with more than two units). Areas where staff work, such as hallways and stairs, are also covered as places of employment. Private residences themselves are exempt unless used as a licensed child care, adult day care or health care facility, so the law does not reach smoking inside a tenant's own unit. Smoking is also presumptively banned within 20 feet of entrances, exits, windows that open and ventilation intakes serving an area where smoking is prohibited. As the person in control, post 'Smoking Prohibited by Law' signs (letters at least one inch high) or the international no-smoking symbol in and at the entrance to those common areas, and tell anyone smoking there that the law forbids it; the smoker faces a fine of up to $50. You may declare additional areas, or the whole property, nonsmoking, and counties may adopt stricter rules (not searched). Hawaii's statutes contain no rule on tobacco smoke drifting between units and none on tenants waiving smoke-drift claims; a lease clause that makes the tenant release you from liability for your own acts or omissions, or those of your agents, is void, and a tenant cannot waive rights under the landlord-tenant code, so do not rely on a smoke-drift waiver. The library's smoking policy is the better tool.

title: Tenant Signs and Flags
bodyText: In a rental agreement for a single family residence, you may not prohibit the tenant from putting up, keeping or displaying an otherwise legal sign or outdoor advertising device urging a vote for or against any person or issue; you may impose reasonable restrictions needed to comply with building and housing laws affecting health and safety. A unit that shares walls counts as a single family residence only if it has direct street access and shares no hot water equipment or other essential facility or service. The rule does not cover apartments or other multi-unit buildings, where your lease and rules govern signs, subject to the usual tests for rules. Hawaii's statutes contain no rule protecting a tenant's display of the United States flag or other flags. Separately, posting a sign or notice on someone else's property without the consent of the owner, holder, lessee or agent is unlawful, which is one reason to say in the lease what the tenant may post on the property. If the unit is in a condominium, the tenant must also follow the association's bylaws. County sign ordinances were not searched, and federal law may also apply.

title: Tenant Cameras and Video Doorbells
bodyText: Hawaii's landlord-tenant code says nothing about tenant-installed security cameras or video doorbells, so the lease's alterations terms and house rules govern installation, mounting and removal; any rule must serve a legitimate purpose, be reasonably related to it, apply fairly and be explicit. Hawaii's criminal law limits what anyone, tenant or landlord, may record. It is a crime to install or use, without consent, a device for observing or recording sounds or events in a private place (a place where one may reasonably expect to be safe from casual or hostile intrusion or surveillance, which does not include places the public or a substantial group has access to), or to use a device outside a private place to pick up sounds from inside it that would not ordinarily be audible outside; recording a person who is undressed or in sexual activity is a more serious offense. Recording a conversation is lawful only if the person recording is a party to it or a party has consented. So a doorbell camera that views a shared hallway is different from one aimed into a neighbor's window or recording a neighbor's conversations. A lease may ban or limit cameras that face other units or private areas, and you should never place cameras inside a rented unit. Federal law may also apply.

title: No Waterbed Statute
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule on waterbeds or other liquid-filled furniture in rentals, so the lease governs. You may require your consent, limit them to ground-floor units, or require proof of insurance, as long as the rule protects the property or tenants' safety, is reasonably related to that purpose, and applies to all tenants fairly. The library's common-area clause already requires your consent for water-filled furniture. The security deposit may cover damage the tenant causes in breach of the tenant's duties.

title: Damages When a Tenant Abandons
bodyText: If a tenant wrongfully leaves the unit and makes clear by words or conduct that the tenant does not intend to come back, Hawaii caps what you can recover for the abandonment at the lesser of two amounts: (1) the entire rent for the rest of the term; or (2) the rent for the period reasonably needed to re-rent the unit at a fair rent, plus the difference between that fair rent and the rent in the old rental agreement, plus a reasonable commission for re-renting. The second measure applies whenever it is lower, whether or not you actually re-rent, so you cannot simply leave the unit empty and claim the whole remaining rent: market the unit promptly at a fair rent, keep records of your efforts, and claim only the re-rental period, any rent shortfall and the commission. If the tenant backs out before moving in, you may recover only the lowest of: all money the tenant deposited with you; one month's rent; or the rent from the agreed start date until you re-rent at a fair rent, plus any rent shortfall, reasonable costs and a reasonable commission. A tenant who is absent for 20 or more days in a row without written notice to you, during a period for which you have not received rent, is treated as having wrongfully quit, and you may keep the entire security deposit; you may also enter a unit that appears abandoned, and you must follow the abandoned-property rules for anything left behind. Tenancy type matters. For a fixed term, the remaining-rent figure runs to the end of the term. For a month-to-month tenancy the statute does not say how the rest of the term is measured; a month-to-month tenant who leaves must give 28 days' written notice and pay rent through the 28th day, so the cautious claim is no more than 28 days' rent after you learn the tenant has gone, less any rent you receive from a new tenant for those days. If you sue for possession you may join claims for rent and damages up to the date of judgment, and rent you accept during the case does not recognize the tenancy if you win.

title: Attorney's Fees in Hawaii Leases
bodyText: Hawaii limits what a lease can say about attorney's fees. For unpaid rent, the lease may make the tenant pay the costs of the suit and reasonable attorney's fees of no more than 25% of the unpaid rent, and only after the tenant defaults and you refer the rent to an attorney who is not your salaried employee (or a salaried employee of your assignee). In all other matters arising under the landlord-tenant code, the lease may provide that reasonable attorney's fees and costs may be awarded to the prevailing party, whichever side that is. A lease fee term outside these two permissions is unenforceable, so do not use a one-way fee clause for non-rent matters, a fee for in-house counsel, or a fee above 25% of the unpaid rent. Separately, in contract actions the court taxes a reasonable attorney's fee against the losing party, capped at 25% of the judgment (or of the amount sued for if the defendant wins), so a tenant who wins a contract claim may recover fees too. If the tenant stops a nonpayment case by paying before the writ of possession issues, the payment must include a reasonable fee for your attorney along with the rent, 8% yearly interest and the costs of the case. Under the prelitigation mediation program for nonpayment notices (in effect from February 5, 2026 until it ends on February 4, 2028 unless extended), each side bears its own mediation costs and fees, but you may ask for all costs of the mediation process, including reasonable attorneys' fees, if the tenant defaults on a mediated agreement or fails to attend a scheduled mediation; after February 4, 2028 that rule ends with the program. The code also awards fees directly in some cases, whatever the lease says: a tenant who is unlawfully removed or excluded, retaliated against, or not given possession at the start of the term may recover attorney's fees; you may recover them if a tenant knowingly gives a false domestic violence early-termination notice, and if a lockout claim fails because you acted with cause or under a court order (only if your attorney is not your salaried employee). Attorneys may not represent either side in a small claims security deposit case. These rules are the same for fixed-term and periodic tenancies. The library's Default by Tenant clause uses exactly the two permitted fee terms.

title: Notice Before Conversion or Demolition
bodyText: If you plan to convert the building to a condominium, you must give each tenant whose tenancy is under a rental agreement written notice at least 120 days before the rental agreement ends. For a month-to-month tenancy, before you end it because you plan to demolish the units, convert the building to a condominium, or change the building's use to transient vacation rentals, you must give written notice at least 120 days before the planned demolition or termination; if you revoke or amend and reissue the notice, the 120 days start again from the reissued notice. During those 120 days the tenant may move out early by telling you the move-out date, and owes only prorated rent for the time actually occupied. A fixed-term lease is not cut short by a planned conversion: give the 120-day notice so that it runs before the term ends, and do not end the term early unless the lease itself lets you. A good-faith plan to demolish or substantially remodel is also an exception to Hawaii's bar on retaliatory evictions. If the rental project was financed with a state housing finance corporation project loan and the loan is prepaid to convert the units to ownership, the loan agreement must give the tenants at that time the first option to buy their units. Hawaii's statutes put no lease statement about conversion at the start of the lease and give tenants no general right of first refusal. County rules on transient vacation rentals may also apply; they were not reviewed.

title: Notice and Cure Periods for Tenant Defaults
bodyText: Hawaii sets separate notice-and-cure tracks for different defaults; the lease cannot shorten them. Unpaid rent: a written demand giving at least 10 calendar days after the tenant receives it (see the nonpayment notice row for the contents and mediation steps that apply until February 4, 2028). Failure to keep up the unit (the tenant's statutory duties on cleanliness, rubbish, plumbing, proper use, damage and landlord-supplied items): written notice of the problem giving at least 10 days after receipt to fix it. You may end the rental agreement on this ground only if the tenant is materially failing to comply with building and housing laws materially affecting health and safety; for other problems you can fix by cleaning, repairing or replacing a damaged item, you may do the work and bill the actual and reasonable cost as rent due on the next rent date (immediately if the tenancy has ended). No time to fix is required when the noncompliance causes or threatens irremediable damage to any person or property. If you cannot serve the notice, you may post it conspicuously on the unit. For a roomer or boarder (a tenant whose unit lacks a major bathroom or kitchen facility shared with other units, in a building where you live), any material noncompliance not fixed in time is a ground to end the agreement. Breach of a rule or other lease restriction on use, occupancy or maintenance: written notice, in substantially this form, giving at least 10 days: "(Name and address of tenant) (date) You are hereby notified that you have failed to perform according to the following rule: (specify rule allegedly breached) Be informed that if you (continue violating) (again violate) this rule after (a date not less than ten days after this notice), the landlord may terminate the rental agreement and sue for possession of your dwelling unit." No time to remedy is required when the breach causes or threatens damage to any person, or violates building and housing laws affecting health and safety, or is wilful damage to the premises by the tenant or someone there with permission. If the breach continues or recurs after the date in the notice, you must file for possession within 30 days after that continued or recurring breach. Unless the lease says otherwise, using the unit for anything other than the tenant's home, or not using it, is a rule breach on this track. Nuisance in a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy: a 24-hour written warning to abate, then a written notice to vacate within five days (see the nuisance rows). Ending without a default: a fixed term ends on its date; a periodic tenancy ends on the notice periods in the termination notice row (45 days, 10 days for tenancies shorter than month to month, 120 days for demolition, condominium conversion or a change to transient vacation rentals). The court's general summary possession complaint form lists the notices it expects: a 10-day non-monetary default notice, a 45-day month-to-month termination notice, or a notice as specified in the rental agreement or statute. Where the older summary possession chapter sets a different notice (10 days for a tenant by parol; 25 days or 5 days for nonpayment in a month-to-month tenancy), the landlord-tenant code controls. Hawaii's statutes say nothing about how many times a tenant may cure; do not promise more cure time than the statute gives for a breach that threatens damage to persons.

title: Emergency Limits on Ending Tenancies
bodyText: When the Governor declares a state of emergency for all or part of the State, a mayor declares a local emergency, or an area is under a severe weather warning, Hawaii's emergency statute can also limit ending tenancies. While that limit is in effect, you may not end any residential tenancy in the affected area except for the tenant's breach of a material term of the rental agreement (failing to perform an obligation that was part of the bargain, including not paying rent on time) or because the unit is unfit for occupancy (the county agency has found the damage makes it dangerous or unsanitary for the occupants or the neighborhood). The limit does not extend a fixed-term lease beyond its end date. A periodic tenancy (such as month to month) may still be ended on 45 days' written notice if you sell the unit to a good-faith buyer for value, or if you or an immediate family member will live in it. On 45 days' written notice you may also require tenants under a fixed-term lease or a periodic tenancy to move out while the unit is repaired to make it fit for occupancy; you must first offer the same tenants reoccupancy when the repair is done, the lease or tenancy is extended by the length of the repair, and the tenants must find their own accommodations meanwhile. The limits last 72 hours after a declaration takes effect (24 hours after a severe weather warning is canceled) unless the proclamation continues them. A violation is an unfair or deceptive practice with civil penalties of $500 to $10,000 per violation. Check the current proclamation: the Thirty-Second Proclamation Relating to Wildfires (August 24, 2026, through October 23, 2026 unless ended or superseded) continues only the rent-increase limit, for the island of Maui only, and suspends the automatic statewide use of this statute, so the termination limits are not now in effect under it. See the emergency rent freeze row for the rent limit. If a disaster damages the unit, the tenant's own statutory rights after a fire or other casualty not caused by the tenant's or family's wilful fault still apply: the tenant may quit and end the agreement as of the date of quitting (telling you within a week), or stay in the usable part and pay only its fair rental value. A separate wildfire mediation statute for nonpayment cases after the wildfire eviction moratorium applied only for a limited time and is repealed no later than December 31, 2026.

title: No Drug-Free Addendum Statute
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule requiring, authorizing or regulating a drug-free housing addendum, and no special category of drug- and alcohol-free recovery housing with its own lease terms or eviction track. If you use an addendum, it works as an ordinary lease rule: it binds the tenant only if it is brought to the tenant's attention when the lease is signed (or later agreed to in writing if it substantially changes the bargain), it must serve the safety or welfare of tenants or protect your property, be reasonably related to that purpose, apply fairly to all tenants and be explicit enough to tell the tenant what is forbidden. You enforce it with Hawaii's written rule-breach notice; no time to fix is needed where the breach causes or threatens damage to any person. The library's optional Criminal Activity clause already covers the manufacture or distribution of illegal drugs and carves out medical cannabis use that Hawaii protects: a lease term allowing eviction of a tenant with a valid medical cannabis certificate is void unless the lease also allows eviction for smoking tobacco and the cannabis is smoked (a condominium or planned community document banning medical cannabis use is the exception). If a federal housing program requires its own addendum, the program's conditions control over Hawaii's landlord-tenant code; federal law may also apply.

title: No Express Bar on Evicting DV Victims
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule that bars you from evicting, refusing to rent to, or treating differently a tenant or applicant because the person is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, and Hawaii's fair housing law does not list victim status among its protected classes. What Hawaii does give victims is a set of tenancy rights: a tenant may end a rental agreement of one year or less early, without fees or liability for future rent, after domestic violence against the tenant or an immediate family member living in the unit; a tenant who stays may require a lock change; and once a court orders the abuser to vacate, the abuser's interest in the tenancy ends and you need not admit the abuser without a police officer. If the abuser is also a party to the rental agreement and the victim ends it early, you may either keep the abuser on the agreement for future rent or end the abuser's interest by written notice at least five days in advance and evict if the abuser does not leave; you may also recover your actual damages from the abuser. Even without an express ban, the cautious course is not to end a victim's tenancy because of the abuser's conduct or because the police were called: act against the person who caused the problem, use the abuser-removal and lock-change routes, and check fair housing rules (for example, a policy that falls more heavily on women may raise sex-discrimination issues). The library's optional Criminal Activity clause excludes crimes of which a tenant or household member is the victim. Federal law may also apply, especially in federally assisted housing.

title: Domestic Violence Early Termination
bodyText: A tenant may end a rental agreement of a term of one year or less early, without any early-termination fee or penalty and without liability for future rent, if the tenant or an immediate family member living in the unit was a victim of domestic violence during the 90 days before the tenant gives you notice. The notice must be given at least 14 days before the early termination date it names, and that date may be no more than 104 days after the most recent act of domestic violence. With the notice the tenant must give you one of the documents the statute lists (a certified or exemplified restraining order, injunction or criminal-case document; documentation from a victim services organization or domestic violence program, shelter or safe house; or documentation from a medical professional, mental health provider, attorney, advocate, social worker or clergy member the victim sought help from) and a written statement that the tenant reasonably believes the abuser knows where the tenant or family member lives, unless the abuser lives in the same unit. If the tenant is the only tenant, the agreement ends on the early termination date; the tenant owes rent through that date and any earlier obligations, payable on or before that date. If there are other tenants, the agreement continues for them if they show, as you determine, that they can pay the rent; if they cannot, you may end it for them by notice at least 14 days before the date you name, without any penalty or fee. You may not charge any fee or penalty for using this right, and you may not disclose what the tenant tells you unless the tenant consents in a signed statement, it is required or relevant in a court case, or other law requires it. The tenant still owes rent and other amounts that were overdue before the termination. If the tenant knowingly gives a false notice or documents, you may recover three months' periodic rent or three times your actual damages, whichever is greater, plus costs and reasonable attorney's fees. Domestic violence means domestic abuse between family or household members: physical harm, bodily injury, assault or the threat of it, extreme psychological abuse, coercive control or malicious property damage. Family or household members include current and former spouses or reciprocal beneficiaries, people with a child in common, parents, children and other blood relatives, people who live or lived together in the unit, and people in a dating relationship, but not adults who were roommates only by an economic or contractual arrangement. Immediate family member is not defined; read it generously. Tenancy type: the right covers fixed terms of one year or less; it does not reach a fixed term longer than one year. A month-to-month tenancy has a term of one month, so treat it as covered. Deposit and prepaid-rent timing after an early termination is in the deposit rows; lock changes and abuser removal are in their own rows.

title: Documents for a DV Early Termination
bodyText: To use Hawaii's domestic violence early termination, the tenant's written notice must come with one of three kinds of documents: (1) certified or exemplified restraining orders, injunctions against harassment, or documents from criminal cases; (2) documentation from a victim services organization or a domestic violence program, agency or facility, including a shelter or safe house; or (3) documentation from a medical professional, mental health care provider, attorney, advocate, social worker or member of the clergy from whom the victim sought help with the domestic violence. The tenant must also give you a written statement that the tenant reasonably believes the abuser knows the address or location where the tenant or the family member lives, unless the abuser lives in the same unit. Any one of the three categories is enough; do not insist on a police report or a court order when another listed document is given, and do not ask for details beyond what the statute requires. Keep the documents confidential: you may disclose them only with the tenant's signed consent, when required or relevant in a court case, or when other law requires. If a tenant knowingly gives false documents, you may recover three months' periodic rent or three times your actual damages, whichever is greater, plus costs and reasonable attorney's fees. A request to change the locks under the domestic violence lock-change rule needs no documents, except that if the abuser is a party to the rental agreement you must have a copy of a court order requiring the abuser to vacate.

title: No Condemnation Rent Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule saying what happens to a residential lease, or to the rent, when the property is taken by eminent domain. Your lease and general law decide; a published case annotated in the code reports that a tenant of land partly condemned was entitled to a proportionate rent reduction, but it was not read. In a condemnation case the court may let tenants of the property appear as parties. If a state agency displaces a tenant by acquiring the property (or by code enforcement), the agency must pay the displaced tenant's reasonable moving expenses or optional fixed payments, and for projects using federal funds the State must give occupants at least 90 days' written notice before they must move and may charge an owner or tenant who stays on short-term only fair rental value. These are the agency's duties, not yours, except that after a code-enforcement displacement the agency may recover what it paid from whoever is responsible for the violation, with a lien on the property if a responsible owner does not pay within 60 days after written demand. Long-term residential land leases (15 years or more) are outside the landlord-tenant code and have their own leasehold-conversion rules. If you want the lease to end, or rent to abate, on a taking, say so in the lease; the library offers no condemnation clause.

title: Who May Represent an Entity Landlord
bodyText: If your rental is owned by a corporation or a limited liability company, plan on having a licensed Hawaii attorney file and handle a summary possession case. Hawaii law lets only licensed attorneys practice in its courts, except as the court rules provide, while letting a person who is a party appear for himself or herself; the District Court's summons form tells defendants that if the defendant is a corporation or a limited liability company, Hawaii law requires it to be represented by a licensed Hawaii attorney, and a case note in the code reports that a corporation generally cannot represent itself. Nothing in Hawaii's statutes gives an owner's member, officer or property manager a right to appear for an entity in district court. The one exception found is small claims, where, with the court's approval, any person may appear for another without pay; but in a small claims security deposit dispute, attorneys may not appear for either side. An individual owner may represent himself or herself. The District Court's own rules add that nothing in them lets a corporation appear as a party without counsel or be represented by someone not licensed to practice law in Hawaii, and the Hawaii Supreme Court's rules give no exception for an owner's member, officer or property manager. Treat a limited liability company the same way.

title: No Environmental-Event Termination Right
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes give neither you nor the tenant a right to end a lease because a sudden environmental or public health event, or a government order, makes occupancy impossible or unlawful. The related rules that do exist: a tenant whose unit is made partly or wholly unusable by fire or other casualty not caused by the tenant's or family's wilful fault may quit, or stay in the usable part and pay only its fair rental value; a tenant deprived of a substantial part of the bargain by a condition may end the agreement after written notice if you do not fix it within a week; and during a declared emergency in which Hawaii's emergency termination limits apply, a unit a county agency finds unfit for occupancy is one of the few grounds for ending a tenancy. A landlord right to end the lease after such an event is a contract term the statutes leave to the lease; the library's optional Fire or Casualty clause covers physical damage that makes the property uninhabitable. The library offers no separate environmental-event clause; if you want one for events that cause no physical damage (for example a government order closing the building), get advice and write it so that it never takes away the tenant's own statutory rights.

title: No Hardship Stay of Eviction
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no general power to delay an eviction because of the tenant's hardship. The stays that do exist are specific. In a nonpayment case the writ of possession must be stayed if the tenant, before the writ actually issues, pays the rent due with 8% yearly interest, the costs of the case and your expenses including a reasonable attorney's fee. The court rules govern other stays of a writ: ordinarily execution waits 10 days after a judgment, but a writ of possession is not stayed during those 10 days unless the court orders otherwise or the tenant obtains the statutory payment stay; the court may stay enforcement while a motion for a new trial or for relief from the judgment is pending, on conditions that protect you; and a tenant who appeals may get a stay by posting a supersedeas bond. The court's form motion to stay execution of a writ lists reasons such as not being served, missing the hearing for a medical emergency, not receiving a proper notice, or having proof of payment. If the tenant's dependents occupy the unit while the tenant serves on state active duty or full-time National Guard duty, no eviction may be made during the service except with leave of court, knowingly evicting otherwise is a misdemeanor, and the court may, and on application must (unless the tenant's ability to pay is not materially affected), stay the case for up to three months. Plan for these routes, and do not change locks or remove belongings yourself while a stay is sought.

title: How Summary Possession Works
bodyText: In Hawaii you recover possession only through a summary possession case in the district court of the circuit where the unit is located. After the required notice period ends, you file a complaint (the Judiciary has temporary forms: one for nonpayment-only cases under the mediation program through February 4, 2028, which must attach the mediation center's proof that it received your notice, and a general form for other cases, which asks you to attach the written rental agreement and the notice you gave). The complaint asks whether the tenant is on active military duty; answer it truthfully, because a court may not enter a default judgment against a servicemember without appointing an attorney, and a knowingly false statement is a crime. The tenant must appear or answer at the next court session at least five days after service in the same circuit (seven days if served in another circuit; ten days after posting and mailing if the tenant cannot be found in the State). In summary possession cases the tenant may answer orally at the first hearing, which counts as a general denial. If a tenant cannot be served in the State, the court may order service by leaving papers with an agent or employee on the premises, posting them conspicuously on the property and mailing them by certified or registered mail. You may join claims for rent, damages and waste arising from the unit, whatever the amount, and the court can hear the tenant's counterclaims about the premises regardless of amount. Either side may ask the court to order disputed rent paid into court while the case is pending. Rent you accept during the case does not recognize the tenancy, and if you win it counts as damages. If you prove your right to possession, you get a judgment for possession and costs, and a writ of possession issues to the sheriff, a deputy sheriff, a police officer or an independent civil process server on the State's list, who removes all persons and their belongings and puts you in possession; the writ cancels the rental agreement. A writ is not delayed by the usual 10-day wait after judgment unless the court orders otherwise, but in a nonpayment case the tenant can stop it by paying the rent, 8% yearly interest, costs and your expenses including a reasonable attorney's fee before it issues. The sheriff's fee for serving a writ of possession and removing a tenant is $40 plus necessary expenses. Never remove a tenant, change the locks or cut utilities yourself.

title: No Eviction Record Sealing Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes and the court rules searched contain no procedure for sealing or expunging summary possession or eviction records, whether the case was dismissed, settled or won by the tenant, and no rule letting you object to sealing. The District Court forms include a petitioner's motion to seal an address and telephone number, which is not a record-sealing procedure for eviction cases. The Judiciary's website lists a "Sealing Court Records" page and the court's public-access rules, which were not reviewed, may govern access to case records; check them before relying on an eviction record in screening. When you screen applicants with court records, apply your criteria the same way to everyone and follow fair housing law.

title: No Lease-Named Agent for Eviction Papers
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule letting the lease name a person to accept court papers for the tenant in a summary possession case, so do not rely on such a clause. Service follows the court rules: the summons and complaint are served on the tenant; if a defendant cannot be served in the circuit, service may be made anywhere in the State; and if a defendant cannot be served within the State, the court may order the papers left with an agent or employee of the tenant found on the premises or in the circuit, posted in a conspicuous place on the property, and mailed by certified or registered mail unless the address is unknown. The District Court's summons may not be personally delivered between 10:00 p.m. and 6:00 a.m. on premises not open to the public unless a judge allows it. The designation Hawaii does require runs the other way: before the tenancy begins you must tell the tenant in writing the name and address of each owner or person authorized to act for the owner for service of process and for receiving rents, notices and demands, and keep it current; the library's Owner and Manager Disclosure clause does this.

title: Faster Routes for Criminal Activity
bodyText: Hawaii has no special fast-track court process for evicting tenants for violent crime or drug activity; the same summary possession case applies. What shortens the timeline is the notice step. A lease rule against criminal activity is enforced with Hawaii's written rule-breach notice, and no time to fix is required when the breach causes or threatens to cause damage to any person, violates building and housing laws materially affecting health and safety, or is wilful damage to the premises; if the breach continues or recurs, file within 30 days. For a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy, if the tenant or the tenant's invitee or employee creates a nuisance as defined in Hawaii's nuisance-abatement law (places used for drug manufacture or distribution, prostitution, non-social gambling and similar offenses), you may deliver a 24-hour written warning to abate and then a written notice to vacate within five days, refunding rent paid in advance for the period after the tenant leaves. A tenant committing waste or a nuisance, or using the unit for an illegal purpose, cannot claim retaliation protection. Government officials, county residents and organizations, including tenant organizations, may also sue to abate a nuisance and bar the persons responsible from the property. The library's optional Criminal Activity clause and the nuisance rows give the details.

title: No Just-Cause Eviction Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no just-cause or good-cause eviction rule for private residential tenancies. A fixed-term lease ends on its end date by passage of time, and you need no reason not to renew; a tenant who stays on afterward without your consent is a holdover (you may sue for possession during the first 60 days; if you do not, a month-to-month tenancy at the old rent begins). A month-to-month tenancy may be ended without stating a reason by written notice at least 45 days before the termination date (at least 120 days if you plan to demolish the units, convert to a condominium or change the building's use to transient vacation rentals), and a tenancy shorter than month to month by notice at least 10 days ahead. Situational limits still apply. You may not end a tenancy in retaliation for a tenant's good-faith complaint to you or a government agency about health-law or landlord-tenant code violations, or a good-faith repair request, while the tenant keeps paying rent, unless a statutory exception applies (such as an earlier notice to end the periodic tenancy, your good-faith own or immediate family use, a good-faith substantial remodel or demolition, or a sale where the buyer makes that representation). A termination notice given to get around the written notice required for a rent increase is void. During a declared emergency in which Hawaii's emergency termination limits are invoked, you may end tenancies only for a material breach or unfitness, with 45-day exceptions for periodic tenancies on a sale or owner or family occupancy. You may not end a tenancy for a reason that violates fair housing or source-of-income law, a lease term allowing eviction of a certified medical cannabis patient is void (unless the lease bans smoking tobacco and the cannabis is smoked), and the court must stay a case against the dependents of a state military servicemember on request unless the tenant's ability to pay is unaffected. Federally subsidized housing may impose good-cause conditions, which control over the landlord-tenant code; federal law may also apply. County ordinances were not reviewed.

title: Tenants and Foreclosure
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not keep a residential lease alive after the landlord's mortgage is foreclosed, and do not require you or the lender to give tenants a special foreclosure notice. After a nonjudicial (power of sale) foreclosure sale, once the foreclosing lender records the required affidavit and the conveyance document, the purchaser is entitled to immediate and exclusive possession, and the mortgagor and anyone claiming through the mortgagor who stays in possession is treated as a tenant at sufferance subject to eviction; the purchaser may bring summary possession, ejectment or trespass, and the court awards the prevailing party its reasonable attorney's fees and costs. A tenant who rents from the owner is likely in that position, so tell tenants promptly if a foreclosure is pending. The same rule applies after a condominium association's nonjudicial foreclosure of its lien. A tenant can bid: in a power of sale foreclosure the public sale is not final for 15 days (up to 45 days if a qualified bidder gives notice of intent), and an eligible tenant buyer (a natural person living in the property as a primary residence under a rental agreement who is not the mortgagor or the mortgagor's child, spouse or parent) may submit a subsequent bid equal to or higher than the winning bid and become the buyer. If you own a condominium or planned-community unit and fall 30 or more days behind on association assessments, the board, after written notice to you by first-class and certified mail and under a policy the owners approved, may demand that your tenant pay rent to the association up to the amount you owe; the tenant's payment counts as rent paid to you, is a complete defense to your nonpayment case, any lease term to the contrary is void, and you may not retaliate against the tenant. In an association's lien foreclosure the plaintiff may have a receiver appointed to collect rent from the tenant. Federal law may also protect tenants after foreclosure.

title: Forfeiture and Relief From It
bodyText: In Hawaii a lease is ended for a tenant's breach through the landlord-tenant code's notices (for nonpayment, failure to maintain the unit, or breach of a rule) and then a summary possession case; the summary possession law covers a tenant who holds over after a tenancy ends by passage of time or by forfeiture under the lease's conditions or covenants. The rental agreement and the landlord-tenant relationship are cancelled only when a writ of possession issues. Until then, in a nonpayment case, the tenant can undo the forfeiture by paying the rent due, 8% yearly interest, the costs of the case and your expenses including a reasonable attorney's fee before the writ actually issues; the lease cannot take that right away, and the library's Default by Tenant clause preserves it (see the writ-stay row for details). Hawaii's statutes give no comparable payment right to cure non-rent breaches after the notice period has passed. Older case notes printed in the code report that equity may relieve a tenant from a forfeiture for nonpayment and that accepting rent with knowledge of a breach can waive the right to forfeit; those cases were not read, so do not accept rent after a breach notice without advice.

title: No Lease Guarantor Statute
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule on guarantors of residential leases: nothing limits a guarantor's liability to the original term, requires a guaranty to state a maximum amount or an end date, or sets special terms for a separate guaranty. General contract and suretyship law, which was not reviewed, governs. The District Court's general summary possession complaint form lets you name a personal guarantor under the rental agreement as a defendant. Practical steps: put the guaranty in writing, signed by the guarantor, on the lease or expressly referring to it; say plainly whether it covers renewals, extensions and any month-to-month continuation after the term, and any rent increases; and give the guarantor a copy. A deposit you take from a guarantor at the start of the tenancy is money received on behalf of the tenant, so keep the total within Hawaii's limit on what you may collect at move-in (the first month's rent plus a security deposit of up to one month's rent, plus any pet deposit allowed).

title: No Lease Waiver of Exemptions
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes neither authorize nor expressly forbid a tenant to waive, in a lease, the exemptions that protect a debtor's property from attachment and execution, and the library offers no waiver clause. Those exemptions include, for example, an interest in one parcel of real property up to $30,000 for a head of family or a person 65 or older ($20,000 for other persons); necessary household furnishings, appliances, books and clothing, plus up to $1,000 of jewelry; one motor vehicle up to $2,575 of equity; tools and equipment needed for the debtor's trade; and wages for services in the 31 days before the proceeding. Some benefits are protected by statutes that void any waiver. A lease clause by which the tenant authorizes anyone to confess judgment on a claim under the rental agreement is void, and the landlord-tenant code gives you no lien on the tenant's belongings. Because a waiver's validity is not settled by statute and courts were not searched, collect a judgment through the ordinary execution and garnishment process and leave the exemptions to the court.

title: No Illness or Care-Move Exit Right
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes give a tenant no right to end a lease early because of illness, disability, age, or a move to a nursing home, assisted living or other care facility. The early-exit rights Hawaii does give are for domestic violence, qualifying military orders, the tenant's death (the tenancy ends 15 days after notice to the tenant's representative or estate, or when paid-up rent runs out, if later), your failure to deliver or maintain the unit, and fire or casualty. A month-to-month tenant may always leave on 28 days' written notice. If a tenant with a disability asks to be let out of a fixed-term lease, or for another change in a rule or policy, treat it as a request for a reasonable accommodation under fair housing law and consider it in good faith. If you want to offer an early-exit option, the library's optional early-termination clause can be used.

title: No Landlord's Lien on Tenant Property
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes give a private residential landlord no lien on a tenant's belongings for unpaid rent and no right to seize or hold them. Hawaii's commercial code states that its secured-transactions article does not apply to a landlord's lien, the old hotel-keeper lien sections have been repealed, and the only statutory rent lien on tenants' personal property belongs to the State's public housing authority in its own low-income projects, which are outside the landlord-tenant code. Do not take or keep a tenant's property to force payment: removing or excluding a tenant without a court order exposes you to two months' rent (or two months' free occupancy) plus costs and attorney's fees, and seizing or holding the belongings of a servicemember who has lawfully ended a lease, to collect later rent, is a crime. A lease clause in which the tenant authorizes anyone to confess judgment is void. Property left behind after the tenant has gone is handled under the abandoned-property procedure, and you may deduct accrued rent from sale proceeds there. Collect unpaid rent through the deposit, a court judgment and ordinary execution.

title: Your Remedies When the Tenancy Ends
bodyText: When a tenancy ends, by notice, breach or expiration, your remedies are these. Possession: a summary possession case in district court, in which you may also claim rent, damages and waste arising from the unit, whatever the amount, and rent and damages up to the date of judgment; the writ of possession cancels the rental agreement. Rent alone: you may sue only for rent at any time after demanding past-due rent and telling the tenant you intend to sue. Damage: you may sue for waste or breach of contract for damage caused by the tenant's wilful or negligent failure to meet the tenant's statutory duties. Abandonment: the lesser of the remaining rent or the re-rental measure (see the abandonment row). Holdover: up to twice the monthly rent, prorated daily, if the tenant stays without your consent, with summary possession available in the first 60 days. Ending the tenancy does not end either side's obligations until all obligations under the rental agreement and the code are discharged, so you still owe the deposit accounting within 14 days and the tenant still owes unpaid rent and damages. Rent you accept while an eviction case is pending does not recognize the tenancy and, if you win, counts as damages. Disputes over rent can be resolved by an order to pay disputed rent into court.

title: Fixing Tenant Damage and Billing It as Rent
bodyText: If a tenant is materially failing to meet the tenant's statutory upkeep duties (keeping the unit clean and safe, disposing of rubbish, keeping plumbing clean, using fixtures and appliances properly, not damaging the premises, keeping landlord-supplied items in fit condition), give written notice describing the problem and allowing at least 10 days after the tenant receives it to fix it. If the tenant does not, and the problem can be remedied by cleaning, repairing, replacing a damaged item or the like, you may do the work and bill the tenant the actual and reasonable cost. The bill is treated by both of you as rent, due on the next regular rent date, or immediately when the tenant receives it if the tenancy has ended. No time to fix is needed when the problem causes or threatens irremediable damage to any person or property. If you cannot serve the notice, you may post it conspicuously on the unit. You still need the tenant's consent and two days' notice to enter to do the work, except in an emergency or where notice is impracticable. Keep invoices: the cost must be actual and reasonable. Ending the tenancy over these problems is allowed only for material noncompliance with building and housing laws materially affecting health and safety; for everything else, self-help repair and billing (or a damage claim) is the remedy. Because the bill is treated as rent, treat any late charge on it with care: the late charge cap is 8% of the rent due and applies only if the lease provides for a late charge. The library's Default by Tenant clause contains this right.

title: No Liquidated Damages Statute
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes neither authorize nor regulate liquidated-damages terms in residential leases. The landlord-tenant code fixes several measures itself, which a lease cannot raise: damages for abandonment are capped at the lesser of the remaining rent or the re-rental measure; a tenant who backs out before moving in owes at most the lesser of the deposits, one month's rent, or the re-rental measure; the holdover charge may not exceed twice the monthly rent, prorated daily; a late charge may not exceed 8% of the rent due; and the domestic violence and servicemember exits allow no fee or penalty. A court may refuse to enforce, or may limit, an unconscionable term. An agreed early-termination fee that the tenant chooses in exchange for being released (the library's optional early-termination clause) is different from a penalty for breach, but any fixed sum for breach is open to challenge; whether a court would enforce one is a question of case law, which was not searched. The library offers no liquidated-damages clause.

title: No Lockouts for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: Hawaii does not allow a lockout for unpaid rent, and a lease cannot authorize one. If you remove or exclude a tenant from the unit overnight without a court order, the tenant may recover possession or end the rental agreement and, either way, recover two months' rent or two months of free occupancy, plus the cost of suit and reasonable attorney's fees; the court may also order other relief. The statute speaks of removal "without cause or without court order", but you also have no right to enter except with notice for the listed purposes, by court order, when the tenant appears to have abandoned the unit, or during an extended absence, and recovering possession by cutting water, electricity, gas or another essential service is an unfair or deceptive practice with minimum damages of three times the monthly rent or $1,000; so treat any lockout as unlawful. Tenants cannot waive these rights in the lease. To recover possession for unpaid rent, give the 10-calendar-day nonpayment notice (until February 4, 2028 it must also carry the statutory contents and go to a mediation center, and filing may have to wait 20 days if mediation is scheduled) and file a summary possession case; the writ is executed by a sheriff, police officer or authorized civil process server.

title: No Rule on Minors in Eviction Cases
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no rule on naming minors as defendants in a summary possession case, and no rule barring a minor tenant from being sued. Name as defendants the adults who signed the rental agreement or otherwise hold the tenancy. The writ of possession removes the defendant and all persons holding under or through the defendant, which includes the tenant's children, so you do not need to name them. Hawaii's screening-fee rule already treats minors differently: you may charge an application screening fee only for an applicant who is 18 or older or an emancipated minor. If a minor is the only tenant, get advice on capacity to contract before renting or suing.

title: Nonpayment Notice and Mediation
bodyText: Before you sue for possession for unpaid rent, you must give the tenant a written notice demanding the rent and stating that the rental agreement will be terminated unless the rent is paid within the time stated, which must be at least 10 calendar days after the tenant receives the notice. You may post the notice in a conspicuous place on the unit (it is received on the date of posting) or mail it by U.S. mail, properly addressed and stamped (it is received two business days after the postmark, unless it comes back undeliverable). The 10-calendar-day period took effect on February 5, 2026 (before then it was five business days) and stays in place after February 4, 2028. From February 5, 2026 until February 4, 2028 (a two-year mediation pilot that ends then unless the Legislature extends it), the notice must also contain: your name and contact information (if possible your phone number, email and mailing address); the address of the unit; the name and contact information of every tenant on the rental agreement; the current rent due as of the notice date after applying all rent paid from all sources; a statement that a copy is being given to a state-funded mediation center, which will contact both of you to schedule mediation on the unpaid rent; a statement that you may file for possession if the rent is not paid and mediation is not scheduled within 10 calendar days after the tenant receives the notice; a statement that you will take part in mediation if it is scheduled; and a bold-type warning substantially in the statute's words. You must give a copy of the notice to a state-funded mediation center that offers free landlord-tenant mediation. The Judiciary's "Ten Calendar Day Notice of Termination for Failure to Pay Rent" form, adopted for use through February 4, 2028, contains every required item; the version attached to the court's order names The Mediation Center of the Pacific, and courts may insert local contact information, so use the version for your circuit. If mediation is scheduled within the 10 days, you may not file until 20 calendar days after the tenant received the notice, unless the tenant fails to appear or cancels; you must take part if the tenant schedules it, and mediation (in person or remote) is to take place within 30 days after the center reaches both of you. The statute ties the 20-day wait to mediation the center schedules and the tenant takes part in, while the bold warning and the court's form tie it to mediation being scheduled, so wait the full 20 days whenever mediation is scheduled within the 10 days unless the tenant has cancelled or failed to appear. Your nonpayment complaint must include the center's document verifying that you sent it the notice (or your affirmation of how you sent it) and, if mediation is scheduled but has not happened, its date; the court's nonpayment complaint form asks for both. Each side bears its own mediation costs and fees, except that you may ask for all of them if the tenant defaults on a mediated agreement or fails to attend. If mediation produces no agreement, you may file after the 20 days without another mediation (the court may order one for good cause). The court may let you cure an unintentional or immaterial defect in the notice without dismissing the case. No notice is needed if you sue for breach of a mediated or other settlement agreement. You may sue for rent alone at any time after demanding it and telling the tenant you intend to sue. After February 4, 2028, the required contents, the copy to the mediation center, the mediation duties and the 20-day wait end unless extended, and the 10-calendar-day notice with the posting and mailing receipt rules remains; check the statute before relying on either regime. These rules apply to every tenancy under the landlord-tenant code, fixed term or periodic: the older five-day notice for month-to-month nonpayment in the summary possession chapter gives way to the code. Put only rent in the amount due; show late fees and other charges separately, as the court's complaint form does, and remember the late charge cap of 8% of the rent due. Get advice before accepting a partial payment during the notice period and then filing. A separate wildfire mediation statute (15-day notice) applied only after the final wildfire eviction moratorium and is repealed no later than December 31, 2026.

title: No Notice Fee Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes neither authorize nor forbid charging a tenant a fee for preparing or serving a nonpayment, rule-breach or termination notice, and the library offers no notice-fee clause.
