The statutes do limit related charges: a lease may shift attorney's fees only within the code's narrow permissions (on unpaid rent, up to 25% of it after referral to an outside attorney; otherwise only prevailing-party fees), and any other fee term is unenforceable; a late charge, if the lease provides one, may not exceed 8% of the rent due; mediation costs under the 2026-2028 nonpayment mediation program can be shifted to the tenant only if the tenant defaults on a mediated agreement or fails to attend; and a tenant who stops a nonpayment case by paying before the writ issues must pay the costs and charges of the proceedings and your expenses. A notice fee could be attacked as an unlawful collection cost or a disguised late charge, so recover your costs through those routes instead.

title: Notices Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: A Hawaii lease cannot waive or shorten the notices the landlord-tenant code requires before you end a tenancy or sue for possession: the 10-calendar-day nonpayment notice (with the mediation contents through February 4, 2028), the notice giving at least 10 days to fix a failure to maintain the unit, the rule-breach notice in the statutory form giving at least 10 days, and the termination notices for periodic tenancies (45 days from you for month to month, 10 days for shorter tenancies, 120 days for demolition, condominium conversion or a change to transient vacation rentals). Tenants and landlords may not waive or agree to give up rights or remedies under the code except where the code itself allows. The code itself dispenses with a notice or cure period in a few cases: no time to fix is required when the tenant's breach or noncompliance causes or threatens damage to persons (and, for maintenance, irremediable damage to property), and no nonpayment notice is needed to sue on a broken mediated or settlement agreement. A dispute claimed in good faith may be settled by agreement, but a settlement in which a tenant gives up statutory rights is invalid if a court finds it unconscionable when made. A tenant's notice to you may be longer than the statutory minimum only if the tenant chooses; a month-to-month tenant may always leave on 28 days' written notice.

title: Nuisance: Owner Exposure and Association Suits
bodyText: Beyond your own remedies against a tenant who creates a nuisance (the rule-breach notice with no cure period where persons are threatened, and the 24-hour warning and five-day notice to vacate for periodic tenancies), Hawaii's nuisance law can reach you as owner. Any building or place used for drug manufacture or distribution, prostitution, non-social gambling, certain fireworks offenses or (until the hemp chapter's scheduled repeal on July 1, 2027) unregistered hemp-product distribution or retailing, or occupied unlawfully by people with no title, lease or other legal claim, is a nuisance. The Attorney General or county prosecutor, any resident of the county, or any organization, including a tenant organization, may sue to abate it and to enjoin the persons causing or permitting it and the owner, lessee or agent from causing, maintaining or permitting it. The court may bar the responsible persons from entering or living in the property and, if that will not end the nuisance, close the property for up to a year; it may also suspend licenses. When a court considers contempt against an owner, it must give appropriate weight to the owner's notice to the lessee that the lease will be revoked if the nuisance continues and other steps taken to end it, so act promptly and in writing. Two more rules matter. In a condominium, the association may itself bring a summary possession case against a tenant who repeatedly violates the governing documents or other occupants' right to quiet enjoyment if you refuse to act; you are named as an additional defendant. And a tenant who is committing waste or a nuisance, or using the unit for an illegal purpose, cannot defeat your possession case by claiming retaliation. Hawaii's statutes create no rent receivership for nuisance properties. See the illegal-use and criminal-activity rows for the notice steps.

title: No Statutory Owner Move-In Right
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes give you no right to end a fixed-term lease early because you or a family member want to move in. For a month-to-month tenancy you need no reason: written notice at least 45 days before the termination date is enough. The owner-use rules that do exist are narrow: a good-faith recovery of the unit for immediate use as your own home or your immediate family's is an exception to the bar on retaliatory evictions, and during a declared emergency in which Hawaii's emergency termination limits are invoked, a periodic tenancy may be ended on 45 days' written notice if you or an immediate family member will occupy the unit (fixed terms cannot be cut short then). If you want the option to end a fixed term early for owner or family occupancy, the lease must reserve it; the library's optional Owner or Family Occupancy clause does so, with a notice period you choose of at least 45 days, a good-faith requirement, and a bar on using it while emergency termination limits apply. A tenant who leaves early under it owes only prorated rent.

title: No End-of-Term Possession Bond
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no bond a tenant can give to guarantee delivering possession at the end of the term, and no possession bond you must post before a writ of possession issues. A lease term by which the tenant authorizes anyone to confess judgment on a claim under the rental agreement is void, so a bond enforced by a confessed judgment is not available. The bonds that appear in Hawaii's procedure are different: a party who appeals a possession judgment may obtain a stay by posting a supersedeas bond approved by the court, and a court may require a plaintiff to post a bond before a default judgment against a defendant in state military service. If a tenant stays after the term without your consent, use the holdover charge and summary possession instead.

title: Belongings Left After a Writ
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes set no special procedure for a tenant's belongings or animals left in the unit after a writ of possession is executed. The writ itself commands the officer to remove the defendant and everyone holding through the defendant, including all personal belongings and properties, and to put you in possession; the officer who executes it may be a sheriff, deputy sheriff, police officer or an independent civil process server on the State's list, and the fee for serving the writ and removing the tenant is $40 plus necessary expenses. The abandoned-property procedure expressly covers a tenant who wrongfully quits or who leaves under a notice to quit or at the end of the term; it does not say whether it reaches property left after a writ. The cautious course is to follow it for anything of value that remains: mail notice to the tenant's forwarding address (or the address the tenant designated, or the last known address) describing the property, where it is and that you intend to sell or donate it; wait 15 days after mailing; sell in a commercially reasonable way after advertising for three consecutive days in a daily newspaper of general circulation in the circuit, store at the tenant's expense, or donate to a charity; and hold the sale proceeds, less accrued rent and storage and sale costs, in trust for the tenant for 30 days. Items of no value may be thrown away. No statute addresses animals left behind; contact the county animal control agency rather than keeping or releasing them. After the writ, a former tenant who knowingly re-enters or remains in the dwelling without your permission may be committing criminal trespass; call the police rather than removing the person yourself.

title: Paying to Stop a Nonpayment Eviction
bodyText: In a summary possession case for unpaid rent, the tenant has a statutory right to stop the eviction by paying before the writ of possession actually issues. To stop it, the tenant (or whoever owes the rent) must pay: the rent due; interest on it at 8% a year; all costs and charges of the proceedings; and all expenses you incurred, including a reasonable fee for your attorney. If that is paid in time, the court must stay the writ, and the court rules expressly preserve this right. The right lasts until the writ issues, not just until the notice period ends, and a lease cannot take it away; the library's Default by Tenant clause preserves it without stating a cap. It applies only to nonpayment cases, not to evictions for other breaches or for holding over after a termination notice. Rent you accept while the case is pending does not recognize the tenancy, and if you win it counts as damages for the period of occupancy. Hawaii's statutes contain no rule requiring special wording when you accept partial rent, and no limit on how often a tenant may redeem; the statute speaks of payment by the person owing the rent and does not address payment by others on that person's behalf, so accept a payment from a charity or agency on the tenant's behalf if it covers the full amount. Under the 2026-2028 nonpayment mediation program, the mediation-cost rule is separate: mediation costs are recoverable only if the tenant defaults on a mediated agreement or fails to attend.

title: Disputed Rent Paid Into Court
bodyText: In any court case where payment or nonpayment of rent is in dispute, either you or the tenant may ask the court to order the tenant to deposit the disputed rent into court as it comes due (and, if a rent increase is in dispute, the rent before the increase). The court must grant the request unless the tenant shows the rent has already been paid to you, or the two of you signed a written instrument agreeing that rent could be withheld or deducted. Depositing does not cost the tenant any defense. If the tenant cannot make the ordered deposits, you are entitled to judgment for possession and a writ issues. The court pays the money to you if it finds the rent was due and the tenant had no basis to withhold it, or to the tenant if the rent was not due, was paid, or could lawfully be withheld or set off; a party who raised the rent issue in bad faith must pay the other side reasonable interest on the deposits. In a summary possession case the district court can hear the tenant's counterclaims that arise out of and refer to the premises, whatever their amount, and a published case annotated in the code reports that a tenant may raise the landlord's breach of the implied warranty of habitability as a defense to nonpayment (not read). Hawaii's statutes do not require the tenant to pay rent into court before raising other defenses, and the court rules make no counterclaim compulsory in district court. Use the rent deposit request early in any case where the tenant is withholding rent.

title: No Uneconomic-Repair Termination
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes give neither you nor the tenant a right to end a lease because a needed repair would cost too much compared with the rent or the property's value. Your duty to keep the unit fit and in repair stays in place whatever the cost. Your options are the ordinary ones: a fixed-term lease ends on its date; a month-to-month tenancy may be ended on 45 days' written notice (120 days if you plan to demolish the units, convert to a condominium or change to transient vacation rentals); and a good-faith plan to substantially alter, remodel or demolish the premises is an exception to Hawaii's bar on retaliatory evictions. If a fire or other casualty makes the unit unusable, the tenant's casualty rights apply, and the library's optional Fire or Casualty clause lets you end the lease if the damage cannot be repaired within a period you choose. The tenant's own repair-and-deduct remedy is capped at $1,000 or one month's rent, whichever is greater, per repair, and three months' rent in any six months, but those caps limit only what the tenant may deduct, not your duty to repair.

title: Retaliation Is Prohibited
bodyText: As long as the tenant keeps tendering the usual rent (or tendering receipts for rent lawfully withheld), you may not sue for possession, otherwise force the tenant out, demand a rent increase, or reduce services the tenant has been getting, after: the tenant has complained in good faith to the Department of Health, to you, to the building department, to the Office of Consumer Protection or to any other government agency concerned with landlord-tenant disputes about conditions in or affecting the unit that violate a health law or regulation or the landlord-tenant code; the Department of Health or another agency has filed a notice or complaint of such a violation; or the tenant has in good faith requested repairs under the code's repair or termination remedies. This applies even if there is no written rental agreement or it has expired. You may still recover possession if: the tenant is committing waste or a nuisance, or using the unit for an illegal purpose or for other than living in it in violation of the rental agreement; you want the unit in good faith for immediate use as your own home or your immediate family's; you want in good faith to substantially alter, remodel or demolish the premises; the complaint concerns only a condition caused by the lack of ordinary care of the tenant, someone in the tenant's household, or someone on the premises with the tenant's consent; the Department of Health has certified that the unit and related facilities complied with health laws on the date of the complaint; you have in good faith contracted to sell and the buyer represents an intent to occupy or remodel; or you are relying on a notice ending a periodic tenancy that was given before the complaint. You may still raise the rent if the Department of Health certified compliance; your property taxes or other operating costs rose substantially at least four months before the increase (and the increase is no more than the prorated net cost increase); you completed a capital improvement (within its straight-line depreciation, prorated among benefited units); the complaint concerned only a tenant-caused condition; or the new rent is no more than other similar units in the building (or market value for a single-family home). A tenant removed in violation of this rule may recover damages, costs and reasonable attorney's fees. The statute sets no time window and no presumption, so document the legitimate reason for any notice or increase that follows a complaint. Tenants may not waive this protection in the lease.

title: No Seasonal Tenancy Rules
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes have no special rules for seasonal tenancies. A rental for a season to someone who lives in the unit is an ordinary tenancy under the landlord-tenant code, with the usual deposit, notice, habitability and eviction rules; a written lease may set any term, so a seasonal lease simply ends on its end date, and a tenant who stays on without your consent is a holdover. The code does not apply to transient occupancy on a day-to-day basis in a hotel or motel. Transient vacation rentals (stays of less than 30 days to visitors) are regulated mainly by the counties, which may phase out transient accommodations in residential zones, and are subject to transient accommodations tax; if you convert a building with month-to-month tenants to transient vacation rentals you must give those tenants at least 120 days' written notice. County short-term rental ordinances were not reviewed.

title: No Self-Help Evictions
bodyText: In Hawaii you may recover possession of a rented home only through a court order. Self-help is barred in several ways. If you remove or exclude a tenant from the unit overnight without cause or without a court order, the tenant may recover possession or end the rental agreement and, either way, recover two months' rent or two months of free occupancy plus costs and reasonable attorney's fees, and the court may grant other relief; if the agreement ends you must return the deposit under the normal 14-day rule. You may not recover or take possession by wilfully cutting off or reducing running water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service, except on abandonment or surrender; doing so is an unfair or deceptive practice with minimum damages of three times the monthly rent or $1,000, whichever is greater, plus civil penalties. You have no right to enter except with notice for inspection, repairs, agreed services or showings, in an emergency, by court order, when the tenant appears to have abandoned the unit, or during an extended absence for inspection, maintenance and safekeeping; repeated unreasonable entry lets the tenant end the agreement and seek an injunction and a fine. A tenant cannot waive these protections. Removing or holding a servicemember's belongings after a lawful lease termination to collect later rent is a crime. The legal route is the statutory notice, a summary possession case, and a writ executed by a sheriff, deputy sheriff, police officer or authorized civil process server. The rules apply to every tenancy under the code; the code does not apply to day-to-day hotel or motel stays and the other excluded arrangements.

title: Servicemember Lease Rights
bodyText: Hawaii gives servicemember tenants two sets of rights. Under the landlord-tenant code, a servicemember tenant (an active duty member of the regular or reserve armed forces, the Coast Guard or the Hawaii National Guard on ordered federal duty for 90 days or more, who is a party to the rental agreement) may end a rental agreement of a term of one year or less, without early-termination fees or penalties or liability for future rent, on receiving military orders to leave civilian housing and move into on-post government quarters, if not moving would forfeit the housing allowance, the commanding officer denied a request to keep the allowance, and the tenant gives at least 30 days' written notice. A month-to-month servicemember tenant with such orders may end the tenancy on at least 15 days' written notice (the commanding-officer denial condition is not repeated for month to month). The notice must come with a copy of the orders or the commanding officer's signed verification, plus the commanding officer's written proof that the housing-allowance request was denied. If a servicemember tenant dies on active duty, an adult family member may end a one-year-or-less or month-to-month agreement on 15 days' written notice with the death certificate and proof of active duty. The tenant owes rent through the termination date and any earlier unpaid amounts, but you may charge no fee or penalty. If there are other tenants, the agreement continues for those who can show they can pay; if they cannot, you may end it for them on at least 30 days' notice without fees. These rights do not apply if the orders result from discipline or a court order. Separately, Hawaii's military civil relief law protects people on state active duty or full-time National Guard duty: you may not evict the dependents of such a person from a home they occupy except with leave of court, and on application the court must stay the case for up to three months unless the tenant's ability to pay is not materially affected (knowingly evicting otherwise is a misdemeanor); such a person who entered service after signing a lease may end it by written notice, effective 30 days after the next rent due date for a monthly lease (otherwise on the last day of the following month, with rent prorated and rent paid in advance refunded), and you may ask the court before the termination date to modify or restrict that relief; and seizing or holding the person's belongings to collect rent after a lawful termination is a misdemeanor. Before taking a default judgment you must tell the court truthfully whether the tenant is in military service; the court's complaint forms ask. The federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act may also apply. Deposit refunds after these terminations are covered in the deposit rows.

title: No Late-Benefit Eviction Defense
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no eviction defense, continuance or stay for a tenant whose Social Security, public assistance, voucher or other benefit payment is late, and no rule reinstating a tenancy when a late government payment arrives. The closest rules are different: a public assistance recipient whose lease makes rent due within three days after the check usually arrives may move the due date once by a prorated payment (see the rent payment row); a tenant can stop a nonpayment eviction by paying all rent due with 8% interest, costs and your expenses including a reasonable attorney's fee before the writ issues, from any source; under the 2026-2028 mediation program the nonpayment notice must state the rent due after applying all rent paid from all sources; and refusing or imposing different conditions on a tenant because the tenant takes part in a Section 8 voucher or permanent supportive housing program is unlawful source-of-income discrimination unless an exemption applies (for example, owners of no more than four units in the State). If you know a payment is delayed, consider waiting or agreeing a payment plan before filing.

title: Tenants' Statutory Early Exits
bodyText: Hawaii's landlord-tenant code gives tenants these statutory ways to end a tenancy early, and a lease cannot take them away. (1) You fail to deliver possession at the start of the term: the tenant may terminate at any time while unable to move in, owes no rent for that time, and may recover substitute-housing costs. (2) First week: if you do not conform to the rental agreement or are materially failing your fitness duties, the tenant may terminate on notice during the first week of occupancy, and later while staying on in reliance on your promise to fix. (3) Any time: if a condition deprives the tenant of a substantial part of the benefit of the bargain, the tenant may give written notice and terminate if you do not remedy it within one week (no notice if the unit is uninhabitable or there is an imminent threat to health or safety), unless the tenant's side caused it. (4) Unlawful removal or exclusion: the tenant may terminate and recover two months' rent or free occupancy plus fees. (5) Fire or other casualty not caused by the wilful fault of the tenant or family: the tenant may quit at once and tell you within a week. (6) Repeated unreasonable entry or an unreasonable entry without consent. (7) Domestic violence, for agreements of one year or less. (8) Qualifying military orders (and the death of a servicemember on active duty), and state military service under the military civil relief law. (9) A month-to-month tenant may leave on 28 days' written notice, and earlier, with prorated rent, within the last 45 days of your own termination notice (or within the 120-day period of a conversion or demolition notice). (10) If the only tenant dies, the tenancy ends 15 days after notice to the representative or estate, or when paid-up rent runs out, if later. When a tenant terminates under (2), (3) or (5) you must return advance rent for the remaining days and any deposit you may not keep within 14 days; mailing by certified mail, return receipt requested, postmarked by the 14th day, complies. Hawaii has no separate statute letting a tenant terminate for your fraudulent misrepresentation, although general fraud and misrepresentation law supplements the code, and no rule forfeiting money for an omitted lease statement.

title: Oral and Indefinite Tenancies
bodyText: Hawaii's landlord-tenant code does not use the term tenancy at will. If there is no written agreement on the term, the tenancy is month to month (week to week for boarders), and an oral lease for up to one year is valid as if written. A month-to-month tenancy ends on your written notice at least 45 days ahead (the tenant may leave earlier within those 45 days with prorated rent) or the tenant's written notice at least 28 days ahead (rent is owed through the 28th day); a tenancy shorter than month to month ends on at least 10 days' notice by either side. The older summary possession chapter speaks of a notice to quit of at least ten days for a tenant by parol (oral agreement) and of 25 days' notice before the end of a month for periodic tenancies; where those conflict with the code, the code's periods control, so use 45 days for an oral month-to-month tenancy. Two other statuses matter: a person who stays after a foreclosure sale is a tenant at sufferance subject to eviction; and a case note in the code reports that a roommate's licensee with no fixed term, whose license was revocable at will, became a trespasser needing no notice to vacate once the licensor's interest ended (not read). Anyone who occupies a unit for dwelling purposes under a rental agreement, written or oral, is a tenant entitled to the code's notices and court process, so do not treat a paying occupant as a mere guest.

title: No Tenant Bankruptcy Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes have no rule of their own on what happens to a tenancy, a security deposit or an eviction when a tenant files for bankruptcy; the landlord-tenant code says only that general principles of law, including bankruptcy, supplement it. Federal bankruptcy law, including the automatic stay, governs what you may do after a tenant files and was outside the searched sources, so get advice before you serve a notice, file or continue a summary possession case, or apply the deposit against prebankruptcy rent once you learn of a filing. If you are the one in financial trouble, note the reverse rule: a tenant's claim to the security deposit comes before the claims of your creditors, including a trustee in bankruptcy, even if deposits are commingled. Federal law may also apply.

title: When a Tenant Dies
bodyText: Hawaii has a set procedure for when a tenant dies. A tenant may designate, in the rental agreement or a separate written instrument, a representative (name and contact information, including a mailing address) authorized to collect or dispose of the tenant's personal property if the tenant dies during the tenancy; the library's optional Representative If Tenant Dies clause does this. When the tenant dies, or all tenants if there is more than one, you must contact the representative by registered mail and by any other contact information the tenant gave you. If there is no written designation, send the notice to the deceased tenant's estate at the unit's address; a person who then gives you a court order showing authority to act for the deceased tenant is the representative; and if no designated or estate representative comes forward, a family member who comes forward (related by blood, marriage, reciprocal beneficiary relationship, civil union, adoption or legal guardianship) is treated as the representative. The notice must state: the deceased tenant's name, the unit address, and that the representative, if any, was identified by the tenant; the approximate date of death; the monthly rent and the date through which rent has been paid; that the tenancy will end 15 calendar days after the notice is mailed or personally delivered, or on the date through which rent has been paid, whichever is later; and that after the tenancy ends you may dispose of remaining property of value by selling it in a commercially reasonable manner, storing it at the estate's expense, or donating it to a charitable organization. If the representative contacts you within 15 calendar days of the mailing or delivery, you must give access to the unit solely so the representative can remove the property in a reasonable manner, and the representative must then surrender the unit; this does not make the representative your tenant. The tenancy ends 15 calendar days after the notice is mailed or personally delivered, or on the paid-through date, whichever is later. You may then dispose of remaining property you determine in good faith to be of value by sale, storage at the estate's expense or donation, at your discretion and without liability if you have followed the procedure; sale proceeds, after accrued rent and the costs of storage, advertising and sale, are held in trust for the representative for 30 calendar days and then belong to you. Trash, perishable food and other items of no value may be disposed of immediately, without notice and without liability. Within 14 calendar days after the tenancy ends, or 14 calendar days after the representative removes the property, account for the security deposit under the normal deposit rules and pay any balance to the representative or the estate. If you comply, you have no further duty or liability to the representative or the estate after the tenancy expires. You need not tell prospective tenants about a tenant's death, or a history of deaths, in the unit. The procedure applies to every tenancy covered by the code, fixed term or periodic; it does not apply while any co-tenant is living.

title: Notice Periods to End a Tenancy
bodyText: Hawaii sets these notice periods for ending a tenancy without a default. Month to month: you must give written notice at least 45 days before the termination date; after your notice, the tenant may move out earlier within the last 45 days before that date by telling you the move-out date, and owes only prorated rent for the time occupied. The tenant may end a month-to-month tenancy by written notice at least 28 days ahead and owes rent through the 28th day. Before ending a month-to-month tenancy because you plan to demolish the units, convert to a condominium or change the building to transient vacation rentals, you must give written notice at least 120 days ahead (restarting if the notice is revoked or amended and reissued), and the tenant may leave earlier within that period with prorated rent. Shorter than month to month (for example week to week, which is the default for boarders): either side may end it by notice at least 10 days ahead. A fixed term ends on its end date without notice. The termination date need not fall at the end of a rental period. A termination notice given to get around the written notice required for a rent increase (45 consecutive days for month to month, 15 for shorter tenancies) is void, and a notice given in retaliation for a good-faith complaint or repair request is barred unless an exception applies (an earlier periodic-tenancy notice is one). The summary possession chapter's 25-day rule gives way to these periods. If a tenant stays after the termination date without your consent, you may charge up to twice the monthly rent, prorated daily, and sue within 60 days; if you do not sue within 60 days, a month-to-month tenancy at the old rent begins. During a declared emergency that invokes Hawaii's emergency termination limits, you may end periodic tenancies only for breach, unfitness, a sale to a good-faith buyer or owner or family occupancy (the last two on 45 days' notice). The library's month-to-month notice clause states these periods for the lease.

title: Removing Unauthorized Occupants
bodyText: Hawaii has no special fast procedure for removing squatters or other unauthorized occupants outside the courts, and no sheriff or police removal on your sworn complaint. The tools are these. Criminal trespass: a person who knowingly enters or remains unlawfully in a dwelling (that is, without being licensed, invited or otherwise privileged) commits criminal trespass in the first degree, a misdemeanor, so you may ask the police to act against a true intruder. Court process: summary possession or ejectment in the district court, and for unlawful occupation by people with no title, lease or other legal claim, a civil nuisance-abatement suit (which a county resident or organization may also bring) for an order barring them from the property. Be careful about who is a squatter. Anyone who occupies a unit as a dwelling under a rental agreement, written or oral, is a tenant entitled to the code's notices and a court order, and an oral lease for up to a year is valid; if you or your tenant accepted rent or let the person move in as a household member, use the eviction process. Removing or locking out a tenant without a court order costs two months' rent or free occupancy plus fees. A guest whom your tenant still welcomes is your tenant's responsibility under the lease; enforce occupancy limits against the tenant with a rule-breach notice. A case note in the code reports that a roommate's licensee with no fixed term became a trespasser needing no notice once the licensor's interest ended (not read).

title: Accepting Rent After a Notice
bodyText: Once you have started a summary possession or ejectment case, accepting rent during the case is not recognition of the tenancy and does not prejudice your rights as they stood when you filed; if you win, the rent counts as damages for the tenant's continued occupancy. Hawaii's statutes say nothing about accepting rent before you file, for example during a notice period or after a breach notice. Older case notes printed in the code report that accepting rent with knowledge of a breach can waive the right to end the lease for that breach (for a continuing breach, only up to the time of acceptance), but those cases predate the landlord-tenant code and were not read; and a case note under the nonpayment section reports a summary possession claim failing where the landlord deposited a payment before the notice period expired (not read). Two statutes turn on acceptance or consent: a holdover charge applies only while the tenant stays without your consent, and if you neither consent nor sue within 60 days of a holdover, a month-to-month tenancy at the old rent begins; and a tenant who keeps tendering the usual rent is protected from retaliation. The cautious course: after serving a nonpayment or breach notice, either refuse rent or accept it only with a written statement that acceptance does not waive the notice, and get advice before filing if you have accepted money. A lease clause cannot make the tenant give up statutory notice rights.

title: Agreed Ways to Give Notice
bodyText: Hawaii's landlord-tenant statutes have no special "actual notice" rule and no provision letting you and the tenant agree on an extra method, such as text messages, that counts for a notice the law requires. The code's general rule decides most questions: a person has notice of a fact when the person actually knows it, has received a notice of it, or has reason to know of it from all the facts and circumstances known at the time. You give notice by taking the steps reasonably required to inform the other person in the ordinary course, whether or not the person actually learns of it. A notice is received when it comes to the person's attention or is delivered at the place of business through which the rental agreement was made or at any place held out as the place for receipt of such communications, so name in the lease the address where each of you receives notices, and keep it current. Where a statute sets the method, follow it: the nonpayment notice may be posted in a conspicuous place on the unit (received on the date of posting) or mailed (received two business days after the postmark), the notice after a tenant's death goes by registered mail, and some refunds go by certified mail, return receipt requested. A text message or e-mail can satisfy a writing requirement only if both of you agreed to deal electronically, and never for notices of default, eviction, the right to cure or utility shutoff (see the e-mail notices section). The two-day notice before entry is not required by the statute to be written, so a text can serve if it actually reaches the tenant; keep a record. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no other rule on agreed notice methods.

title: Claims and Foreclosures Against the Property
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not require a tenant to tell you when the tenant receives court papers or a notice of a claim against the property by someone else, do not void a tenant's agreement to recognize someone else as landlord, and do not require you to tell a tenant or applicant that the property is in foreclosure. If you want to be told, put that duty in the lease or your rules. Two related rules apply. You must deliver possession at the start of the agreed term, and you may bring an action for possession against any person wrongfully in possession, including a holdover tenant. If your mortgage is foreclosed by power of sale, once the purchaser's affidavit and conveyance document are recorded, anyone claiming through you who stays in possession is treated as a tenant at sufferance whom the purchaser may remove by summary possession, ejectment or another action, with fees awarded to the winner; see the foreclosure rows for what that means for your tenants, and note that federal law may also apply. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no other rule on this.

title: Automatic Renewal Clauses
bodyText: Hawaii's landlord-tenant code has no automatic-renewal rule. A written lease may set any term, and with no agreed term the tenancy is month to month. Hawaii's general consumer law on automatic renewal clauses may also reach a lease that renews itself: it covers anyone who sells products or services to a consumer under a contract with a term of more than one month that renews for a further term of more than one month unless the consumer cancels, and the consumer-protection definitions it borrows treat leasing as a purchase. No case applying it to a residential lease was searched, so treat it as applying. If your lease renews automatically for another fixed term: state the renewal clause and how the tenant cancels clearly and conspicuously (larger type, contrasting type or color, or set off by a box or marks); give the tenant an acknowledgment the tenant can keep showing the renewal terms and how to cancel; offer an easy way to cancel, such as e-mail or a postal address; and, if the term is twelve months or more, send a written reminder no less than 30 and no more than 60 days before the cancellation deadline saying the lease will renew unless cancelled, how to cancel and the deadline (by e-mail only if the tenant agreed to electronic notices). Do not charge a card or account for a renewal term without the tenant's affirmative consent to the renewal terms, and give a clear notice before any material change to them. A knowing violation is an unfair or deceptive practice. A month-to-month tenancy continues automatically by law until ended by written notice (at least 45 days from you, at least 28 days from the tenant, 120 days for demolition, condominium conversion or a change to transient vacation rentals), and a tenancy shorter than month to month ends on 10 days' notice; state these ways to end it clearly in the lease. If a fixed term ends and the tenant stays without your consent, the holdover rules apply instead (see the holdover sections).

title: Arbitration Clauses in Leases
bodyText: No Hawaii statute deals with arbitration clauses in residential leases. Hawaii's Uniform Arbitration Act applies: an agreement contained in a record to arbitrate an existing or later dispute is valid, enforceable and irrevocable except on a ground that exists at law or in equity for revoking a contract, such as unconscionability. Before a dispute arises, neither party may waive the right to be represented by a lawyer at the arbitration, and certain court protections (including provisional remedies, court jurisdiction to enforce the agreement and appeals) cannot be waived or varied. An arbitrator may award attorney's fees only if the law would allow them in court for the same claim or the parties agreed. Be cautious before using an arbitration clause. Neither you nor the tenant may waive or agree to forego rights or remedies under the landlord-tenant code, and the code's remedies run through the courts: you bring summary possession in the district court of the circuit where the property is, either of you may take a security deposit dispute to the small claims division (where neither side may be represented by an attorney), and the district court may issue injunctions in landlord-tenant cases. For nonpayment of rent, from February 5, 2026 through February 4, 2028 you must send your 10-calendar-day notice to a state-funded mediation center and mediate if mediation is scheduled before you file; on February 4, 2028 that mediation regime ends unless the legislature extends it, while the 10-calendar-day notice and its posting and mailing rules stay. Case notes under the Act report Hawaii courts refusing to enforce arbitration terms found unconscionable, including discovery limits and cost-splitting (those cases were not read). If you use an arbitration clause at all, keep possession cases, small-claims deposit disputes and the statutory mediation out of it, preserve the tenant's statutory remedies and right to a lawyer, and avoid terms that make arbitration costlier for the tenant than court. The rules are the same for fixed-term, month-to-month and shorter tenancies. Federal law may also apply. Federal law also matters here: the Federal Arbitration Act overrides state rules that block arbitration directly or indirectly (for example, a rule against giving up a jury), and the U.S. Supreme Court has held that renting out real estate is activity it reaches. On that basis the library now offers an optional clause, `arbitration-agreement`: money claims only, with possession, small claims, security-deposit, injury, emergency and government-agency matters kept out, every remedy and the right to a lawyer kept, the arbitration fees above a court filing fee paid by you, a 30-day opt-out for the tenant, and separate initials from both of you. Because state law points the other way, a court here could still refuse to enforce it; if one did, the dispute would simply go to court.

title: Other Rules Hawaii Does Not Have
bodyText: Three rules some states have do not exist in Hawaii's statutes. (1) No statute gives you a special right to end a tenancy because the rental application was false. The lease's application-accuracy section makes a material falsehood a breach of the lease, which you enforce through the code's ordinary notices: for a breach of the tenant's statutory duties, written notice and at least ten days to remedy, with termination only for a material failure to comply with building and housing laws affecting health and safety; for a rule breach, written notice in the statutory form with at least ten days to stop. (2) No Hawaii statute requires smoke or carbon monoxide alarms in rentals, so there is also no statute making alarm compliance inadmissible in an injury case or limiting what an insurer may do because of it; county building and fire codes may require alarms (not covered here), and you must comply with building and housing laws materially affecting health and safety. (3) No statute bans renting the same unit to two tenants for the same period; if you cannot put a tenant into possession at the start of the agreed term, the tenant owes no rent for that time, may terminate, and may recover reasonable substitute-housing costs (see the double-letting row). Hawaii's statutes and court rules were searched; case law, administrative rules and county codes were not.

title: Checked Across the Whole Code
bodyText: We searched all of Hawaii's statutes, its constitution and the court rules, not only the landlord-tenant code, for three things landlords ask about. (1) Squatters: Hawaii has a remedy outside the landlord-tenant code. A building or place used for a criminal trespass offense that involves someone unlawfully living on or occupying property to which the person has no title, lease or other legal claim is a nuisance that can be enjoined and abated; the attorney general, the county prosecutor, any citizen living in the county or an organization may sue, the court may issue a temporary injunction, and the final order permanently bars the occupants who are parties from living on or entering the property. Separately, you may bring an action for possession against any person wrongfully in possession. Never use self-help against anyone you rented to; see the unauthorized-occupant row. (2) Receipts: Hawaii requires you to give a written receipt for rent at the time it is paid, whatever the method, though a canceled check counts and for a check you need give a separate receipt only on request (see the rent receipts row). (3) Registration: no state statute requires you to register or license a long-term residential rental, or to prove registration before you can win possession, but an out-of-state limited liability company that owns income-producing real property in Hawaii is transacting business here, and it may not maintain an action or proceeding, an eviction included, until it has a certificate of authority; the lease stays valid (HRS §§ 428-1003(b) and 428-1008). An out-of-state corporation that transacts business here faces the same bar until it obtains a certificate of authority, though owning property without more is not transacting business for a corporation (HRS §§ 414-431 and 414-432). You do need a general excise tax license to do business, and transient accommodations need a separate tax registration. Counties regulate short-term and transient vacation rentals and may have their own registration rules, which were not searched.

title: Domestic Violence Citations Check
bodyText: Hawaii has not moved its protective-order laws. The landlord-tenant code's domestic violence protections (early termination, lock changes and court orders to vacate) define domestic violence by pointing to the definition of domestic abuse in the domestic abuse protective orders chapter, and that definition is still in place. It covers physical harm, bodily injury, assault or the threat of imminent physical harm, injury or assault, extreme psychological abuse, coercive control or malicious property damage between family or household members, and certain offenses against a minor family or household member. Family or household members include spouses and former spouses, reciprocal beneficiaries, people with a child in common, parents, children and other relatives, people who live or lived together, and people in a current or past dating relationship, but not adult roommates who share a unit only for economic or contractual reasons. Coercive control was added in 2020, so older forms and policies may use a narrower definition; update them. The documents a tenant may give you for early termination include restraining orders, injunctions against harassment (issued by the district court) and documents from criminal cases, documentation from a victim services organization, or documentation from a medical professional, mental health provider, attorney, advocate, social worker or member of the clergy. 2026 laws amended some protective-order and harassment-injunction procedures but not the definition the code uses. The early-termination right applies to rental agreements of one year or less.

title: No Emergency Contact Law
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not require you to give tenants an emergency or 24-hour telephone number. Three rules make one wise. You must disclose in writing, at or before the start of the tenancy, the name and address of each person authorized to manage the property and of each owner or person authorized to receive notices, rent and legal papers for the owner, and keep that information current. If you or the owner live off the island where the unit is, you must name an on-island agent in the written rental agreement. And for repairs to electrical, plumbing or other facilities, including major appliances you provide, that are needed for sanitary and habitable living conditions (other than repairs needed because of the tenant's misuse), you must start repairs within three business days after oral or written notice, or tell the tenant the reason for any delay beyond your control and set a reasonable tentative start date; otherwise the tenant may make the repair and deduct up to $1,000 or one month's rent, whichever is greater. Because oral notice counts, give tenants a number they can reach. You may also enter without the usual two days' notice in an emergency. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no other rule on emergency contacts.

title: No Energy Data Release Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes have no energy-benchmarking program for private rental buildings and no provision letting a lease clause authorize a utility to release a tenant's energy usage data to you. Hawaii's benchmarking and energy-usage-data statutes apply to public buildings and state-owned facilities, and the utility regulator's performance measures consider a customer's access to the customer's own energy use data. If you need a tenant's usage information, ask the tenant to share it or sign the utility's own release. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no other rule on this; utility tariffs and commission rules were not searched.

title: Where Lease Disputes Are Heard
bodyText: Hawaii's landlord-tenant code applies to every residential rental agreement for a unit in Hawaii, wherever the agreement was signed, and a lease cannot move Hawaii cases elsewhere. A summary possession case must be brought in the district court of the circuit where the property is. The district courts hear civil cases up to $40,000 (and exclusively up to $10,000, not counting fees, interest and costs), may decide a tenant's counterclaim about the premises in a possession case regardless of its amount, and may issue injunctions in landlord-tenant cases. District courts try cases without a jury; if a party is entitled to a jury and demands one on time under the court rules, the case moves to the circuit court. Either you or the tenant may take a dispute over the security deposit to the small claims division, where neither side may be represented by an attorney. So do not put a clause in the lease choosing a court in another state or county for these cases. Neither of you may waive rights or remedies under the code, and a jury-waiver clause is covered separately. These rules are the same for fixed-term, month-to-month and shorter tenancies.

title: Mediation and Informal Dispute Resolution
bodyText: No Hawaii statute authorizes or regulates a lease clause requiring you and the tenant to try to resolve a dispute informally before going to court. Neither of you may waive or agree to forego rights or remedies under the landlord-tenant code, so do not use a clause that delays or conditions the tenant's statutory remedies or your own possession case. Hawaii does require mediation in one situation. From February 5, 2026 through February 4, 2028, before filing a summary possession case for nonpayment of rent you must give the tenant a written notice allowing at least 10 calendar days after receipt to pay, with the contents the statute lists (including a bold-type warning), and give a copy to a state-funded mediation center. If mediation is scheduled within the 10 days, you may file only after 20 calendar days from the tenant's receipt of the notice, unless the tenant fails to appear or cancels; you must take part if mediation is scheduled; mediation takes place within 30 days after the center contacts both of you, in person or remotely. Each side pays its own mediation costs, but if the tenant defaults on a mediated agreement or fails to attend, you may ask for your costs, including reasonable attorney's fees. If mediation fails you may file without more mediation, though the court may order another session for good cause; no further notice or mediation is needed for a case based on breach of a mediated or settlement agreement. On February 4, 2028 this mediation regime ends unless the legislature extends it; the 10-calendar-day notice, posting and mailing rules stay. Possession cases for reasons other than nonpayment do not require this mediation. Separately, the state Office of Consumer Protection may receive, investigate and try to resolve any dispute under the landlord-tenant code, and Hawaii's mediation statute protects mediation communications as privileged in most mediations by a professional mediator or agreed in a record. Condominium and planned-community association disputes have their own mediation rules.

title: Registration and Licenses for Landlords
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes create no statewide rental registry and no state license for renting a dwelling long term. The state requirements are these. (1) Tax license: anyone with income taxed under the general excise tax law, which includes rent, must obtain a general excise tax license from the Department of Taxation before doing business (a one-time $20 fee) and display it; doing business without one can bring a fine of up to $500, or $500 to $2,000 for a cash-based business. (2) Transient rentals: if you furnish transient accommodations, you must also register each place of business for the transient accommodations tax and display the registration with your local contact's name, telephone number and e-mail address. (3) Managers: a person who rents, leases or manages real estate for others for compensation must be a licensed real estate broker (or work under one), unless an exception applies, such as an owner managing the owner's own property, a custodian or caretaker of the property, or a hotel operator. (4) Off-island owners: if you or the owner live outside Hawaii or on a different island from the unit, you must name an on-island agent in the written rental agreement (see that clause). (5) Out-of-state entities: an out-of-state limited liability company that owns income-producing real property in Hawaii is transacting business here and must obtain a certificate of authority; until it does it may not maintain an eviction or other court action, it is liable for the fees and penalties it would have paid, and it may be served by registered or certified mail at any address it uses for its business (HRS §§ 428-1002, 428-1003(b), 428-1008 and 428-110(b)). An out-of-state corporation that transacts business here needs a certificate of authority too, with the same bar on suing, though owning property without more is not transacting business for a corporation (HRS §§ 414-431 and 414-432). If someone collects rent for you, your written rental collection agreement needs a tax statement on its first page (see that row). Counties regulate short-term and transient vacation rentals and may require their own registration or permits; check your county's rules.

title: No Statutory Rule on Blank Spaces in a Lease
bodyText: Hawaii has no statute requiring every blank in a residential lease to be filled in or making an incomplete lease a breach; Hawaii's blank-space rules apply to credit sale contracts and rent-to-own agreements for goods, not leases. Complete every blank before signing anyway. A residential lease for a term of five years or less must be written in a clear and coherent manner using words with common and everyday meanings and divided and captioned by sections, and a blank leaves a term unclear. Some blanks also carry legal duties: the name and address of the manager and of the owner or the owner's agent for notices and legal papers must be disclosed in writing at or before the start of the tenancy, an off-island owner must name an on-island agent in the written rental agreement, and failing to provide a required disclosure within ten days after the tenant demands it costs $100 plus reasonable attorney's fees. Strike out any blank that does not apply.

title: Give the Tenant a Copy of the Lease
bodyText: If the rental agreement is in writing, you must give the tenant a copy of it. The statute sets no deadline, so give each tenant a signed copy at signing or promptly after everyone signs. If you fail to provide it within ten days after the tenant properly demands it, you may owe the tenant $100 plus reasonable attorney's fees; Hawaii's statutes do not make a missing copy a defense to enforcing the lease. Give each tenant a copy of the move-in inventory you both sign, and give the tenant any written rules at signing, because rules bind the tenant only if brought to the tenant's attention when the tenant enters the rental agreement or, if they substantially change the bargain, the tenant consents in writing. An electronic copy is enough only if you both agreed to deal electronically and the tenant can print or store it. Keep your own copy: the court's complaint forms for a possession case ask you to attach the written rental agreement. A special rule applies to a lease made through a distressed property consultant or purchaser (a sale-leaseback of a home in foreclosure): each lessee must get a copy immediately after everyone signs, and the lease is not effective until all parties sign. For an oral rental agreement there is no copy to give, but the required disclosures still apply.

title: No Initials Requirement
bodyText: No Hawaii statute requires a tenant to initial a lease term, including a notice period, for it to bind the tenant; the tenant's signature on the lease is enough as far as the statutes go. Hawaii's initialing rules apply to other documents, such as vehicle dealers' door-to-door sale notices, seller-financing disclaimers, statutory power of attorney forms and changes in recorded instruments. Initials do not make an unlawful term lawful. Hawaii's notice periods are set by statute and neither party may waive them: a month-to-month tenancy ends on at least 45 days' written notice from you (120 days for demolition, condominium conversion or a change to transient vacation rentals) or at least 28 days' written notice from the tenant, and a tenancy shorter than month to month on at least 10 days' notice from either side. A lease cannot shorten those periods, and requiring a month-to-month tenant to give more than 28 days is unsettled, so don't. A fixed-term lease ends on its end date without notice unless it says otherwise. If your lease renews itself automatically, make the renewal term stand out instead (see the automatic renewal section). Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no other rule on initials.

title: Lease Length Limits
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes set no maximum length for a residential lease: you and the tenant may agree in writing to any period as the term. If you do not agree on a term, the tenancy is month to month (week to week for boarders). Length still matters in four places. An oral lease is valid for up to one year; a longer lease must be in writing and signed (see the written lease row). A lease for more than one year must be recorded at the Bureau of Conveyances to be good against a later good-faith buyer, lessee or mortgagee who has no actual notice of it. The plain-language law covers residential leases for terms of five years or less. A lease of improved residential land for fifteen years or more, measured from the start of the lease, is outside the landlord-tenant code (unless set up solely to avoid it). No statute caps a tenancy formed by conduct: the code treats any written or oral agreement on the use and occupancy of a unit as a rental agreement, and a periodic tenant who stays past the end of a period without either side giving notice creates a tenancy for another period.

title: No Lease Type-Size Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes set no minimum type size for a residential lease, and no statute bars you from relying on a lease or part of one because the print is small. The lease must still be written clearly and coherently in everyday words and divided and captioned by sections if its term is five years or less. Hawaii's type rules for rentals reach other documents: a written agreement with someone who collects rent for you must carry a general excise tax statement on its first page in bold ten-point type (a transient accommodations version applies to vacation rentals); the first page of a lease made through a distressed property consultant or purchaser must give the property description and the lessor's name, address and telephone number in at least fourteen-point boldface type; and, until February 4, 2028, the nonpayment notice you give a tenant must include a warning in bold type about the state-funded mediation step (on February 4, 2028 the mediation rules end and the warning requirement ends with them). If your lease renews itself automatically, print the renewal clause so it stands out from the surrounding text. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no other type-size rule for leases.

title: How Hawaii Notices Must Be Delivered
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes set a delivery method for only a few landlord-tenant notices, and you or your agent may deliver them yourselves; no statute requires a sheriff or process server for a notice (court papers are served under the court rules). The general rule: you give notice by taking the steps reasonably required to inform the other person in the ordinary course, and a notice is received when it comes to the person's attention or is delivered at the place held out for receiving such communications. Specific methods: (1) Nonpayment notice: deliver it, post it in a conspicuous place on the unit (received on the date of posting), or mail it by the U.S. Postal Service, properly addressed with postage (received two business days after the postmark unless returned undeliverable). From February 5, 2026 through February 4, 2028 a copy also goes to a state-funded mediation center. (2) Notice of a breach of the tenant's statutory duties: if the tenant cannot be served as required, you may post it in a conspicuous place on the unit. (3) After a tenant dies: registered mail to the named representative, plus any other contact information the tenant gave, or notice to the estate at the unit's address if no one was named. (4) Refunds when a tenant terminates in the first week because you did not conform to the lease or keep the unit fit, for a serious condition, or after a fire or other casualty: mailing to the tenant's address by certified mail, return receipt requested, postmarked by midnight of the fourteenth day, complies. (5) Deposit accounting at move-out: mailing to the address the tenant supplied, with acceptable proof of mailing and postmarked before midnight of the fourteenth day, is presumptive proof. (6) Abandoned property: mail notice to the tenant's forwarding address, a designated address or the previous known address, and wait 15 days. Other written notices, such as termination of a month-to-month tenancy, rent increases and rule-breach notices, may be delivered by any method that gets them to the tenant; hand delivery or mail with proof is safest. E-mail works only as the e-mail notices section allows. A delivery method in your lease does not replace any method the law requires.

title: Extra Terms in Move-Out Notices
bodyText: Hawaii has no statute governing a move-out notice form you ask a tenant to sign and no required warning if the form adds terms the lease does not contain. Keep such a form to the move-out date and a forwarding address. A new term in it is only a proposed change to the agreement, and neither party may waive rights or remedies under the landlord-tenant code; an agreement settling a dispute in which a tenant gives up code rights is invalid if a court finds it unconscionable when made. Related rules: a month-to-month tenant ends the tenancy by written notice at least 28 days ahead and owes rent through the 28th day; after you give a month-to-month tenant your 45-day notice (or 120-day notice for demolition, condominium conversion or a change to transient vacation rentals), the tenant may move out earlier within that period by telling you the move-out date and paying prorated rent; and the security deposit may be used as the last month's rent only if you and the tenant both agree in writing and the tenant gives 45 days' notice of vacating. A form you want the tenant to sign cannot take away any of these. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no other rule on this.

title: Where Hawaii Law Lets Your Lease Decide
bodyText: Several Hawaii rules depend on what the lease says, and a silent lease takes the statutory default. (1) Rent is payable at the time and place agreed; otherwise the whole rent is due at the start of a term of one month or less, and in equal monthly installments at the start of each month for longer terms. (2) You may charge a late charge only if the rental agreement provides for one, and it may not exceed 8% of the rent due. (3) You may agree in writing to any term; with no agreed term the tenancy is month to month (week to week for boarders). (4) The tenant may sublet or assign without your consent unless a written rental agreement requires your consent (units administered, owned or subsidized by the government are different). (5) The tenant pays your attorney's fees only if the lease provides for them, and only within the statutory limits. (6) A tenant must tell you of an extended absence (no later than its first day) only if the rental agreement requires it; a tenant who then makes no reasonable effort to do so must indemnify you for any damage resulting from the absence. (7) Unless the rental agreement provides otherwise, using the unit other than as the tenant's home, or not using it, is a breach of the tenant's duties. (8) You and the tenant may agree that the tenant performs specified repairs, maintenance and minor remodeling, on conditions. (9) A pet deposit of up to one month's rent may be agreed for a pet that lives in the unit. (10) The security deposit counts as last month's rent only if you both agree in writing and the tenant gives 45 days' notice of vacating. (11) Where the code requires action within a reasonable time, you may fix any time that is not manifestly unreasonable. (12) The tenant may name a representative to handle the tenant's belongings after death, in the lease or a separate writing. (13) A lease term allowing eviction of a tenant certified for medical cannabis is void unless the lease also allows eviction for smoking tobacco and the cannabis is smoked (condominium or planned community rules banning medical cannabis aside). (14) You must deliver possession in the agreed condition unless you agree otherwise before delivery. (15) After a good-faith sale to a buyer not connected with you, with the rental agreement disclosed in writing in the sale contract, or the end of a manager's role, the seller or manager is released from later liability unless otherwise agreed. Everything else in the code applies whatever the lease says, because neither party may waive rights or remedies under it.

title: Plain Language Required; No Waiver Statement
bodyText: Hawaii's plain-language law covers your lease. Every written lease of space to be occupied for residential purposes for a term of five years or less, entered into on or after July 1, 1981, must be written in a clear and coherent manner using words with common and everyday meanings, and appropriately divided and captioned by its sections. There is no dollar limit for leases, no readability score or test, no required statement listing the rights a tenant gives up, and no attorney general preapproval. If you fail to comply, you are liable for any actual damages the tenant suffers plus a $50 penalty; in a class action the total penalty is capped at $10,000. No action may be brought after both parties have fully performed, and a lessor who tries in good faith to comply is not liable for the penalties. Noncompliance does not make the lease void or voidable and is not a defense to enforcing it. The law does not apply to a separate document referred to in the lease that has its own independent purpose, to a legal description of the property, or to words or forms required, authorized or approved by state or federal law or a government agency, so statutory notice forms and required disclosures may be used as written. The attorney general or the director of the Office of Consumer Protection may sue to stop violations. Use short sentences, define terms, and give each section a heading.

title: Hawaii Rules That Depend on Size or Building Type
bodyText: Hawaii's landlord-tenant code applies to small and large landlords alike; its list of exclusions does not include small landlords. Only one Hawaii statute turns on how many units you own: the ban on source-of-income discrimination against housing voucher and permanent supportive housing participants does not apply to a landlord who owns not more than four dwelling units in the State, but that exemption is lost if the owner, individually or through a business, owns more than a ten percent interest in more than four units in the State. Read both parts together. Other rules turn on the building, not your portfolio. The fair housing law and the source-of-income law do not apply to renting a unit in a building with no more than two families living independently where the owner or lessor lives in one of them, or to renting a room or up to four rooms in a home where the owner or lessor lives; the source-of-income law also does not apply to an affordable housing project subsidized by public funds or lands. Your duties to provide garbage receptacles and removal and running water do not apply to a single family residence (including a unit with its own street access that shares no hot water equipment or other essential facility), and the rule that you may not ban lawful political signs applies only to a single family residence. Roomers and boarders (a unit lacking a major bathroom or kitchen facility, sharing one with other units, in a building where you live) default to week-to-week tenancies and may be evicted for any material noncompliance after notice. In a multi-unit building you may post the owner and manager information in the elevator or common areas and in the unit instead of giving it to each tenant. Student housing run by a private dorm company offering at least fifty beds is outside the code. Federal fair housing law has its own exemptions and may also apply.

title: Renter's Insurance Is Unregulated in Hawaii
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes neither require renter's insurance nor regulate a lease that requires it. There is no rule on which insurer the tenant uses, no force-placed insurance procedure, no required statement that your insurance does not cover the tenant's belongings, and no specific ban on using the tenant's policy for repairs you owe. You may make renter's insurance a lease requirement (see the renter's insurance section). Three rules limit how you use it. A lease term exempting or limiting your liability, or making the tenant indemnify you, for damage to persons or property caused by your own acts or omissions or those of your agents or employees, is void, so an insurance clause cannot shift that liability. Your repair and habitability duties stay yours whether or not the tenant is insured. And at the start of the tenancy you may require or receive only the first month's rent and the security deposit, so do not collect insurance premiums or fees for coverage you arrange yourself at move-in; have the tenant buy the policy directly. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no other rule on renter's insurance; insurance division rules were not searched.

title: Selling the Property or Changing Managers
bodyText: When you sell, the buyer takes over the rental agreement: a new owner who buys the property is liable under the rental agreement and the landlord-tenant code. The name and address of each manager and of each owner or owner's agent for notices, rent and legal papers that you disclosed at the start of the tenancy must be kept current, and that duty is enforceable against any successor landlord, owner or manager, so tell tenants in writing of the new owner or manager and where to pay rent. A person who fails to make the disclosure becomes the agent of each landlord for receiving notices, rent and legal papers and for performing the landlord's duties. Unless otherwise agreed, a landlord who sells in good faith to an unconnected buyer, with the written disclosure in the sale contract, is relieved of liability for events after the conveyance, and a manager is relieved for events after the management ends. Deposits must be accounted for to the buyer and each tenant notified within 20 days (see the deposit on sale row). While selling, you may enter to show the unit to prospective buyers or lenders on at least two days' notice during reasonable hours, and the tenant may not unreasonably refuse. A good-faith sale contract in which the buyer represents that the buyer or the buyer's immediate family will live in the unit, or will substantially alter, remodel or demolish it, lets you recover possession even after a tenant's protected complaint. Converting to a condominium needs at least 120 days' notice before the tenancy ends. If the property is foreclosed, see the foreclosure rows.

title: What Hawaii's Landlord-Tenant Code Covers
bodyText: Hawaii's Residential Landlord-Tenant Code applies to every residential rental agreement, written or oral, for a dwelling unit in Hawaii, wherever the agreement was made. It does not apply to: residence at an institution incidental to detention or to medical, geriatric, educational, religious or similar services; student or faculty housing controlled by a college or university (or on land leased from it by a nonprofit for that purpose), or run by a private dorm company offering at least fifty beds to students; occupancy under a bona fide contract to buy the unit; fraternal organization housing run without profit; transient day-to-day occupancy in a hotel or motel; an employee whose occupancy depends on employment (or a pensioner, or up to four years under a plan to transfer the unit to the occupant); a lease of improved residential land for fifteen years or more; a buyer before transfer or a seller after transfer; homeless facilities and programs; Hawaii Public Housing Authority housing; and transitional facilities for abused family or household members. An exclusion does not apply if the arrangement was created solely to avoid the code. Roomers and boarders are tenants with some special rules. Where the code is silent, the summary possession chapter and general principles of law and equity apply, and the code controls if the two conflict. In a federally subsidized program, federal program conditions control over an inconsistent code provision. A condominium association may bring a possession case against a tenant who repeatedly violates its governing documents if the landlord refuses to act. Hawaii's statutes contain no separate landlord-tenant act for mobile home parks. On Hawaiian home lands, a homestead lessee may not sublet the lot or improvements, though with the department's approval the lessee may rent lodging in the home or in a separate dwelling unit on the lot to native Hawaiians. Counties regulate short-term and transient vacation rentals, which are not covered here.

title: When a Lease Must Be in Writing
bodyText: In Hawaii an oral lease for up to one year is valid and enforceable as if it were in writing. No lawsuit may be brought on an agreement that is not to be performed within one year, or on a contract for an interest in land, unless it, or a note or memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by the person to be held to it or by someone that person authorized in writing, so put any lease longer than one year in writing and have every tenant sign. Separately, a lease for a term of more than one year must be recorded at the Bureau of Conveyances, or it is void against a later buyer, lessee or mortgagee who acts in good faith, pays value, has no actual notice of it and records first; that is a priority rule, not a rule that the lease is invalid between you and the tenant. Even for shorter tenancies, some lease choices count only in writing: the term itself (otherwise the tenancy is month to month), a requirement that the tenant get your consent to sublet or assign, and an agreement to use the security deposit as the last month's rent. Electronic signatures satisfy a signature requirement if both of you agreed to sign electronically. Courts have recognized exceptions such as part performance (cases not read), so do not rely on an unsigned long lease.

title: Forms and Required Wording Hawaii Supplies
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes prescribe no general lease form; you write your own, in plain language (in a project under the state housing finance corporation's rental assistance program, the corporation sets standards for the lease form owners use). Hawaii supplies or requires specific wording for these documents. (1) Rule-breach notice: when a tenant breaks a rule, your written notice must give at least ten days (no time to remedy is needed when the breach causes or threatens damage to any person or breaks the tenant's duty to obey building and housing laws or not to wilfully damage the premises) and be in substantially this form: "(Name and address of tenant) (date) You are hereby notified that you have failed to perform according to the following rule: (specify rule allegedly breached) Be informed that if you (continue violating) (again violate) this rule after (a date not less than ten days after this notice), the landlord may terminate the rental agreement and sue for possession of your dwelling unit." (2) Nonpayment notice: from February 5, 2026 through February 4, 2028, your 10-calendar-day notice must list your name and contact information, the unit address, the name and contact information of every tenant on the rental agreement, the rent due after all payments from all sources, the facts about the copy sent to the mediation center and when you may file, a statement that you will take part in mediation if it is scheduled, and a warning in bold type in substantially the wording the statute gives; the Judiciary has published a ten-calendar-day notice form for that period, and complaint forms for possession cases. (3) Death of a tenant: the notice to the representative or estate must state the tenant's name, the unit address, that the representative was identified by the tenant, the approximate date of death, the monthly rent and paid-through date, that the tenancy ends 15 calendar days after the notice is mailed or delivered or on the paid-through date, whichever is later, and how you may dispose of remaining belongings of value. (4) If someone collects rent for you, the written rental collection agreement must show on its first page the owner's name, address, social security number and, if available, general excise tax number, the property address, and this statement in bold ten-point type: "HAWAII GENERAL EXCISE TAXES MUST BE PAID ON THE GROSS RENTS COLLECTED BY ANY PERSON RENTING REAL PROPERTY IN THE STATE OF HAWAII. A COPY OF THE FIRST PAGE OF THIS AGREEMENT, OR OF FEDERAL INTERNAL REVENUE FORM 1099 STATING THE AMOUNT OF RENTS COLLECTED, SHALL BE FILED WITH THE HAWAII DEPARTMENT OF TAXATION." (a transient accommodations version applies to vacation rentals). (5) A lease made through a distressed property consultant or purchaser must show on its first page, in at least fourteen-point boldface type, the property description and the lessor's name, address and telephone number and payment address. Use statutory wording as written; the plain-language law does not apply to wording required or approved by law.

title: Tenant Portals and Electronic Dealings
bodyText: Hawaii has no statute on tenant portals as such, but its electronic transactions law limits how you use one.
