It applies only between parties who have each agreed to deal electronically, judged from the context and the parties' conduct; that a tenant once paid rent electronically is not enough. If your lease is on paper, an agreement to do business electronically may not be in the lease itself: put it in a separate and optional agreement, and do not make the lease conditional on it. A tenant who agrees to deal electronically may refuse to conduct other transactions electronically, and that right cannot be waived, so a lease term requiring that every future document, signature or notice go only through the portal will not hold; keep a paper route. When the law requires information in writing, an electronic record satisfies it only if the tenant can print or store it when received; a record the portal prevents the tenant from printing or saving cannot be enforced against the tenant. Notices of default, eviction, the right to cure and utility shutoff are outside the electronic transactions law, so deliver them as the statutes require (see the notice delivery row). Electronic signatures and records are valid for the lease and other documents once both sides have agreed. Hawaii's statutes do not say whether you may require rent to be paid only through a portal; offer at least one other way to pay, give a written receipt for each payment at the time of payment (for a payment by check, when the tenant asks for one), and never require postdated checks. If the portal stores tenants' social security, driver's license or financial account numbers, Hawaii's data-security laws apply (see the tenant records row).

title: Tenant Records and Data Security
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not require you to keep a rent ledger or give a tenant a payment history, but several record duties apply. Give a written receipt for rent at the time of payment (a canceled check counts; for a check, give a receipt if asked). If you charge an application screening fee, give the applicant a receipt and a breakdown of the costs on request, and return any unused part within 30 days after you submit the screening requests. When you keep any of a deposit, your written notice must include written evidence of the costs, such as estimates, invoices or cleaning receipts. Keep the signed move-in inventory. Do not disclose information a tenant gives you to end a lease because of domestic violence unless the tenant consents in a signed statement, it is required or relevant in a court case, or other law requires it. Hawaii's data-security laws reach anyone doing business who holds a person's name together with a social security number, driver's license or state ID number, or a financial account, card number, access code or password: you must take reasonable measures to protect the records when you dispose of them (shredding or burning paper, erasing or destroying electronic media, and a written disposal policy, or a contract with a records-destruction business you check); if there is a security breach, you must notify the affected people without unreasonable delay (and the Office of Consumer Protection and the credit bureaus if more than 1,000 people are notified at once); and you may not make anyone's full social security number public, print it on materials mailed to the person (unless an exception applies, and even then never on a postcard or other mailer without an envelope), or require it to be sent over the internet without a secure or encrypted connection. Violations can bring penalties of up to $2,500 each plus the person's actual damages.

title: Changing Lease Terms Mid-Tenancy
bodyText: Hawaii has no general statute letting you change lease terms by notice. What you may change depends on the kind of tenancy. Fixed term: the lease binds both of you until it ends; change a term only by written agreement, or as the lease itself allows (for example a mid-term rent increase clause or rules). Month to month: you may raise the rent by written notice given at least 45 consecutive days before the increase; for a tenancy shorter than month to month (such as week to week), at least 15 consecutive days. Because Hawaii lets the parties agree to any consideration as rent, treat an increase in any recurring charge the tenant pays you as needing the same notice. To change other terms of a periodic tenancy, get the tenant's written agreement, or end the tenancy with the required notice (at least 45 days for month to month, 10 days for shorter periods) and offer a new agreement; but a termination notice given to evade the rent-increase notice periods is void. Rules: new or changed rules bind the tenant if brought to the tenant's attention, but a rule that substantially modifies the tenant's bargain needs the tenant's written consent, and every rule must serve a legitimate purpose, be reasonably related to it, apply fairly to all tenants and be explicit. You may not raise the rent or reduce services to retaliate for a tenant's good-faith complaint or repair request (with listed exceptions). Oral changes are part of the rental agreement too, but put every change in writing.

title: Tenant Laws With Expiration Dates
bodyText: As of October 18, 2026, three Hawaii landlord-tenant rules are temporary. (1) Nonpayment mediation: from February 5, 2026 through February 4, 2028, before filing a possession case for nonpayment you must send your 10-calendar-day notice to a state-funded mediation center as well as the tenant, include the listed contents and bold warning, mediate if mediation is scheduled, and, if the mediation center schedules mediation within the 10 calendar days and the tenant takes part, wait until 20 calendar days after the tenant's receipt to file (unless the tenant fails to appear or cancels). On February 4, 2028 that program ends and the earlier text of the nonpayment section returns, except that the 10-calendar-day notice period and the rules on when a posted or mailed notice is received stay. The Judiciary's matching notice and complaint forms are approved for the same period. Check whether the legislature extends the program before relying on the end date. (2) Wildfire mediation: a separate mediation procedure for tenancies covered by the wildfire emergency proclamations took effect when the final wildfire eviction moratorium expired and is repealed on December 31, 2026 or one year after that expiration, whichever comes first; the state consumer protection office indicated in February 2025 that the termination restrictions had ended, so this procedure has likely already lapsed. (3) Maui rent freeze: under the current wildfire emergency proclamation, rents for residential dwellings on the island of Maui may not exceed the rents in effect on August 9, 2023, except for documented added operating expenses and increases in a written agreement the tenant signed before that date, with an exception for certain regulated affordable housing projects; the proclamation runs through October 23, 2026 unless terminated or superseded, and these proclamations have been renewed repeatedly, so check the current one. No other core Hawaii landlord-tenant statute is scheduled to expire (the housing authority's state rent supplement program for kupuna is set to end June 30, 2028).

title: No Lease Translation Requirement
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not require a private landlord to translate a lease or notice, even if you advertise or negotiate in another language, and no statute prescribes translated notices for tenants. One exception may matter if you receive state money to provide housing services: Hawaii's language access law requires state agencies and covered entities (persons or organizations receiving state financial assistance, such as grants or purchase-of-service contracts, to render services to the public, but not tax credits, loan guarantees, procurement contracts or licenses) to take reasonable steps to give limited English proficient persons meaningful access to their services, including competent oral language services and written translations of vital documents such as applications and notices of rights or denials for any limited English proficient group making up five percent or one thousand people, whichever is less, of those served or likely to be affected. If that describes your program, check with the agency funding it. Otherwise, a translation you provide is a courtesy: say in it which version controls, and remember that the lease must be clear and coherent to the tenant. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no other translation rule for leases.

title: Notices That Must Be in Writing
bodyText: Many Hawaii landlord-tenant notices must be in writing, and a lease cannot replace them with spoken notice, because neither party may waive rights or remedies under the code. Your notices that must be written: the owner and manager names and addresses at or before the start of the tenancy; the move-in inventory; rent receipts; a rent increase (45 consecutive days ahead for month to month, 15 for shorter periods); ending a month-to-month tenancy (at least 45 days, or 120 days for demolition, condominium conversion or a change to transient vacation rentals); the nonpayment notice; a notice of the tenant's failure to meet statutory duties; a rule-breach notice in the statutory form; a nuisance warning and the following notice to vacate; the deposit accounting at move-out; a buyer's notice of the deposit amount within 20 days after a transfer; the notice after a tenant's death; ending the interest of a household member who committed domestic violence (at least five days); and the abandoned-property notice, which is mailed. The tenant's notices that must be written: ending a month-to-month tenancy (at least 28 days); a notice of a condition before terminating for it; a repair request that starts the 12-business-day repair period; a servicemember's or survivor's early-termination notice; and notice of an absence of 20 days or more, since without it the tenant is treated as having wrongfully quit while no rent is paid for that time. The statutes do not require writing for your two days' notice before entry or for a tenant's notice of an urgent repair to essential facilities (oral notice starts the three-business-day period), or for the 10-day notice ending a tenancy shorter than month to month; give that last one in writing anyway, because the summary possession chapter requires written notice for periodic tenancies. A text or e-mail counts as writing only if both of you agreed to deal electronically, and never for notices of default, eviction or the right to cure.

title: Association Documents and Tenants
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not require a lease of a condominium, cooperative or planned-community unit to disclose the association's obligations, and do not require you to give the tenant the declaration, bylaws or house rules. Two rules make delivery wise anyway. A condominium tenant must comply with the association's bylaws, and every tenant of a condominium owner must comply strictly with the declaration, bylaws and house rules; the association can fine the tenant directly after notice and a chance to be heard, and you, as owner, remain responsible for the tenant's conduct and fines. And the rules you want to enforce yourself bind the tenant only if they are brought to the tenant's attention when the tenant enters the rental agreement, or, if they come later and substantially change the bargain, the tenant consents in writing. So give the tenant copies of the house rules and other governing documents at signing and list them in the lease (the association compliance clause can serve). Seller disclosure rules require association documents only for sales, which include a lease with an option to buy a home of one to four units or a condominium or cooperative unit; if you give such an option, those rules apply to it. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no other association disclosure rule for leases.

title: Renting in a Condominium or Planned Community
bodyText: If you rent out a unit in a condominium or planned community, Hawaii's association laws reach your tenant directly. Your tenant, like you, is bound by the condominium declaration, bylaws and house rules, and a condominium tenant must comply with the bylaws. If your tenant violates them, the association may, besides acting against you, charge late fees and levy reasonable fines against the tenant directly after giving you and the tenant notice and a chance to be heard; you remain responsible for your tenant's conduct, for any fine levied against the tenant and for the association's legal fees in enforcing against the tenant. After notifying both of you and allowing ten days to cure (no notice is needed where the breach causes or threatens damage to any person or violates the tenant's duty to obey building and housing laws or not to damage the premises), the association may also enforce any right you as landlord could have used under the lease, including eviction. An association may also bring its own possession case against a condominium tenant who repeatedly violates the governing documents or other occupants' quiet enjoyment when you refuse to act, naming you as a defendant. Unless the lease provides otherwise, these powers do not change your own rights to enforce the lease. Associations in both kinds of community may recover their enforcement costs and attorney's fees from a tenant. If you fall 30 or more days behind on assessments, the board may demand that your tenant pay the association, up to the rent due, and the tenant's payment counts against the rent; see the foreclosure section for how that works. The association's rules may restrict leasing of residential units only as far as needed to meet the underwriting requirements of institutional mortgage lenders, unless the declaration or bylaws provide otherwise, so check the declaration and bylaws for rental limits before you lease. Condominium units sold under the state community development authority's leasehold program in urban redevelopment sites have been limited to owner occupancy and may not be rented; a 2026 act lets the authority's rules make exceptions and lets some units be sold without an owner-occupancy requirement, so check the unit's sale terms and the authority's current rules before renting one. Where the bylaws let owners keep pets, they may not bar tenants' pets if you consent in writing (see the condominium pet section). A tenant may not serve on the condominium board. Hawaii's statutes set no cap on association lease-approval or move-in fees, no rule on an association deposit from tenants, and no limit on the tenant information an association may request. Remember that you may not require from or on behalf of a tenant at the start of a rental agreement any money other than the first month's rent and the security deposit, so an association charge you pass on at move-in must fit within those limits. County rules on rentals may also apply.

title: No Lead-Safe Certificate
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes create no state lead-safe certificate, lead registry or lead inspection requirement for rental housing, and no certificate to attach to the lease. For housing built before 1978, federal law requires the lead disclosure in the library's lead-based paint section. Hawaii's lead law is a Department of Health program: the department reviews lead abatement plans, inspects abatement projects, may set lead hazard exposure standards and work-practice and notification requirements for lead abatement in dwellings, and may require records and reports from the owner or operator of a lead abatement activity. If you hire anyone to abate lead paint, use a contractor who meets the department's certification rules. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no lead certification requirement for leases; the department's own rules were not reviewed here.

title: No State Lead Notices
bodyText: Beyond the federal lead disclosure for housing built before 1978, Hawaii's statutes require no state lead notice, tenant-rights packet, inspection certificate or renewal re-notice for rentals. Use the library's lead-based paint section for the federal disclosure. Hawaii's statutes have no rule requiring you to abate lead hazards because a child is found to have lead poisoning, and no state lead standard written into the landlord-tenant code; peeling or deteriorating paint is handled under your general duties to comply with building and housing laws materially affecting health and safety and to keep the premises habitable. If a state or county agency notifies you in writing of a health or safety violation, you must start repairs within seven calendar days (or tell the tenant the reason for a delay beyond your control and set a reasonable tentative start date). The Department of Health regulates lead abatement work and may order immediate action where lead hazards create an imminent peril to public health and safety. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no other state lead notice for leases; the department's own rules were not reviewed here.

title: No Bed Bug Disclosure Requirement
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no bed bug disclosure requirement: you need not tell a prospective tenant about past infestations, and no statute sets inspection or treatment timelines or assigns treatment costs. The general rules apply: you must keep the premises habitable and comply with building and housing laws materially affecting health and safety, so a known infestation must be treated; the tenant must keep the part of the premises the tenant occupies as clean and safe as conditions permit. If the tenant's lease or rules require cooperation with treatment, see the bed bug cooperation section. If a prospective tenant asks about infestations, answer truthfully. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no other bed bug rule.

title: No Occupancy Certificate Disclosure
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not require you to give tenants a certificate of occupancy or a notice about one, and no state statute bars collecting rent for a unit without one. Certificates of occupancy are issued by the counties under their building codes; in the state statutes they appear only in other settings, such as when a condominium owner's share of common expenses begins, when construction counts as complete, and affordable housing credits and tax exemptions. What matters for a rental is your duty at all times during the tenancy to comply with all applicable building and housing laws materially affecting health and safety; if a county agency finds the unit unlawful to occupy, that duty and the tenant's repair, termination and retaliation protections apply. Check with the county before renting a new, converted or accessory unit. County building codes were not searched. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no certificate of occupancy disclosure rule.

title: No Drywall Disclosure
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no defective or corrosive drywall disclosure requirement for leases. If you know a unit has drywall that corrodes wiring or plumbing or gives off sulfur odors, the general duties apply: you must keep the premises habitable, comply with building and housing laws materially affecting health and safety, and keep the electrical, plumbing and other facilities you supply in good working order. If you give the tenant an option to buy, the seller disclosure rules for sales apply and require you to disclose material facts, including defects, within your knowledge. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no other drywall rule.

title: No Electric Submetering Disclosure
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no lease disclosure requirement when you submeter electricity or bill tenants for it, and no prescribed form or rate limit for ordinary landlord billing. The one regulated arrangement is power from a renewable energy system on your property (such as rooftop solar) that you sell to tenants: the lease must then state the rate schedule or formula and the other disclosures in the library's on-site renewable power clause. For any other resale or allocation of utility-company electricity, read the library's section on billing tenants for utilities before you start: whether you could be treated as a public utility is not settled by statute. If you do bill for electricity, state in the lease how the charge is measured and when it is due, and never interrupt service to force the tenant out. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no other submetering disclosure rule.

title: No Flood Disclosure Requirement
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not require you to tell a tenant whether a rental is in a flood zone or tsunami inundation area, has flooded before, or needs flood insurance, and give the tenant no right to end the lease over a missing flood notice. Hawaii's flood disclosure rule is in its seller disclosure law, which treats a lease with an option to buy a home of one to four units or a condominium or cooperative unit as a sale. If you give a tenant such an option, your disclosure statement must say, where county maps designate the property by tax map key, whether it lies within a federal special flood hazard area, an airport noise exposure area, a military air installation compatible use zone, a tsunami inundation area or the state's sea level rise exposure area; you must deliver the signed statement within ten calendar days after the contract is accepted, and the buyer then has fifteen calendar days to rescind. For an ordinary lease, telling tenants about known flood or tsunami risk is good practice. Your duty to keep the premises habitable still applies after a flood. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no other flood disclosure rule for leases.

title: No Foreclosure Disclosure Duty
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not require an owner facing foreclosure to tell a prospective tenant before signing a lease, or to tell current tenants that a foreclosure has started. The foreclosure notice of default goes to the borrower, mortgagor and guarantors; in a power of sale foreclosure, the public notice of the sale must be posted on the property, which is often how a tenant learns of it. Because a residential lease likely does not survive a power of sale foreclosure sale (the buyer is entitled to immediate possession and anyone claiming through the owner who stays is a tenant at sufferance), and an eligible tenant may bid to buy the property for a short time after the sale, tell prospective and current tenants promptly and honestly if a foreclosure is pending; the foreclosure section explains the tenant's position. Federal law may also apply. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no foreclosure disclosure rule for landlords.

title: No Good Cause Notice
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no good-cause or just-cause eviction rule, so there is no notice telling a tenant whether the unit is covered by one. A month-to-month tenancy may be ended by your written notice at least 45 days before the termination date (the tenant may leave earlier within those 45 days, paying prorated rent), and by the tenant's written notice at least 28 days ahead; you need 120 days' written notice if you plan to demolish the units, convert to a condominium or change the building to transient vacation rentals; a tenancy shorter than month to month ends on 10 days' notice by either side; a fixed-term lease ends on its end date. Limits still apply. A termination notice given to evade the rent-increase notice rules is void. While the tenant keeps paying the usual rent, you may not recover possession, raise the rent or cut services in retaliation for good-faith complaints to a government agency or to you about health or code violations, an agency's notice of violation, or good-faith repair requests, except for the reasons the statute lists. During a declared emergency, the emergency statute can bar ending tenancies in the affected area except for breach of a material term or an unfit unit (see the emergency limits section). Federally subsidized tenancies follow their program's rules. County ordinances were not searched. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no good-cause notice requirement.

title: No Contamination Disclosure Duty
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not require you to disclose hazardous-substance or radioactive contamination to a tenant before signing, and do not require recorded environmental restrictions to be written into residential leases. One rule reaches occupants. When contaminated land is cleaned up under a state or federal program, the Department of Health may approve an environmental covenant restricting its use; the covenant is recorded, runs with the land and binds later owners and occupants, and a copy must be provided, by the person and in the manner the agency requires, to each person in possession of the property. If your rental is subject to an environmental covenant, give the tenant a copy, follow any notice duties the covenant itself sets (for example before a change in use or site work), and make the tenant's use limits part of the lease or rules. The department keeps a registry of environmental covenants. If you give the tenant an option to buy, the seller disclosure rules for sales apply and require you to disclose known material facts. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no other contamination disclosure rule for leases; the department's rules were not reviewed here.

title: No Code-Order Disclosure Duty
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not require you to give prospective tenants copies of outstanding inspection, code-violation or condemnation orders. The duties that matter are these. At all times during the tenancy you must comply with building and housing laws materially affecting health and safety. If the Department of Health or another state or county agency notifies you in writing of a health or safety violation, you must start repairs within seven calendar days, with a good-faith effort to finish as soon as possible (or tell the tenant the reason for a delay beyond your control and set a reasonable tentative start date); otherwise the tenant may have the work done and deduct up to $1,000 or one month's rent, whichever is greater (no more than three months' rent in any six months, and never for a condition caused by the want of due care of the tenant, a family member or a guest). A tenant may end the rental agreement during the first week of occupancy if you are in material noncompliance with your duty to keep fit premises or fail to conform to the agreement, and keeps that right while staying in reliance on your promise to fix the condition. You may not retaliate after an agency files a notice or complaint of a violation. During a declared emergency a unit the county finds unfit for occupancy is treated separately. Because a tenant can terminate early and recover from these conditions, disclose open orders affecting the unit before signing. County codes were not searched. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no code-order disclosure rule.

title: No Landlord Insurance Mandate
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not require residential landlords to carry liability insurance and create no statewide rental registration that asks for proof of coverage. Where Hawaii statutes require insurance near this subject, it is for other parties: a condominium association must, unless its declaration or bylaws provide otherwise, keep property insurance on the common elements and general liability insurance of at least $1,000,000, plus flood insurance if the property is in a special flood hazard area. Your lender, an association's governing documents, a housing program or a county may still require coverage. Remember that a lease clause exempting you from, or limiting, your liability for damage to persons or property caused by your own or your agents' or employees' acts or omissions, or requiring the tenant to indemnify you for it, is void, so insurance, not the lease, is how you manage that risk. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no landlord insurance mandate.

title: On-Bill Energy Charges
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not require you to tell a new tenant that the utility account for the unit carries a charge to repay energy-efficiency or renewable energy improvements, and give the tenant no rent deduction for one. Hawaii does allow on-bill repayment: the public utilities commission may run an on-bill program that lets an electric utility customer pay for a renewable energy system or energy-efficient device through a charge on the electricity bill, with penalties for nonpayment that may include disconnection, and the state's green infrastructure loan program uses a commission-approved on-bill repayment tariff. If an on-bill charge stays with the meter of your rental and the tenant will pay the electric bill, tell the tenant in writing before signing what the charge is, how much it is and how long it lasts, and say in the lease who pays it; the general law of misrepresentation supplements the landlord-tenant code. Commission orders and tariffs were not searched. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no meter conservation charge notice.

title: No Drug Lab Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no duty to disclose that a rental was used to manufacture methamphetamine or other drugs, no state decontamination standard or occupancy ban for former drug labs, and no duty on a landlord to report a suspected lab. Manufacturing methamphetamine is a crime, punished more severely near schools. If you know or suspect a unit was used as a drug lab, the general duties apply: before renting it you must be able to comply with building and housing laws materially affecting health and safety and keep the premises habitable, so have the unit assessed and cleaned by qualified professionals, and do not conceal the history from an applicant who asks. Illegal activity by a tenant is covered in the library's criminal activity clause. Department of Health rules were not searched. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no other drug lab rule for rentals.

title: No Military Zone Disclosure
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not require you to tell a tenant that a rental is near a military installation or airport, or within an air installation compatible use zone or airport noise area, and give the tenant no right to end a lease over a missing disclosure. Those zones appear in Hawaii's seller disclosure law, which treats a lease with an option to buy a home of one to four units or a condominium or cooperative unit as a sale: if you give a tenant such an option, your disclosure statement must say, where county maps designate the property by tax map key, whether it lies within the noise exposure area on the state's airport noise maps or the Air Installation Compatible Use Zone of any Air Force, Army, Navy or Marine Corps airport (along with the flood, tsunami and sea level rise areas). For an ordinary lease, telling an applicant about known aircraft noise is good practice. County zoning may add rules near bases and airports; county ordinances were not searched. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no military zone disclosure rule for leases.

title: No Mold Disclosure Requirement
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no mold disclosure requirement, mold information pamphlet, mold testing duty or indoor mold standard for rental housing. Mold is handled under the general duties. You must comply with building and housing laws materially affecting health and safety, keep the premises habitable, and keep the plumbing and other facilities you supply in good working order, so fix leaks and ventilation failures that cause mold. The tenant must keep the part of the premises the tenant occupies as clean and safe as conditions permit and keep plumbing fixtures as clean as their condition permits. For repairs to plumbing or other facilities needed for sanitary and habitable living conditions you must start within three business days after oral or written notice; other defects within twelve business days after written notice; otherwise the tenant may repair and deduct within the statutory limits. Note known mold and its treatment on the move-in inventory. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no other mold rule.

title: No Ordnance, Demolition or Meter Disclosure
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not require you to tell prospective tenants about a former military ordnance or munitions site nearby, a planned demolition of the building, or a shared utility meter. Related rules still matter. Before you end a month-to-month tenancy because you plan to demolish the dwelling units, convert to a condominium or change the building to transient vacation rentals, you must give the tenant at least 120 days' written notice; a revoked or reissued notice starts the period again, and the tenant may leave earlier within that period on notice, paying prorated rent. For a fixed-term tenancy, a planned condominium conversion also requires 120 days' notice before the rental agreement ends. If you know of a demolition plan at signing, say so. If a meter serving the unit also serves other areas, say in the lease who pays for what; see the utility billing section. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no ordnance, demolition or shared-meter disclosure rule.

title: No Pesticide Notice Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not require you to give tenants notice before pesticides are applied in or around a rental, or to give them pest control company notices before signing. Hawaii's pesticide statutes regulate the products, their labels and use, and the licensing of applicators and pest control operators; users of restricted use pesticides must report their use to the Department of Agriculture and Biosecurity each year, and the department publishes that information online (except for structural pest control, such as termite and household pest work). If you need to treat a unit, give the tenant the two days' notice of entry the law requires (except in an emergency or where impracticable), enter at reasonable hours, and tell the tenant what will be applied and when the area is safe to reenter; use a licensed operator where the law requires one. Department of Agriculture and Biosecurity rules were not searched. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no pesticide notice rule for rentals.

title: No Private Well Testing Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not require you to test a private well or rainwater catchment system serving a rental, or to give test results to tenants. The Department of Health runs a voluntary program: any resident of a legal dwelling that relies on a water catchment system may, subject to the department's procedures and available program funds, have the water tested once a year for lead and copper for $25, and may get technical assistance on improving water quality. Separately, every cesspool in the State must be upgraded or converted to an approved wastewater system, or connected to a sewer, before January 1, 2050, unless the department grants an exemption; that is an owner's duty, not a disclosure rule. Your duties to tenants come from the landlord-tenant code: comply with building and housing laws materially affecting health and safety, keep the premises habitable, keep the plumbing you supply in good working order, and, except for a single family residence or a building not required by law to be equipped for it, provide running water as reasonably required. If the unit relies on a well or catchment, say so in the lease, test the water before a new tenancy, and share the results. Department of Health rules were not searched. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no other well testing rule.

title: No Chemical Exposure Warning Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes have no counterpart to California's Proposition 65. No Hawaii statute requires you to warn tenants that a building or unit contains chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm, and there is no private enforcement scheme for missing warnings. Hawaii's chemical-related rules for rentals are narrower: the federal lead disclosure for housing built before 1978, environmental covenants on cleaned-up contaminated land (a copy goes to people in possession as the health department requires), and the Department of Health's lead and asbestos abatement rules for work you hire. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no chemical exposure warning rule for rentals.

title: No Property Tax Rent Statement
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not require you to tell tenants what part of the rent pays real property taxes, or to give an annual rent or tax statement. One state tax credit touches it: a low-income resident who pays rent for a home in Hawaii may claim a refundable income tax credit if adjusted gross income is under $30,000 and more than $1,000 in rent was paid during the year, but only if the rental property is not partially or wholly exempt from real property tax. The credit is $50 for each qualified exemption (doubled for a taxpayer 65 or older), and rent for this purpose excludes charges for utilities, parking, storage, yard services and furniture. Tenants claiming it may ask whether the property is tax-exempt, and you must give every tenant your general excise tax number for this purpose (see the general excise tax number clause). Real property tax is a county tax; county rules were not searched. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no property tax rent statement requirement.

title: No Radon Disclosure Requirement
bodyText: Hawaii has no statute requiring a radon disclosure, radon test or radon mitigation for rental housing, no floor-level rule and no radon-resistant construction mandate in its statutes. The word does not appear in Hawaii's statutes, constitution or court rules. Testing is not a legal requirement; your general duty to keep the premises habitable and comply with building and housing laws affecting health and safety still applies. Building codes adopted by the State and counties were not reviewed here.

title: Hawaii Lease Disclosure Checklist
bodyText: Hawaii's required written items for a residential lease are these. (1) Owner and manager: at or before the start of the tenancy, give the tenant in writing the name and address of each person authorized to manage the premises and of each owner or person authorized to act for the owner for service of process and for receiving and receipting for rents, notices and demands, and keep it current (in a multi-unit building a posted notice may be used instead). (2) On-island agent: if you or the owner live outside Hawaii or on another island, name in the written rental agreement an agent living on the island where the unit is. (3) General excise tax number: give every tenant your general excise tax number for filing for the low-income renters' credit. (4) Copy: give the tenant a copy of a written lease. (5) Move-in inventory: before initial occupancy, make a written record of the condition of the premises and any furnishings or appliances, signed in duplicate by you and the tenant, with a copy to each tenant. (6) Rules: rules bind the tenant only if brought to the tenant's attention at signing, or later with written consent where they substantially change the bargain. (7) Plain language: a lease for a term of five years or less must be clear, coherent, in everyday words, and divided and captioned by sections. (8) If you sell power from an on-site renewable energy system to the tenant, the lease must state the rate schedule or formula and the other required disclosures. (9) If the lease gives an option to buy, the seller disclosure law applies (disclosure statement, flood and noise zones, association documents). For housing built before 1978, federal law also requires the lead disclosure. Optional items the law lets the lease set: a notice-of-absence requirement, a late charge (up to 8% of the rent due), attorney's fees within the statutory limits, a tenant-death representative, a consent requirement for subletting, and tenant repair agreements. Later notices with fixed periods (rent increases, ending a tenancy, 120 days for demolition, condominium conversion or a change to transient vacation rentals) are not lease disclosures. Hawaii's statutes require no state tenant-rights statement in or with the lease. If you fail to give a required owner, manager, agent or tax-number disclosure within ten days after the tenant's proper demand, you owe $100 plus reasonable attorney's fees, and the same may apply to the lease copy and rent receipts.

title: No Rights Guide Delivery Duty
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not require you to give tenants a state-published guide to landlord and tenant rights, at signing or at renewal, or to get a signed acknowledgment of one. The state does publish guidance you may share: the Department of Commerce and Consumer Affairs publishes a landlord-tenant handbook and a landlord-tenant information webpage, and the state Office of Consumer Protection may receive, investigate and try to resolve any dispute under the landlord-tenant code. Giving the handbook is a courtesy, not a substitute for the disclosures the code requires (see the disclosure checklist). Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no rights guide delivery rule.

title: No Tenant Rights Statement
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes require no state-agency statement of tenant rights in or with the lease: no attachment, no first-page placement, no signature on each page, and no rule barring a suit until one is given. The statutory notices Hawaii does prescribe come later and have their own contents: the notice of a rule violation must be in substantially the form the statute sets, and, until February 4, 2028, the nonpayment notice must include the listed contents and a bold warning (on February 4, 2028 the mediation version of the statute ends and the earlier text returns, except that the 10-calendar-day notice period and the posting and mailing receipt rules stay; see the statutory forms section). What Hawaii requires at the start of the tenancy is the disclosure checklist: owner and manager names and addresses, an on-island agent where needed, your general excise tax number, a copy of the lease and a signed move-in inventory. The state's landlord-tenant handbook may be shared as a courtesy. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no tenant rights statement requirement.

title: No Truth-in-Renting Act
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no truth-in-renting act requiring a statement in the lease, or penalizing a landlord simply for offering a lease with terms that violate tenant rights. Its own rule is that such terms do not work. Except where the landlord-tenant code allows, neither you nor the tenant may waive or agree to give up rights or remedies under it. A lease term exempting or limiting your liability, or requiring the tenant to indemnify you, for damage caused by your own or your agents' or employees' acts or omissions is void; so is a tenant's authorization to confess judgment; an attorney's fee term outside the statutory limits is unenforceable; a term allowing eviction of a certified medical cannabis patient is void except as the statute allows; and a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable term. A lease for a term of five years or less must also be clear and coherent in everyday words, with sections divided and captioned (see the plain language section). Draft only enforceable terms; a void term invites a dispute and can mislead. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no truth-in-renting statute.

title: No Code Variance Notice
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not require you to give tenants a copy of a health, sanitary or housing code variance or waiver, or to attach one to the rental agreement. Variances in Hawaii's statutes are granted by agencies under their own programs (for example, the Department of Health's lead and asbestos program and county zoning and shoreline setback variances) and none is tied to tenant notice. A variance does not change your duties under the landlord-tenant code: comply with building and housing laws materially affecting health and safety and keep the premises habitable. If a variance affects the unit, telling the tenant in the lease is good practice. Department of Health and county rules were not searched. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no code variance notice rule.

title: No Sex Offender Registry Notice
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not require a lease to include a sex offender registry notice, or require you to tell tenants that a registered offender lives in the building or nearby. The registry is public: the State provides public internet access, and on-site access at the Hawaii criminal justice data center and designated police stations, to the public information about covered offenders, with a posted warning that anyone who uses the registry information to injure, harass or commit a criminal act against a listed person may face criminal prosecution, civil liability or both. You may tell tenants the registry exists and how to search it. Do not use registry information to harass anyone. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no sex offender notice rule for leases.

title: No Occupancy Notice Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule requiring a single-family home lease to carry an occupancy notice, and no presumption that an occupant lacks lawful occupancy unless the lease is notarized or signed by a licensed manager. They also set no general type-size or first-page rule for residential leases (see the type-size section). To deal with someone living in the unit without right, use the ordinary remedies: you may bring an action for possession against any person wrongfully in possession, including a holdover tenant, and a person who knowingly enters or remains unlawfully in premises commits trespass, which the police handle. A signed written lease naming every occupant, with your current contact information, is the best evidence of who has the right to be there. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no single-family occupancy disclosure rule.

title: No Shoreline Access Disclosure
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not require a landlord to tell a tenant about public access to a shoreline or beach next to a rental, or about limits on the tenant's own access. Two rules matter for shoreline rentals. If you give the tenant an option to buy property adjacent to the shoreline, the seller disclosure law treats it as a sale and requires you to disclose all permitted and unpermitted erosion control structures on the parcel, the expiration dates of any permits, any notices of alleged violation and any fines. And no one, landlord or tenant, may intentionally prevent the public from traversing a public right-of-way, transit area or beach transit corridor to the sea or shoreline, by gates, fences, walls, rubbish, guard dogs or animals or, for a landowner, encroaching vegetation; that is a misdemeanor, with minimum fines for repeat convictions. If the property borders a public access way, tell the tenant not to block it. Shoreline setback rules are county matters; county ordinances were not searched. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no shoreline access disclosure for leases.

title: Housing Voucher and Source-of-Income Rules
bodyText: Hawaii bars landlords from discriminating against people who use a housing assistance program, meaning a Section 8 housing choice voucher program or any permanent supportive housing program. You may not: say in any advertisement that you will not rent to a program participant (so no "No Section 8"); discourage a person from applying because of participation; refuse to rent because of participation or the program's requirements; or impose different rental conditions on participants. Exemptions: you may still verify the source and amount of an applicant's income and evaluate stability, security and creditworthiness in a commercially reasonable way; the rule does not apply to a landlord owning no more than four dwelling units in the State (unless the owner, directly or through a business entity, holds more than a ten percent interest in more than four units), to a case where the program has not approved the tenancy within 21 days after a good-faith request for tenancy approval (including the unit inspection), to an owner-occupied building with no more than two units, to an owner-occupant renting one to four rooms, or to subsidized affordable housing projects. Penalties: a court may impose a civil penalty of up to $2,000 for a first violation and $2,500 for a later one, and order injunctive or other relief; no one is fined twice for the same violation, and no attorney's fees or costs are awarded. The state housing authority runs incentives for voucher landlords, subject to its rules: up to one month's contract rent when a unit sits vacant between voucher tenancies or when you first switch a unit to the voucher program; a signing bonus of up to one month's contract rent when you first join the program and secure a voucher tenant (not combined with the first-switch vacancy payment); and reimbursement of verified repair costs for tenant-caused damage that exceeds the security deposit, if you claim within 30 calendar days after the tenant vacates, subject to funding and a licensed contractor's estimate above the amount the authority sets. These are incentives, not duties. Hawaii's fair housing law protects other classes separately. County ordinances were not searched.

title: No Sprinkler Disclosure Duty
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not require a lease to say whether a building has fire sprinklers, or require a sign about a missing system. Sprinklers are a building and fire code matter. Until June 30, 2027, no county may require automatic fire sprinklers to be installed or retrofitted in a new or existing detached one- or two-family dwelling used only for residential purposes (except new homes that need a variance from access road or firefighting water supply requirements). A state loan program, open for new loans until June 30, 2027, can finance condominium associations' installation, repair or replacement of fire sprinklers and other fire safety measures. Your duty is to comply with building and housing laws materially affecting health and safety, which includes any county sprinkler or fire code that applies to your building. Telling a tenant whether the building is sprinklered is good practice. The State Fire Code and county codes were not searched. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no sprinkler disclosure rule.

title: Deaths and Other Events at the Property
bodyText: You have no obligation to tell a prospective tenant that a tenant has died in the rental, or about the history of tenant deaths in the unit. Hawaii's statutes say nothing about other events, such as a crime on the property or an earlier occupant's illness, for an ordinary lease, so no statute requires those disclosures either; but do not misstate facts if an applicant asks, because the general law of misrepresentation supplements the landlord-tenant code. If you give the tenant an option to buy, the seller disclosure law applies, and its own rule is similar: you may leave out of the disclosure statement that an occupant had AIDS or AIDS-related complex or was tested for HIV, and that the property was the site of an act or occurrence that had no effect on its physical structure, physical environment or improvements; those facts are not material facts for the statement. If a real estate licensee rents or manages the property for you, the licensing law separately requires the licensee to find out and disclose all material facts about the property (the fact that an occupant has AIDS or ARC or was tested for HIV is not a material fact), and the Real Estate Commission may discipline a licensee who fails to; the Commission's rules were not searched. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no other stigmatized-property rule.

title: Housing for Your Employees
bodyText: Hawaii has no statute requiring an employer-landlord to give an employee a signed disclosure of occupancy and vacating terms, or to offer a rental agreement when the job ends. The key rule is scope: the landlord-tenant code does not apply to occupancy by your employee whose right to occupy is conditional upon that employment (or by your pensioner, or for up to four years afterward under a plan to transfer the unit or property to the occupant), unless the arrangement was created solely to avoid the code. If an employee's housing is not conditional on the job, for example an employee who rents from you on ordinary terms, the code applies in full. Where the code does not apply, recovering the unit after the job ends falls under the general summary possession law, which lets the person entitled to the premises be restored to possession from someone holding without right after the tenancy ends, and the arrangement's own written terms; no published case was searched on how courts treat these occupancies, so put the terms in writing: that occupancy depends on the job, when it ends, how long the employee has to leave, and any rent or charge (the optional employee housing clause can serve). If you count housing as part of pay, Hawaii's wage law counts the reasonable cost of lodging customarily furnished by an employer as wages, and minimum wage rules allow reasonable deductions for it; check the labor department's rules before deducting. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no other employee housing disclosure rule.

title: No Tenant Protection Act Notice
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no statewide tenant protection act like California's, so there is no notice telling tenants that rent caps or just-cause rules apply. They set no state rent control and no just-cause eviction rule; the summary possession law's reference to county rent control ordinances points to repealed county powers. Rent increase rules are about notice, not amount: for a month-to-month tenancy you must give written notice at least 45 consecutive days before an increase takes effect, and for a tenancy shorter than month to month at least 15 consecutive days; a fixed-term lease's rent changes only as the lease provides. During a declared emergency, the emergency statute can freeze rents in the affected area (see the emergency rent section). Hawaii's statutes also give tenants no general right to buy the building when you sell or convert it. Instead you must give at least 120 days' notice before ending a tenancy because you contemplate a condominium conversion, demolition or a change to transient vacation rentals. In rental projects financed with a state housing finance agency project loan, the financing agreement must give all tenants the first option to buy their units if the loan is prepaid to convert the rentals to ownership units. County ordinances were not searched. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no tenant protection act notice.

title: No Utility Disclosure Attachment
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes require no utility disclosure attachment to the lease, such as a form explaining how a shared bill is apportioned, a submeter certificate, or a notice of energy-improvement charges on the bill. The only lease disclosures Hawaii's statutes prescribe for utilities apply when you sell tenants power from a renewable energy system on your property; the library's on-site renewable power clause carries them. If you bill tenants for utilities in any other way, put the method, the utilities covered and the due dates in the lease (see the utility billing and on-bill charge sections). If you provide a utility that is not included in the rent, the security deposit may cover what the tenant owes you for it under the rental agreement. If the lease gives an option to buy, the seller must also give a good-faith declaration of electricity cost for the most recent three months the property was occupied, where the owner pays the electric bills directly. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no utility disclosure attachment rule.

title: Accessory Dwelling Units
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes push counties to allow accessory dwelling units (ADUs) and protect renting them long term. Each county must adopt ordinances allowing at least two ADUs, or the reasonable equivalent, on residentially zoned lots (lots in zones principally reserved for single-family and two-family detached homes, not rural or low-density zones), or instead designate districts that allow them. If a county has not done so by December 31, 2026, it may not deny a permit for up to two ADUs on a single-family lot just because the lot would exceed the maximum number of units, though it may still deny on infrastructure, design or development standards. No county may prohibit using any dwelling unit on a residentially zoned lot as a separately leased long-term rental, as each county defines that term. A private covenant recorded after May 28, 2024 may not limit the number of ADUs below what the statute allows, or limit long-term rental of units, on such a lot; covenants recorded earlier are not affected. These rules do not apply outside the State urban district, within special management areas, or in areas a county deems at high risk of flooding, lava or fire, and ADUs remain subject to county development standards. The statute neither requires nor forbids owner occupancy of the lot; check your county's ADU ordinance, which was not reviewed. Once rented, an ADU is an ordinary residential tenancy under the landlord-tenant code. If you live on the lot, do not assume the fair housing and source-of-income exemptions for an owner-occupied building with no more than two units cover a detached ADU: they speak of a single building, so treat the rental as covered. Condominium or planned-community documents recorded before May 28, 2024, and county short-term rental rules, may still limit how an ADU is used.

title: Alarm Tampering: No Fee Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule letting a lease charge a fee when a tenant removes, disables or tampers with a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm, and no statute on rental alarms at all (see the smoke and carbon monoxide alarms row). Recover the cost, not a penalty. A tenant must not wilfully destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the premises, its facilities or equipment, or let anyone on the premises with the tenant's permission do so, and must keep landlord-supplied facilities and appliances in fit condition, reasonable wear and tear excepted. If a tenant's disabling of an alarm is a material failure to meet those duties, give written notice and at least ten days after receipt to remedy it (no time is needed when the failure threatens irremediable damage to a person or property); if the tenant does not, you may fix it yourself and bill the actual and reasonable cost, which is treated as rent due on the next regular rent date, or immediately if the tenancy has ended. A flat tampering fee is not authorized by statute and could be attacked as a penalty or an unauthorized charge. Fire law reaches tenants as well as owners: an owner, occupant or other person in control of a building who violates any law, ordinance or rule relating to protection from fire loss may be fined up to $2,500 or jailed up to 30 days, or both, each day a separate offense. You, as owner, may not permit occupancy of a building that is not reasonably safe from fire loss, so test alarms at each turnover and promptly replace any a tenant disables. County fire and building codes, which may require alarms, were not searched.

title: Asbestos: No Rental Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule requiring you to inspect a rental for asbestos, disclose asbestos to a tenant, or give a tenant notice before asbestos work. Asbestos is regulated as a pollution and work-safety matter. The Department of Health may set asbestos exposure standards and work practice and notification requirements for demolishing and renovating buildings that contain asbestos (its administrative rules were not searched), and no person may engage in any activity that causes a violation of the asbestos and lead law; a county may regulate asbestos matters the department's rules do not cover. Work that removes, encloses, encapsulates, repairs, demolishes or otherwise disturbs friable asbestos, or asbestos material that may become friable during the work, generally must be done by a licensed asbestos specialty contractor; some incidental work, such as on vinyl asbestos floor materials or asbestos pipe or sheets, is excepted when done without a health hazard. Your general duties still apply: comply with building and housing laws materially affecting health and safety, and make the repairs needed to keep the premises habitable. The cautious course: before renovating, sanding or demolishing in an older building, have suspect materials tested and use a licensed contractor; tell tenants in writing about any known asbestos hazard and planned work; and give at least two days' notice before entering, except in an emergency. Lead-based paint is covered by its own row. Federal law may also apply.

title: Balconies and Lanais: No Inspection Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes set no schedule of periodic inspections, engineering reports or repair deadlines for balconies, lanais, decks, exterior stairways or other elevated elements of rental buildings. Your ongoing duties cover them: comply with building and housing laws materially affecting health and safety; keep common areas of a multi-unit property clean and safe; and make all repairs needed to keep the premises habitable. Separately, every owner or person in control of a building must keep it reasonably safe from loss of life or injury by fire, and county fire chiefs inspect buildings other than the interiors of private dwellings. Tenants must report a defective condition they have reason to believe you do not know about as soon as practicable. If you rent a condominium unit, a balcony or lanai designed to serve only that unit but outside its boundaries is, unless the declaration says otherwise, a limited common element, so check the declaration and the association's maintenance responsibilities before you schedule repairs. The cautious course: have elevated wood or metal elements looked at periodically by a qualified professional, repair promptly, and keep a record. County building codes may impose more and were not searched.

title: Casualty and Mitigation Rules Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: Hawaii's casualty and abandonment rules are part of the landlord-tenant code, and neither you nor a tenant may waive or agree to give up rights or remedies under the code, except where the code itself allows it. Neither rule contains such an exception. Casualty: if fire or other casualty makes the unit, or any part of the premises reasonably necessary to its use, partly or wholly unusable, and it happened without wilful fault of the tenant or a member of the tenant's family, the tenant may (1) move out immediately and notify you of that choice within one week after leaving, in which case the rental agreement ends on the move-out date (if the tenant does not notify you, rent runs until you actually learn of the move-out or that further occupancy is impossible), or (2) if continued occupancy is lawful, stop using the unusable part and owe no more than the fair rental value of the part still used. A lease cannot remove or shorten these choices; the library's fire or casualty clause follows them. Only wilful fault by the tenant or the tenant's family bars the remedy, not ordinary carelessness or a guest's fault. Mitigation: when a tenant wrongfully quits and clearly shows by words or deeds that it will not resume the tenancy, you may recover only the lesser of the rent for the rest of the term, or the rent for the period reasonably needed to re-rent at fair rent plus the difference between the fair rent and the agreed rent and a reasonable commission; the second measure applies whether or not you actually re-rent. A tenant who backs out before moving in owes the lesser of the money deposited, one month's rent, or the re-rental measure plus reasonable costs. A lease cannot enlarge these measures (see the abandonment damages row). Tenancy type: the rules apply to fixed-term and periodic tenancies alike; the remaining-term figure matters most in a fixed term. They do not reach occupancies the code excludes, such as transient day-to-day hotel or motel stays and housing directly controlled by the Hawaii Public Housing Authority.

title: Children in the Household
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes have no list of lease terms you must include about children, and no statewide occupancy standard (such as persons per bedroom) for private rentals; county building and housing codes may set space or occupancy limits and were not searched. What Hawaii does have is a ban on familial-status discrimination. Familial status covers a parent with legal custody living with a minor child, a person living with a minor child with the parent's written or unwritten permission, a pregnant person, and anyone in the process of getting legal custody of a minor. You may not refuse to rent, or set different terms, conditions, privileges, facilities or services, because a household includes children, and you may not advertise, use an application form, or make a record or inquiry indicating a limitation, specification or preference against children. List every occupant, including children, in the lease, and apply the same occupancy rules to every household, basing any limit on the unit's size and applicable codes, not on age. Rules aimed at children, such as pool or play-area rules, must serve tenants' safety or welfare, be reasonably related to that purpose, and apply to all tenants in a fair manner. The protected class of age covers adults (people over the age of majority and emancipated minors). Exemptions: the discrimination ban does not apply when you rent a unit in a building with no more than two units and you live in the other, or rent up to four rooms in a home you live in; on the statute's wording the advertising and inquiry ban still applies even then. The familial-status and age rules do not apply to housing for older persons as defined by federal law. Federal law may also apply.

title: No Confession of Judgment
bodyText: A tenant may not authorize anyone to confess judgment on a claim arising out of a rental agreement for a dwelling unit, and any such authorization is void. Do not use a cognovit or warrant-of-attorney clause, a pre-signed stipulation to judgment for possession, or a pre-signed consent judgment, whether in the lease or in a separate paper. To recover possession or money you must bring a summary possession case or other court action in which the tenant can be heard. A settlement reached after a dispute arises is different: a claim disputed in good faith may be settled by agreement, and any claim may be settled for less than the amount claimed, but a settlement in which a party gives up rights under the landlord-tenant code is invalid if a court finds it was unconscionable when made, taking into account the party's competence, any deception or coercion, the legal advice received, and the value given. Hawaii's statutes and court rules contain no separate rule on confessed ejectment for residential leases. The ban covers every tenancy under the landlord-tenant code; the library offers no confession clause for any tenancy.

title: Consumer Protection Act
bodyText: Hawaii's consumer protection act makes unfair methods of competition and unfair or deceptive acts or practices in the conduct of any trade or commerce unlawful. Only a consumer, the attorney general or the Office of Consumer Protection may sue over an unfair or deceptive practice. A consumer is a natural person who, primarily for personal, family or household purposes, purchases or attempts to purchase goods or services, and the act's definitions count a lease or contract to lease as a purchase or sale. Whether a residential tenant renting a home is a consumer under the act is a question of case law, which was not searched; the cautious course is to assume that deceptive advertising, misstatements about the unit, fees or the tenant's rights, and abusive collection practices can be challenged under it. A consumer who wins recovers at least $1,000 or three times actual damages, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney's fees and costs (an elder may be awarded at least $5,000 instead), and may seek an injunction; the State may seek a civil penalty of $500 to $10,000 for each violation, each day a separate violation. A contract made in violation of the act is void. Two landlord acts are unfair or deceptive practices by statute: recovering possession by wilfully interrupting or reducing water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service (except after abandonment or surrender), which also carries minimum damages of three times the monthly rent or $1,000, whichever is greater; and violating the emergency price and termination limits while they are in force. Collecting a fee or charge that neither the agreement nor the law authorizes, or claiming that a debt may be increased by fees that cannot legally be added, is a prohibited collection practice for anyone who regularly collects consumer debts owed to them, and is treated as an unfair or deceptive act (see the void lease term row). Hawaii's statutes do not make leaving blank spaces at signing, or failing to give a copy at signing, an unlawful practice for residential leases (those rules cover credit sales, door-to-door sales and lease-purchase of goods), though you must give the tenant a copy of a written lease (see the lease copy row). The Office of Consumer Protection may also investigate and try to resolve any dispute under the landlord-tenant code. Federal law may also apply.

title: Domestic Violence Information Is Confidential
bodyText: If a tenant gives you notice and documents to end a rental agreement early because of domestic violence, you may not disclose any information the tenant reported to you under that law unless the tenant consents in a signed statement, the information is required or relevant in a court case, or other law requires the disclosure. Keep those papers apart from the general tenant file, limit who can see them, and do not share them with other tenants, the abuser, references or screening companies. The same care fits the other domestic violence rights. You must change the locks within three days of a victim tenant's request, at the tenant's expense, but not where the abuser is a party to the rental agreement unless a court order requiring the abuser to vacate has been furnished to you; and once a court orders the abuser to vacate, you have no duty to let that person in unless a law enforcement officer is with them, or to give them keys. Hawaii's address confidentiality program lets victims of domestic abuse, sexual offenses or stalking use a substitute address, but it binds state and county agencies, not private landlords. Hawaii's statutes contain no other confidentiality rule for domestic violence information a landlord holds. Tenancy type: the early termination right, and with it this disclosure ban, covers rental agreements of a term of one year or less (treat month-to-month tenancies as covered); keep the same confidentiality for any tenant. The early termination right itself is in the domestic violence early termination row, and lock changes in their own row. Federal law may also apply, especially in federally assisted housing.

title: Calls for Police or Emergency Help
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule giving tenants a non-waivable right to call police or emergency services, and none barring a lease from penalizing those calls. The retaliation ban protects a tenant's good-faith complaints to you or to the Department of Health, the building department, the Office of Consumer Protection or another agency concerned with landlord-tenant disputes about conditions violating health laws or the landlord-tenant code, and good-faith repair requests; it does not list calls to police or emergency services. Even so, do not write a lease term that limits, discourages or penalizes calls for police, fire or medical help, or that treats a tenant who is a crime or domestic violence victim as in breach because help was called; a court may refuse to enforce a term it finds unconscionable, and the library's criminal-activity clause expressly protects emergency calls and crime victims (see the crime-free lease row). Domestic violence victims have specific early termination, lock-change and vacate-order protections. Federal law may also apply, and county nuisance rules were not searched.

title: No Eviction Penalty Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule that specifically voids a lease clause imposing a penalty because you served an eviction notice or filed a possession case. Other rules reach most such clauses. A lease may make the tenant pay costs of suit and reasonable attorney's fees for unpaid rent, but the fees may not exceed 25% of the unpaid rent and apply only after default and referral to an attorney who is not your salaried employee; in all other matters under the landlord-tenant code the lease may provide only for reasonable fees and costs to the prevailing party, and any other fee term is unenforceable. In contract cases the court taxes reasonable attorney's fees against the losing party, capped at 25% of the judgment. A late charge, if the lease provides one, may not exceed 8% of the rent due. Holdover charges, abandonment damages and the damages for backing out before move-in are capped by statute, and the domestic violence and servicemember early exits allow no fee or penalty. A tenant who pays before the writ of possession issues in a nonpayment case must pay the rent, interest at 8% a year, the costs and charges of the proceedings and your expenses, including a reasonable attorney's fee, which you recover through the court, not through a lease penalty. A court may refuse to enforce, or limit, a term it finds unconscionable. The library offers no eviction-penalty clause; recover only actual, documented costs through these routes (see the attorney's fees, notice fee and liquidated damages rows).

title: No Waiver of Landlord Liability
bodyText: A lease term that exempts or limits your liability, or requires the tenant to indemnify you, for damage to persons or property caused by your acts or omissions, or those of your agents, servants or employees, in or about the unit or the rest of the premises, is void. This covers hold-harmless, release, waiver-of-liability and tenant-indemnity clauses aimed at your own negligence or that of your staff and contractors acting for you, whether in the lease, the house rules or an addendum. A separate rule voids any agreement exempting you from liability for damage caused by entries into the unit (for example, theft or damage during an entry the tenant refused, an entry without consent while the tenant was present, or a negligent entry), except a tenant's consent to a particular entry. What you may do: require the tenant to carry renters insurance for the tenant's own belongings and liability, make the tenant responsible for damage the tenant, household members or guests cause, and rely on the statutory rule that a tenant who fails to give a lease-required notice of an extended absence must indemnify you for resulting damage. Clauses allocating risks you do not cause (such as the tenant's own property losses from events outside your control) are not covered by the ban, but draft them narrowly; a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable term. The ban applies to every tenancy under the landlord-tenant code, fixed-term or periodic.

title: Fair Housing in Hawaii
bodyText: Hawaii's fair housing law applies to owners, anyone engaging in a rental, and anyone (licensed or not) who rents or leases property for pay, and their employees and agents. Protected classes: race; sex, including gender identity or expression; sexual orientation; color; religion; marital status; familial status; ancestry; disability; age (adults); and HIV infection. The chapter defines national origin (it includes an ancestor's national origin) but its list names ancestry, not national origin; federal law protects national origin, so treat it as covered. Banned practices include refusing to rent or negotiate; different terms, conditions, privileges, facilities or services; saying a unit is unavailable when it is not; steering; requiring an HIV test; refusing reasonable modifications or accommodations for a disability (with limits on what you may ask; see the disability accommodation row); failing to meet accessible design rules for covered multifamily housing first occupied after March 13, 1991; retaliating against, coercing, intimidating or interfering with anyone using these rights; inserting a discriminatory restriction in a lease or other instrument; attempts; and any advertisement, sign, application form, record or inquiry indicating a limitation or preference. Exemptions: the main ban does not apply when you rent a unit in a building with no more than two units and you live in the other, or rent up to four rooms in a home you live in; religious housing may limit by sex, sexual orientation or marital status; housing for older persons is exempt from the familial-status and age rules. The exemption names only the main ban, so on the statute's wording the advertising and inquiry ban still applies to an exempt owner (no court decision was searched); never advertise a preference. There is no small-landlord exemption. Source of income: separately, you may not advertise that you will not rent to, discourage, refuse, or set different conditions for a person in a section 8 voucher or permanent supportive housing program. That rule has its own exemptions that cover advertising too: commercially reasonable verification of income and credit; owning four or fewer units in the State (unless the owner holds more than a 10% interest in more than four); no program approval within 21 days of a good-faith request, including the unit inspection; the owner-occupied two-unit building and up to four rooms; and subsidized affordable projects. Its penalties are up to $2,000 for a first violation and $2,500 after, with no attorney's fees. Enforcement: the Civil Rights Commission investigates complaints; after it finds reasonable cause, the complainant, the respondent or an aggrieved person may elect within 20 days to go to court instead of an administrative hearing, and the commission represents the complainant. A person may also sue within two years of the practice. Remedies include orders to rent, damages (which may be set at $500 for each violation unless more is proven), punitive damages in court, and attorney's fees. Hawaii's statutes do not make a landlord's sexual harassment of a tenant or applicant a crime or a separate housing violation, but demands for sexual favors tied to a tenancy can be challenged as discrimination in terms or conditions because of sex, and other criminal laws may apply. The state constitution has no equal-dignity clause adding classes such as social origin. Federal law may also apply.

title: Fire Code Duties
bodyText: Hawaii has a state fire code, adopted by the state fire council, setting minimum requirements for protecting people and property from fire loss, including control of conditions hazardous to life or property in the design, use or occupancy of buildings.
