The state fire code becomes part of the Hawaii state building codes, and each county must amend and adopt those codes for its own area within two years; the county fire and building codes in force are the standard for your property (the code texts and county ordinances were not searched). As owner, you must construct, keep and make the building reasonably safe from loss of life or injury to persons or property by fire, given its construction and use; you may not permit occupancy of a building that is not reasonably safe from fire loss; and you must furnish reasonably adequate fire protection and safeguards and do everything else reasonably necessary to prevent fire loss. The county fire chief inspects buildings and premises, but not the interiors of private dwellings, at least once every five years or as often as the chief finds necessary, and may serve a written order on the owner, occupant or person responsible to correct a violation or unreasonable fire risk within a set time; you may appeal to the county fire appeals board within five days. An owner, occupant or person in control who violates a fire-protection law, ordinance, rule or order may be fined up to $2,500 or jailed up to 30 days, or both, each day a separate offense, and counties may add civil penalties. The landlord-tenant code makes code compliance a continuing duty for both you and the tenant: you must comply with all applicable building and housing laws materially affecting health and safety, and so must the tenant. After a government agency's written notice of a violation, you must begin repairs within seven calendar days (see the repair rows).

title: Fire Sprinklers
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes impose no fire sprinkler installation or retrofit duty on residential landlords. Instead, until June 30, 2027 (when the provision is scheduled to be repealed), no county may require the installation or retrofitting of automatic fire sprinklers or a sprinkler system in any new or existing detached one- or two-family dwelling unit in a structure used only for residential purposes; the bar does not cover new homes that need a variance from access road or firefighting water supply requirements. For apartment buildings, condominiums and other multi-unit structures, sprinkler requirements come from the state fire code, the Hawaii state building codes and county building and fire codes, which were not searched; county codes may also address existing high-rise buildings. Whatever the code requires, you must keep the building reasonably safe from fire loss and comply with building and housing laws materially affecting health and safety, and if a building has sprinklers you must keep landlord-supplied facilities in good working order. If you rent a condominium unit, sprinkler work in the building is normally the association's responsibility; check the declaration and any assessments.

title: No Foreign Ownership Restriction
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no restriction on foreign persons, foreign governments or foreign adversaries owning or leasing residential property, no alien land law, and no rule requiring a lease to a nonresident alien to state that fact or give the alien's name and address. You may rent to, and buy from or sell to, a foreign national on the same terms as anyone else, and you may not treat an applicant differently because of ancestry (see the fair housing row). A territorial-era provision on homestead leases of public lands, printed with the historical Organic Act, does not govern private residential leases today. Federal law may also apply, including federal tax withholding when a foreign person sells real property.

title: Which Code Edition Applies
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes generally do not freeze building and fire standards at a named edition. The Hawaii state building codes are based on the state fire code, the Uniform Plumbing Code, the International Building, Residential and Energy Conservation Codes, the National Electrical Code and other national standards, named without an edition. The state building code council must adopt each code within two years of its official publication date; if it does not, the new code automatically becomes part of the Hawaii state building code until the council adopts an amended version. Each county must amend and adopt the state codes within two years after state adoption; if it does not, the state codes apply as an interim county building code. The state fire council reviews and amends the fire code every year. So the standard that applies to your building depends on the county code in force when the work was permitted and on any later retrofit rules, not on a date written in the statute; check with your county building department (county codes were not searched). A few statutory rules are tied to dates rather than editions: accessible design rules apply to covered multifamily housing first occupied after March 13, 1991; county codes must require pressure-balance or thermostatic shower valves (unless the water serving showers is limited to 110 degrees Fahrenheit) in new dwelling units with building permits issued after December 31, 1992; and a new single-family home permitted on or after January 1, 2010 generally must include a solar water heater unless a variance is approved.

title: Passing Government Fines to Tenants
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule that specifically bars or allows passing a government fine imposed on you through to a tenant. General rules decide it. Your duty to comply with building and housing laws materially affecting health and safety cannot be shifted by the lease (except through a good-faith repair agreement that does not cover code violations you must cure), so a lease term making the tenant pay fines for conditions you are responsible for is likely unenforceable. At the start of the tenancy you may collect only the first month's rent and the security deposit, and any new recurring charge is a rent change that needs the proper notice (see the government fee row). Where the tenant's own breach caused the violation (for example, the tenant's failure to comply with codes, or wilful or negligent damage), you may recover your resulting damages from the tenant: give written notice and time to remedy, bill the actual and reasonable cost of a remedy you perform, or sue for waste or breach. Keep the fine notice and proof that the tenant caused the condition. Some fines fall on the occupant directly: fire-protection penalties reach any owner, occupant or person in control who violates a fire law, rule or order. County fines and ordinances were not searched.

title: Immigration Status: No State Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule requiring or forbidding a landlord to ask about an applicant's or tenant's immigration or citizenship status, no rule making it unlawful to rent to a person without lawful immigration status, and no immigrant tenant protection act. Hawaii's fair housing law protects ancestry; it defines national origin (including an ancestor's national origin) but does not list national origin among its protected classes, and federal law protects national origin. The cautious course: do not ask about immigration status unless a government housing program requires it; ask every applicant for the same kind of identification and income proof; and accept any reliable photo identification. Hawaii issues limited purpose driver's licenses and identification cards to residents who cannot prove authorized presence in the United States, and a lease or rental agreement is among the documents an applicant may use to prove Hawaii residency for one. Never threaten to report a tenant's status to force a move or payment; that could be retaliation, interference with fair housing rights, or a crime under other laws. Federal law may also apply.

title: Jury Waivers: No Statute
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes neither allow nor forbid a jury-trial waiver in a residential lease, and there is no standard-form contract statute making a jury or class-action waiver presumptively unconscionable. Most landlord-tenant cases never reach a jury: district courts try all cases without a jury, and a summary possession case is brought in district court. If a party demands a jury in a civil matter triable of right by a jury, in the manner and time the court rules require, the case is transferred to circuit court. The state constitution preserves the right of trial by jury in suits at common law where the value in controversy exceeds $5,000, and a party who does not demand a jury on time under the court rules waives it. Whether a jury waiver in a lease is enforceable, and against whom, is a question of case law, which was not searched; a case note printed with the statutes reports that an express jury waiver in a lease did not bind third-party leasing agents who were not parties to it. The jury right is not a right under the landlord-tenant code, so the code's non-waiver rule does not itself void a waiver, but a court may refuse to enforce a term it finds unconscionable. The library offers no jury waiver clause.

title: Using a Void Lease Term
bodyText: Hawaii's landlord-tenant code attaches no special penalty to putting a prohibited term in a lease or knowingly using such a lease. The offending term is simply void or unenforceable, and the rest of the lease stands. Two narrower rules can still make it costly. First, inserting a discriminatory restriction on occupancy or leasing into a lease or other written instrument is itself a discriminatory practice under fair housing law, with damages that may be set at $500 for each violation unless more is proven. Second, collecting under a void term can be an unfair or deceptive practice. The collection practices law covers anyone who, in the regular course of business, collects consumer debts owed to that person (which on its wording can include a landlord collecting rent and charges from an individual tenant), and makes it a prohibited practice to represent that a debt may be increased by attorney's fees, service fees or other charges that may not legally be added, or to collect any interest, charge, fee or expense incidental to the debt unless the agreement or the law authorizes it. A collection agency collecting for you faces parallel bans, and may not collect a collection fee from the tenant, or an attorney's fee except after suit is filed and then no more than 25% of the unpaid principal. Each prohibited practice is treated as an unfair or deceptive act under the consumer protection act: the State may seek a civil penalty of $500 to $10,000 for each violation, each day a separate violation, and a consumer who sues recovers at least $1,000 or three times actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees. Whether these laws reach a particular landlord, and whether merely offering a lease with a void term is itself deceptive, are questions of case law, which was not searched. The cautious course: remove void terms (for example, fees beyond the statutory caps), never demand or collect a charge the law does not allow, and correct any notice or ledger that adds one.

title: What a Hawaii Lease Must Include
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no single list of terms a residential lease must contain, and an oral rental agreement is valid. Specific rules require items in or with the lease. (1) If you, as owner or landlord, live outside the State or on another island, you must designate on the written rental agreement an agent who lives on the island where the unit is (for an oral agreement, give the tenant a written statement on demand). (2) In writing at or before the start of the tenancy, give the name and address of each person authorized to manage the premises and of each owner or person authorized to act for the owner for service of process and receiving rent, notices and demands, and keep it current (in multi-unit buildings a posted notice may be used instead). (3) Give the tenant a copy of a written lease. (4) Give tenants your general excise tax number. (5) Before initial occupancy, make a written inventory of the condition of the premises and any furnishings and appliances, signed by you and the tenant, with a copy to each tenant. (6) Write a lease of five years or less in plain language with section captions. Some rights exist only if the lease provides for them: a late charge (capped at 8% of the rent due); attorney's fees, within the statutory limits; your consent to subletting or assignment (in a written agreement); notice from the tenant of an extended absence no later than its first day; a term changing the default rule that using the unit other than as the tenant's home, or not using it, is a breach; a term other than month to month (agreed in writing); applying the deposit to the last month's rent (a written agreement when the tenant gives 45 days' notice); a pet deposit; and a tenant repair agreement. The tenant may also designate, in the lease or a separate writing, a representative to collect or dispose of the tenant's belongings if the tenant dies. House rules bind the tenant only if brought to the tenant's attention at the start, or later consented to in writing when they substantially change the bargain. Each item has its own row in the library. Federal law may also require disclosures, such as for lead-based paint.

title: Code Rights Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: Hawaii's landlord-tenant code has a chapter-wide non-waiver rule: except as the code itself provides, neither a tenant nor a landlord may waive or agree to give up rights or remedies under the code. It covers every section of the code and binds both sides. The code's own exceptions are specific: a reasonable time for an action may be fixed by agreement if not manifestly unreasonable; rent is payable at the time and place agreed; the term may be any period agreed in writing; a written agreement may require your consent to subletting or assignment; you and the tenant may agree, in good faith, that the tenant performs specified repairs, maintenance and minor remodeling, but not work needed to cure your failure to meet building and housing laws; the deposit may be applied to the last month's rent only by written agreement; the lease may require notice of an extended absence and may change the rule on use other than as the tenant's home; the lease may provide for attorney's fees within the statutory limits; a tenant may consent to a particular entry; you and the tenant may agree before delivery to a condition other than the agreed one; and a seller's or manager's release from later liability applies unless otherwise agreed. Disputes may be settled: a claim disputed in good faith may be settled by agreement, and any claim may be settled for less than claimed, but a settlement giving up code rights is invalid if a court finds it unconscionable when made, considering the party's competence, any deception or coercion, the legal advice received, and the value given. A term that breaks the rule is unenforceable; it does not by itself void the rest of the lease. The rule reaches only rights and remedies under the landlord-tenant code; rights under other laws (such as fair housing or consumer protection) depend on those laws. It does not apply to occupancies the code excludes, such as transient hotel stays and housing directly controlled by the Hawaii Public Housing Authority.

title: Plain Language Leases
bodyText: Hawaii's plain-language law covers residential leases. Every written lease of space to be occupied for residential purposes for a term of five years or less, entered into on or after July 1, 1981, must be written in a clear and coherent manner using words with common and everyday meanings, and be appropriately divided and captioned by its sections. A residential lease longer than five years falls outside that clause but may still be covered as a consumer agreement for personal, family or household purposes if it involves less than $25,000; for a lease, that means total rent for the term, not counting option or extension periods, under $25,000 (assume the highest fixed rent for any period when rent is not fixed). Liability, the good-faith defense, the exclusions for separate documents and government-approved forms, and enforcement are in the plain language statement row. Use short sentences, define terms, and give each section a heading.

title: Pools: No State Safety Statute
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no pool barrier, fence, gate, drain-cover, lifeguard or safety-notice duty for residential landlords, and no pool notice at lease signing. Pools at apartment buildings, condominiums and other shared residential properties may be subject to Department of Health rules for swimming pools and to county building codes; neither was searched. Your general duties apply: comply with building and housing laws materially affecting health and safety, keep common areas of a multi-unit property clean and safe, and keep landlord-supplied facilities in good working order. Pool rules bind tenants only if they promote the tenants' convenience, safety or welfare or protect the property, are reasonably related to that purpose, apply to all tenants in a fair manner, are explicit enough to follow, and were given at move-in or, if a later rule substantially changes the bargain, consented to in writing. Rules about children's pool use should rest on safety and not single out families with children beyond what safety requires. The cautious course: a fence with a self-closing, self-latching gate, posted rules, regular inspection of drains and equipment, and liability insurance. Premises-liability case law was not searched.

title: Terms a Hawaii Lease Cannot Contain
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no single list of banned lease terms; the bans are spread through the landlord-tenant code and other laws. In a residential lease these are void or unenforceable: (1) any waiver of rights or remedies under the landlord-tenant code, except where the code allows it (see the non-waiver row); (2) a term exempting or limiting your liability, or making the tenant indemnify you, for damage caused by your or your agents' or employees' acts or omissions; (3) a tenant's authorization to confess judgment; (4) attorney's fee terms other than fees for unpaid rent of up to 25% of it after referral to an outside attorney, or prevailing-party fees in other code matters; (5) a late charge over 8% of the rent due; (6) collecting anything at the start beyond the first month's rent and the security deposit, a deposit above one month's rent plus an agreed pet deposit of up to one month's rent (never for an assistance animal), or deposit uses beyond the statutory list; (7) requiring postdated checks or other negotiable instruments for rent; (8) a term allowing eviction of a tenant certified for medical cannabis, unless the lease also allows eviction for smoking tobacco and the cannabis is smoked (not where condominium or planned-community documents ban medical cannabis); (9) in a single-family residence, a ban on lawful political signs; (10) waivers of your liability for abusive or harmful entries, other than consent to a particular entry; (11) a termination notice given to evade the rent-increase notice rules; (12) a restriction on occupancy or leasing based on a protected class (inserting one is itself a discriminatory practice); (13) fees or penalties for a domestic violence or servicemember early termination, and extra rent, fees or deposit because an abuser is excluded; (14) shifting your repair and fitness duties to the tenant, except a good-faith agreement for specified repairs, maintenance and minor remodeling that does not cover code violations you must cure or reduce your duties to other tenants; (15) rules adopted after move-in that substantially change the bargain, unless the tenant consents in writing, and any rule that fails the statutory tests. Hawaii's statutes contain no specific ban on passing home-warranty deductibles or copays to tenants, but charging a tenant for repairs you must make conflicts with your non-waivable duties; charge only for damage the tenant, household or guests caused. Outside the code, a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable term, recovering possession by cutting off utilities is an unfair practice, and general contract law (case law, not searched) may limit penalties. There is no general money penalty for using a banned term, though collecting a charge the law does not allow can be an unfair collection practice (see the void-term row).

title: Questions You May Not Ask Applicants
bodyText: Separate from the ban on discriminating, Hawaii's fair housing law bars using an application form, or making a record or inquiry in connection with a prospective rental, that indicates directly or indirectly an intent to limit, specify or discriminate because of race; sex, including gender identity or expression; sexual orientation; color; religion; marital status; familial status; ancestry; disability; age; or HIV infection. On the statute's wording this ban is not subject to the owner-occupant exemptions, which excuse only the main discrimination ban. Specific limits: you may not ask an applicant to be tested for HIV. If a disability is not readily apparent and a person asks for an accommodation, you may ask for information verifying that the person has a physical or mental impairment that substantially limits a major life activity, but you may not ask for medical records or access to health care providers, or ask about the diagnosis, nature or severity of the disability; for an assistance animal you may ask for verification from the person's treating health care professional, mental health professional or social worker. You also may not discourage a person from applying because the person uses a section 8 voucher or permanent supportive housing program, unless a source-of-income exemption applies. What you may ask, of every applicant alike: income and its source (in a commercially reasonable way), rental history, credit, references, and how many people will live in the unit. Do not ask about marriage, plans to have children, religion, ancestry, sexual orientation or medical history. You may confirm an applicant is an adult before charging a screening fee or signing a lease. A written inquiry, form or record that appears to be yours is prima facie evidence that you authorized it, so review your forms and your agents' scripts. Federal law may also apply.

title: Registered Offenders: No Occupancy Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule restricting where registered sex offenders (called covered offenders) may live, no duty for a landlord to check the registry, disclose that a registrant lives on the property, or refuse to rent to one, and no crime for leasing a unit where one or more registrants live. Registry information is public: the attorney general and county police release a registrant's name and aliases, birth year, physical description and photograph, residence address and length of residence, employment location, vehicles and offenses, online and at designated police stations, except for registrants with only one misdemeanor offense not committed against a minor. The registry carries a warning that anyone who uses the information to injure, harass or commit a criminal act against a registrant may face criminal prosecution, civil liability, or both. If you use the registry in screening, adopt a written policy, apply it to every applicant the same way, and base decisions on the information, not on assumptions about other household members. Hawaii's fair housing law does not list criminal history as a protected class, but federal law may also apply. County rules were not searched.

title: Renting in Single-Family Zones
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes do not limit renting homes in single-family zones, and they protect long-term rentals instead. No county may prohibit using any dwelling unit on a residentially zoned lot (a lot in a zone principally reserved for single-family and two-family detached homes) as a separately leased long-term rental, as each county defines that term, and a private covenant recorded after May 28, 2024 may not limit long-term rental of residential units on such a lot. These protections do not apply outside the State urban district, in special management areas, or in areas a county deems at high risk of flooding, lava or fire, and covenants recorded before May 28, 2024 are not affected. Hawaii's statutes set no statewide owner-occupancy requirement for renting. Other limits can apply. If you bought a new condominium unit by signing an owner-occupant affidavit, you may not lease, rent or offer to rent it until at least 365 consecutive days after the purchase was recorded. County rules on short-term and transient vacation rentals, and condominium or planned-community documents, may limit shorter rentals or set minimum terms; they were not reviewed. See the accessory dwelling unit row.

title: Steam Radiators: No Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule on steam radiators, radiator covers or steam heat in rentals, and no lease rider for them; they also set no heating standard for rentals (see the heating row). If a building has a boiler, radiators or other heating equipment you supply, you must keep it in good working order and comply with building and housing laws materially affecting health and safety. County building codes were not searched.

title: Voucher Inspections and the 21-Day Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's source-of-income law ties directly to program inspections. You may not refuse to rent to, or set different conditions for, a person because the person uses a section 8 housing choice voucher or a permanent supportive housing program, or because of the program's requirements; but that protection does not apply if the source of income is not approved within 21 days after the person submits a good-faith request for tenancy approval, which includes the inspection of the unit. So do not refuse or delay a voucher holder because of the program's approval and inspection process; but if the approval, including the inspection, is not completed within 21 days of a good-faith request, the protection no longer applies and you may rent to someone else. Keep a record of the request date and of your cooperation. The rule also does not apply to landlords owning four or fewer units in the State (unless the owner holds more than a 10% interest in more than four), to an owner-occupied building with no more than two units, to renting up to four rooms in a home you live in, or to subsidized affordable housing projects; you may verify income and creditworthiness in a commercially reasonable way. Violations bring a civil penalty of up to $2,000 for a first violation and $2,500 for later ones, plus court orders, but no attorney's fees. Once a subsidized tenancy starts, the program's conditions, including its periodic inspections, control over the landlord-tenant code where they conflict. A tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to your entry to inspect, and is liable for damage caused by unreasonably refusing access; give at least two days' notice and enter at reasonable hours. Hawaii's statutes contain no rule letting you end a tenancy because a tenant refuses a program inspection; rely on the program's rules and the ordinary breach notices. Federal law may also apply.

title: Protecting Tenant Personal Information
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no general rule barring you from disclosing information about a tenant, and no consent rule for sharing it, except for information a tenant gives you to end a lease because of domestic violence (see the domestic violence confidentiality row). Two data laws apply to tenant files. Social security numbers: a business may not intentionally make an individual's entire social security number available to the general public, print it on mailings unless an exception applies (and never visibly, or on a postcard or other mailer without an envelope), or require it to be sent over the internet without a secure connection or encryption; using it to run background checks, obtain a credit report, or collect a debt is allowed. Records disposal: any business that holds a Hawaii resident's name with a social security number, driver's license or state ID number, or a financial account, card number or access code must take reasonable measures against unauthorized access when disposing of the records, including policies for burning, pulverizing, recycling or shredding paper and destroying or erasing electronic media, described in a written policy; you may instead contract with a records-destruction business after due diligence and monitor it. Each violation can bring a penalty of up to $2,500 in an action by the attorney general or the Office of Consumer Protection, plus the injured person's actual damages, and the court may award attorney's fees to the prevailing party. These laws speak of a business, which includes a sole proprietorship; treat your rental activity as covered. Security-breach notice duties are in the tenant records row.

title: Tenant Organizing: No State Right
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule protecting tenants' right to form or join a tenant organization, meet in common areas, or distribute materials, and no rule barring you from interfering with organizing. The retaliation ban protects a tenant's good-faith complaints to you or to a government agency about conditions violating health laws or the landlord-tenant code, and good-faith repair requests, while the tenant keeps paying rent; a complaint made jointly with other tenants is still a complaint. It does not mention organizing itself. Tenant organizations do have one statutory role: any organization, including a tenant organization, may sue in its own name to abate a drug, prostitution or similar nuisance in its county. Fair housing law separately bars intimidating or threatening anyone who encourages others to use fair housing rights. The cautious course: treat organizing activity neutrally, apply common-area rules to all tenants in a fair manner, and never raise rent, cut services or end a tenancy in response to a joint complaint. County rules were not searched.

title: Screening Applicants in Hawaii
bodyText: Hawaii regulates tenant screening only in pieces; there is no separate screening statute. Fees: you may charge an application screening fee only to cover the costs of getting information about an applicant 18 or older or an emancipated minor (such as reference checks, tenant reports, criminal background checks and credit reports), give a receipt and cost breakdown on request, and return any unused part within 30 days after submitting the screening requests (see the application fee row). Fair housing: apply the same criteria to every applicant and ask nothing that indicates a preference based on a protected class; you may not require an HIV test or ask about the diagnosis, nature or severity of a disability. Source of income: unless an exemption applies (for example, you own four or fewer units in the State), you may not refuse or set different conditions for a section 8 voucher or permanent supportive housing participant, though you may verify the source and amount of income and evaluate creditworthiness in a commercially reasonable way; Hawaii's statutes do not limit a minimum-income test to the tenant's share of the rent, so apply any income test in a commercially reasonable way that does not screen out voucher holders as such. Criminal history: Hawaii's statutes contain no limit on considering criminal history in rental screening, no conditional-offer or look-back rule, no rule on erased or expunged records in housing, and no negligence shield for renting to a person with a record. Apply a written, consistent policy. Sex offender registry information is public (see the registered offenders row). Data: you may collect social security numbers to run background checks and credit reports, but must protect them and dispose of screening records securely (see the tenant information row). Federal law, including the Fair Credit Reporting Act, may also apply.

title: No Exemption Notice Needed
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule requiring a lease statement or notice telling tenants that a property is exempt from rent caps, just-cause eviction rules or a tenant opportunity-to-purchase law, because Hawaii's statutes contain no general rent cap, just-cause eviction rule or tenant purchase right for private rentals (see the rent control and just-cause rows). The narrow rules that do exist need no exemption notice: the temporary emergency limits on rent increases and terminations apply only while a proclamation invokes them; condominium conversion, demolition and transient vacation rental conversion require 120 days' notice; and tenants of rental projects financed with certain state housing finance corporation project loans get a first option to buy their units if the loan is prepaid to convert them to ownership (see the conversion notice row).

title: Unconscionable Terms
bodyText: In any court case about a rental agreement, if the court finds as a matter of law that the agreement or any of its terms was unconscionable when made, it may refuse to enforce the agreement, enforce the rest without the unconscionable term, or limit the term's application to avoid an unconscionable result. Before deciding, the court must let the parties present evidence of the term's setting, purpose and effect. A practice the landlord-tenant code expressly permits is not unconscionable in itself, so terms that track the code (such as a late charge within the 8% cap or attorney's fees within the statutory limits) are on firm ground. The same test applies to settlements: a settlement in which a party gives up rights under the code is invalid if a court finds it unconscionable when made, considering the party's competence, any deception or coercion, the legal advice received, and the value given. Hawaii's statutes do not declare any particular lease clause, such as one on misrepresenting an animal's status, fully enforceable regardless of unconscionability; misrepresenting a service animal is dealt with separately (see the service animal misrepresentation row). Unconscionability is judged by courts case by case; case law was not searched. Draft terms in plain language, keep them balanced, and do not bury significant obligations.

title: No Veterans Rental Incentive
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no tax credit, payment, deposit guarantee or other incentive for landlords who rent to veterans. Servicemembers have their own early termination rights (see the servicemember row). State and federal veterans' agencies and programs may offer rental help to veterans, which counts as a source of income you consider like any other; federal programs were not searched, and a veteran using a section 8 voucher is protected by the source-of-income law unless an exemption applies.

title: Water Heater Temperature
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule requiring you to set a water heater to a maximum temperature before a new tenant moves in, and no scald-prevention notice. Two building rules touch the subject: county building codes must require that showers in new dwelling units (building permits issued after December 31, 1992) have individual pressure-balance or thermostatic mixing valves unless the water serving the showers is limited to 110 degrees Fahrenheit; and a new single-family home permitted on or after January 1, 2010 generally must include a solar water heater system unless a variance is approved. You must keep landlord-supplied plumbing and appliances, including the water heater, in good working order. The cautious course: set tank water heaters to about 120 degrees Fahrenheit at turnover, check any mixing valves, and note the setting on the move-in inventory. County codes were not searched.

title: Window Guards: No Rule
bodyText: Hawaii's statutes contain no rule requiring window guards, window stops or other fall-prevention devices in rentals, and no window-guard lease notice. Your general duties apply: comply with building and housing laws materially affecting health and safety, keep common areas of a multi-unit property safe, and make the repairs needed to keep the premises habitable, including windows, screens and lanai railings. If a tenant with young children asks for window stops or guards, consider installing them, choosing devices that can be released from inside for emergency escape. County building codes were not searched.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Hawaii follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (HRS § 490:3-311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (HRS § 490:1-308(b)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Hawaii's landlord-tenant act imposes a duty of good faith: every duty under the chapter, and every act that must be done before using a right or remedy under it, carries an obligation of good faith in its performance or enforcement (HRS § 521-10). That binds you and the tenant alike. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.

title: Renting Out a Home on Hawaiian Home Lands
bodyText: Hawaii has no general rule requiring a government officer to approve residential leases of communal or tribal land, but one land system has its own rule: Hawaiian home lands. The Department of Hawaiian Home Lands leases these tracts to native Hawaiians, and title stays with the State (Hawaiian Homes Commission Act, 1920, § 207(a)-(b)). Every homestead lease is subject to conditions that apply whether or not the lease states them, and one of them is that the lessee may not sublet the tract or the improvements on it (HHCA § 208(5)). The only exception is that the lessee, with the department's approval, may rent lodging to a native Hawaiian or Hawaiians, either within the lessee's existing home or in a separate dwelling unit built on the premises (HHCA § 208(5)). So if you are a homestead lessee, don't rent the home, a room or an accessory unit to anyone until the department has approved it, and only to a native Hawaiian tenant. What happens to a homestead lease after a forbidden rental is set by the department's rules, which this library has not reviewed. If you are renting from someone whose home is on Hawaiian home lands, ask to see the department's written approval. This library's lease clauses assume land the landlord may lease freely.

title: Recording a Lease Longer Than One Year
bodyText: Hawaii requires leases for a term of more than one year to be recorded in the Bureau of Conveyances (HRS § 502-83). An unrecorded lease stays valid between you and the tenant, but it is void against a later buyer, lessee or mortgagee of the property who acts in good faith, pays value, has no actual notice of the lease, and records first (HRS § 502-83). Whether a tenant's possession counts as notice to a later buyer is a question of case law this library has not reviewed. No Hawaii statute in the Residential Landlord-Tenant Code makes recording a condition of the tenant's or your rights under that Code, and most residential leases of a year or less need not be recorded. If you sign a lease longer than one year, the cautious course is to record it, or a memorandum of it, and to tell any buyer or lender about it in writing. Land registered in the Land Court has its own registration rules, which this library has not reviewed.

title: Community Facilities District Taxes and Your Lease
bodyText: No Hawaii statute requires a residential lease to state that the property is in a special district or gives a tenant a vote or seat in one. Hawaii's main special-district tool is the county community facilities district: a county with a charter may create these districts by ordinance and levy a special tax on property in them, and the tax is a lien on the property (HRS § 46-80.1(a)-(b)). The tax falls on the property, but the statute speaks to leases that pass it to a lessee. The county ordinance must say that if a lease requires the lessee to pay the proposed special tax, the owner may waive that requirement in writing, and if the owner does not, the notice, hearing and protest rights pass to the lessee (HRS § 46-80.1(c)(3)). The ordinance must also provide notice to buyers or lessees who would be required to pay the special tax (HRS § 46-80.1(c)(4)). If your property is in a community facilities district and your lease makes the tenant pay any part of the special tax, read the county ordinance and give the tenant whatever notice it requires before signing. This library's standard lease does not pass district taxes to the tenant.

title: Renting to Students
bodyText: A student who rents a house or apartment from a private landlord is an ordinary tenant under Hawaii's Residential Landlord-Tenant Code; no Hawaii statute in that Code sets special rules for student leases. The Code's student-housing rule is an exclusion. The Code does not apply to residence in a structure directly controlled and managed by the University of Hawaii or another college in the State for housing its own students or faculty, or in a structure on land leased from the college by a nonprofit for the exclusive purpose of housing its students or faculty (HRS § 521-7(2)(A)). It also does not apply to residence in a structure directly controlled and managed by a private dorm management company that offers at least fifty beds to students of a college in the State (HRS § 521-7(2)(B)). None of these exclusions applies if the arrangement was created solely to avoid the Code (HRS § 521-7). If you rent a few rooms or a house to students, the full Code applies, and the cautious course is to use an ordinary residential lease.

title: Hunting on Rented Land
bodyText: This library does not cover farm leases. If you rent out a home that comes with land, Hawaii's wildlife law decides who gives hunting permission: no person may enter land held or occupied by another to hunt or take wildlife without permission, and once the owner has let another person occupy or hold the land, the permission must come from that occupier or holder (or the occupier's agent), not the owner (HRS § 183D-26(a)). So once the land is rented, a hunter needs your tenant's permission, not just yours. A prosecution under that section can be brought only on the sworn complaint of the owner, occupier or holder, or their agent (HRS § 183D-26(b)). If you want to keep hunting rights or bar hunting on the property, say so in the lease.

title: Time Limit to Sue for Rent or Damages
bodyText: Hawaii's Residential Landlord-Tenant Code sets no deadline of its own for suing a tenant; the general time limits apply. A suit to recover a debt founded on a contract, which includes unpaid rent under a lease, must be brought within six years after the claim accrued (HRS § 657-1(1)). A suit for compensation for damage or injury to property must be brought within two years (HRS § 657-7). Which period a court applies to damage claimed as a breach of the lease is a question of case law this library has not reviewed, so the cautious course is to sue for property damage within two years after the damage happened. Treat each missed rent payment as starting its own clock, and don't count on a partial payment to restart the period.

title: Banning a Non-Tenant from the Property
bodyText: Hawaii's criminal trespass law can help you keep out a person who is not your tenant, but it is never a way to remove a tenant from possession. A person enters or remains unlawfully when not licensed, invited or otherwise privileged to be there; on premises open to the public, the person is privileged unless they defy a lawful order not to enter or remain, personally communicated by the owner or another authorized person (HRS § 708-800). Knowingly entering or remaining unlawfully in a dwelling, or in or upon the premises of an apartment building, is criminal trespass in the first degree, a misdemeanor (HRS § 708-813(1)(a), (4)); an apartment building is any structure with one or more dwelling units that is not a hotel or a single-family residence (HRS § 708-800). Knowingly entering or remaining unlawfully on any other premises is simple trespass, a violation (HRS § 708-815). A tenant's guest is invited by the tenant, so whether your order alone makes a guest's presence unlawful is a question of case law this library has not reviewed. The cautious course is to give a banned non-tenant a written, dated notice that names the person and the property, keep a copy, and call the police rather than removing anyone yourself.

title: Leases From a Life Tenant or Other Limited Owner
bodyText: Hawaii law has no civil-law usufruct; the closest interest is a life estate. Hawaii's Residential Landlord-Tenant Code has no rule on a lease made by a life tenant or another owner whose interest may end during the tenancy, and its table of contents has no section on the subject (HRS chapter 521). Other Hawaii statutes and case law on life estates were not reviewed. If you hold only a life estate or another interest that may end during the lease, the cautious course is to have the remainder owner sign the lease or consent to it in writing, and to tell the tenant in the lease what happens if your interest ends.
